3. **`orderBy` / pagination context sugar** — the fragment DSL supports `where`; `orderBy` works through
   the same `GraphQuerySpec`, but the `query.<prop>`-style order sugar isn't separately covered here.

title: Full-text search primitive — `loadMatching` — 0.0.68
body:
Full-text search primitive — `loadMatching` — 0.0.68
Maintainer handoff for a first-class full-text **search** operation on `GraphObjectManager`, the exact
mirror of `loadNearest` (vector). Drivine already owned the full-text **index** (`@FullTextIndex` +
`FullTextIndexSpec` + per-engine DDL, 0.0.60); this adds the search side so consumers stop hand-writing
per-engine full-text Cypher and score normalization.

```kotlin
// Vector (already there)
gom.loadNearest<ChunkNode>(queryVector, topK = 20, threshold = 0.7): List<Scored<ChunkNode>>

// Full-text (new) — same shape
gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>("graph databases", topK = 20): List<Scored<ChunkNode>>
```

`loadMatching` resolves the model's full-text index, runs the engine-appropriate query, and returns
**scored, typed, `[0, 1]`-normalized** results — cross-engine, no consumer Cypher, polymorphic dispatch
included.

title: Using it — exact syntax and the trip-ups (read this first)
body:
Using it — exact syntax and the trip-ups (read this first)
### Non-filtered — any `@NodeFragment` or `@GraphView`

```kotlin
import org.drivine.manager.loadMatching   // the reified extension

gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>("graph databases", topK = 20)                    // fragment, returns List<Scored<ChunkNode>>
gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>("graph databases", topK = 20, threshold = 0.5)   // drop hits below 0.5 normalized
gom.loadMatching<ContentElementNode>("graph", topK = 20)                     // sealed base → each hit typed to its subtype
gom.loadMatching<ChunkView>("graph", topK = 20)                             // view → projected view per hit
```

- `threshold` defaults to **`0.0`** (keep everything), not nullable like `loadNearest` — full-text
  scores are already normalized to `[0, 1]`, so `0.0` is the natural floor.
- `topK` is applied as a trailing **`LIMIT`** (the full-text `CALL` takes no `k`, unlike the vector
  index `CALL`). It is a hard cap on rows returned.

### Filtered — full-text **plus** a `where { }` predicate, one query

```kotlin
import org.drivine.query.dsl.query

// fragment (generated ChunkNodeQueryDsl):
gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>("graph databases", topK = 20) {
    where { query.containerSectionId eq "sec-1" }
}
// explicit subtype/3-arg form (same rule as the 0.0.67 fragment DSL — a subtype's own property needs this):
gom.loadMatching(ChunkNode::class.java, ChunkNodeQueryDsl.INSTANCE, "graph databases", topK = 20) {
    where { query.containerSectionId eq "sec-1" }
}
```

- ❌ The filtered `loadMatching<Sub> { }` on a **subtype of a sealed fragment** binds to the base DSL —
  filter a subtype-only property with the explicit 3-arg form, exactly as [[fragment-query-dsl-0.0.67]]
  documents for `loadAll`.
- The generated filtered `loadMatching` extension is emitted **only** for `@FullTextIndex`-bearing
  views/fragments (the gate `loadNearest` uses for `@VectorIndex`). Import it from the fragment/view's
  package alongside the other generated extensions.

### Java — fluent `.match(...)`

```java
import org.drivine.manager.Scored;
import static org.drivine.query.dsl.JavaQueryBuilderKt.query;

List<Scored<ChunkNode>> hits = query(gom, ChunkNode.class)
    .filterWith(ChunkNodeQueryDsl.class)
    .where(q -> q.getContainerSectionId().eq("sec-1"))   // KSP DSL from Java → bean getter
    .match("graph databases", 20);
```

- `match(query, topK)` / `match(query, topK, threshold)` is the Java fluent form; it returns
  `List<Scored<T>>`. It works for both views and fragments.

### Query syntax & escaping

The `query` string is passed through to the engine's full-text query language (**Lucene** on Neo4j:
`AND` / `OR` / `"phrase"` / `field:term`; RediSearch on FalkorDB; Tantivy on Memgraph). Raw user input
is **not** escaped — if it may contain query-syntax metacharacters, wrap it (the naive `"\"$q\""`
phrase-wrap) or escape before calling. Honour `@FullTextIndex(analyzer = …)` at **index** time (it is
baked into the index; the search procedures take no query-time analyzer).

title: 1. Annotation
body:
1. Annotation
`@FullTextIndex` already existed (0.0.60) and is unchanged — property-level (single-property) or
class-level (`@Repeatable`, multi-property via `properties`), with optional `name` / `analyzer`. There
is **no `group` attribute** (the original prompt suggested one); multi-property indexes are declared
class-level:

```kotlin
@NodeFragment(labels = ["Chunk"])
data class ChunkNode(@NodeId val id: String, @FullTextIndex val text: String, …)

@FullTextIndex(properties = ["name", "description"])   // one index spanning two fields
@NodeFragment(labels = ["Entity"])
data class EntityNode(@NodeId val id: String, val name: String, val description: String)
```

The same annotation drives schema `ensure` **and** search resolution — one source of truth, as
`@VectorIndex` is for vectors.

title: 2. Runtime
body:
2. Runtime
`GraphObjectManager` gains (mirroring the `loadNearest` overloads):

- `loadMatching(class, query, topK, threshold = 0.0)` and `loadMatching(class, property?, query, topK, threshold)`
  — `@GraphView` searches its root fragment's index and returns the projected view; `@NodeFragment`
  searches and returns itself; `property` disambiguates when a fragment has several indexes.
- `loadMatching(class, Q, query, topK, threshold, spec)` — filtered, for **both** views and fragments.
- reified extensions in `GraphObjectManagerExtensions.kt`: `loadMatching<T>(query, topK, threshold)`,
  `loadMatching<T>(property?, …)`, `loadMatching<T, Q>(query, topK, threshold, spec)`.

Index resolution is a new `FullTextIndexResolver` (mirror of `VectorIndexResolver`): reads
`@FullTextIndex` (property- **and** class-level) off the root fragment, derives the index name
`${label}_${onDiskProperties joined by _}_fulltext` — matching `FullTextIndexSpec.defaultName()`, so the
searched name equals the created name on the name-keyed engines. `FullTextQuerySpec` carries `label`
(FalkorDB keys by label) + `indexName` (Neo4j/Memgraph key by name) + the bound param names.

Query builders `FragmentFullTextSearchBuilder` / `GraphViewFullTextSearchBuilder` mirror their vector
twins, adding the trailing `LIMIT $topK`. The filtered fragment form renders its `where` against the
node alias `n` (the same `FragmentQueryBuilder` alias the 0.0.67 DSL uses); the filtered view form
renders in projected-collection mode like filtered `loadNearest`.

**Architecture — planners + one executor.** Query construction lives in `ScoredSearchPlanner.kt`
(`org.drivine.query`): `VectorSearchPlanner` and `FullTextSearchPlanner`, each with `plan(...)`
(unfiltered) and `planFiltered(...)`, returning a `ScoredSearchPlan(cypher, bindings)`. They are pure
(grammar + inputs, no session/persistence) and own their bound-param names + support checks. The
manager keeps only thin public overloads that build the `GraphQuerySpec`, call a planner, and hand the
plan to one shared private `executeScoredSearch(graphClass, plan)` — which registers subtypes,
transforms each `{ value, score } AS row` with the same `TransformPostProcessor` `loadAll` uses, and
snapshots for dirty tracking. Both search kinds (and both filter forms) funnel through that one
executor, so `loadNearest` and `loadMatching` stay a few lines each and the manager stopped growing.

title: 3. Score normalization (centralized — this bit the consumers)
body:
3. Score normalization (centralized — this bit the consumers)
Raw full-text scores are unbounded (Lucene) and not comparable across engines, and FalkorDB can yield
`0/0 = NaN`. Every grammar's `fullTextSearchHead` routes its `CALL` through one shared helper,
`CypherGrammar.normalizedFullTextHead`, which is **identical across engines**:

```cypher
<engine CALL … YIELD node, score>
WITH collect({node: node, score: score}) AS _ftResults, max(score) AS _ftMax
UNWIND _ftResults AS _ftRow
WITH _ftRow.node AS <root>, (CASE WHEN _ftMax > 0 THEN _ftRow.score / _ftMax ELSE 1.0 END) AS <score>
```

- Divides each hit by the batch max → `[0, 1]`, top hit always `1.0` (a deterministic test anchor).
- `CASE WHEN _ftMax > 0 … ELSE 1.0` is the FalkorDB `maxScore == 0` / NaN guard, applied on **all**
  engines for safety (the consumers only guarded FalkorDB and hit NaN elsewhere later).
- The head's output contract — bind node→rootAlias, normalized score→scoreAlias — is byte-for-byte the
  same shape as `vectorSearchHead`, which is why the builders are near-verbatim mirrors.

Per-engine `CALL`:

| Engine | Procedure | Addressed by |
|---|---|---|
| Neo4j | `db.index.fulltext.queryNodes(name, query)` | index **name** |
| FalkorDB | `db.idx.fulltext.queryNodes(label, query)` | node **label** (no index names) |
| Memgraph | `text_search.search_all(name, query)` | index **name** |

title: 4. Codegen
body:
4. Codegen
KSP (`drivine4j-codegen`): emits the filtered `loadMatching(query, topK, threshold, spec)` reified
wrapper — for a **view** whose root fragment has a `@FullTextIndex` (`rootFragmentHasFullTextIndex`),
and for a **fragment** that has one (`fragmentHasFullTextIndex`, subject to the same root-only
`emitExtensions` gate the 0.0.67 fragment DSL uses to avoid sealed-hierarchy overload ambiguity). Only
the filtered form is generated; the non-filtered reified `loadMatching<T>` is hand-written.

Java APT: **no change** — Java has no reified extensions and uses the runtime fluent
`query(T).filterWith(TQueryDsl).match(…)` path, which composes with the `<Fragment>QueryDsl` the APT
processor already generates (0.0.67).

title: 5. Backend support
body:
5. Backend support
Verified cross-engine (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) in `FullTextSearchCrossEngineTest`: fragment
ranking + `topK` + normalized `threshold`, the view projection path, a class-level multi-property
index, polymorphic per-node dispatch on a sealed base, and the filtered (full-text + property
predicate) form. Engines with no native full-text index (Neptune / base openCypher) leave
`supportsFullTextSearch = false` and `loadMatching` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

**Memgraph note:** text search is **GA** on `memgraph/memgraph:latest` — no experimental flag. (In this
version `--experimental-enabled` only accepts `planner-v2`; passing `text-search` makes the container
refuse to start.) `text_search.search_all(index, query)` yields `node, score`.

**Neo4j note:** full-text indexes populate asynchronously — after seeding, `CALL db.awaitIndexes()`
before searching (the cross-engine test does this for Neo4j only).

title: 6. Tests
body:
6. Tests
- `query/grammar/FullTextSearchGrammarTest` — each grammar's `fullTextSearchHead` (procedure,
  name-vs-label, the shared normalization tail + guard); Neptune/openCypher throw.
- `manager/FullTextSearchCrossEngineTest` — the runtime, all three engines (fixtures in
  `sample/fulltext/`, incl. a hand-written `ArticleNodeQueryDsl` for the filtered form since the test
  source set isn't KSP-processed).
- `drivine4j-sample/GeneratedLoadMatchingTest` — asserts the KSP-generated `loadMatching` extension is
  emitted for the full-text view + fragment (`SampleFullTextView` / `SampleArticleNode`) and **absent**
  for a non-full-text view (the gating decision). The full-text mirror of `GeneratedLoadNearestTest`.

title: 7. Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
body:
7. Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
The store can delete its entire hand-written full-text Cypher path and call `gom.loadMatching`:

- Delete `RagDialect.chunkFullTextSearchCypher()` / `entityFullTextSearchCypher()` per-engine templates,
  the FalkorDB `CASE WHEN maxScore > 0 … ELSE 1.0` / Neo4j-Memgraph `score/maxScore` normalization, and
  the `$fulltextIndex` / `$chunkLabel` / `$searchText` name-vs-label binding split — all now inside the
  primitive.
- `GraphObjectManagerStore.textSearch` → `gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>(request.query, request.topK, request.similarityThreshold)`;
  `textSearchWithFilter` → the filtered form (`loadMatching(ChunkNode::class.java, ChunkNodeQueryDsl.INSTANCE, query, topK, threshold) { where { … } }`),
  translating the metadata/entity `PropertyFilter` into `where { }` predicates.
- `cypherSearch.chunkFullTextSearch` / `chunkFullTextSearchWithFilter`, `ChunkSimilarityMapper`, and the
  legacy `resources/cypher/*_fulltext_search.cypher` files become dead — remove them. Combined with
  `loadNearest`, the store's retrieval surface is then **100% object-manager**, no hand-written Cypher.
- One behaviour to preserve: the store phrase-wraps the facet query (`"\"$q\""`) but not the others —
  `loadMatching` does **no** escaping, so keep whatever wrapping the caller relied on at the call site.
- The `@FullTextIndex` the store already declares for schema now drives search too — no new annotation.

title: 8. Follow-ups
body:
8. Follow-ups
1. **Query escaping helper** — a small `FullText.escape(userInput)` (or an `escaped: Boolean` flag) so
   callers get safe raw-input search without reinventing Lucene escaping.
2. **`orderBy` on scored results** — `loadMatching` orders by relevance; a secondary sort (e.g. recency
   tie-break) isn't exposed.

_Done in this change:_ the vector + full-text search dispatch was extracted from `GraphObjectManager`
into `VectorSearchPlanner` / `FullTextSearchPlanner` (`ScoredSearchPlanner.kt`), leaving the manager
with thin delegating overloads over one shared `executeScoredSearch` — see §2.

title: Dynamic property predicates + full operator parity in `where { }` — 0.0.69
body:
Dynamic property predicates + full operator parity in `where { }` — 0.0.69
Maintainer handoff for a runtime-key escape hatch in the type-safe query DSL — `property(path)` and
`predicate(path, operator, value)` — **plus** the operators/conditions needed to express embabel's
entire `PropertyFilter` model (`NOT IN`, regex, case-insensitive, `not { }`, `hasAnyLabel`). Together
they let a consumer translate an arbitrary runtime filter into `where { }` and run filtered search
through the object manager, retiring hand-written filter Cypher. Value binding stays parameterized.

> Scope note: this doc covers the original "Phase A" (dynamic key access) **and** "Phase B" (full
> operator parity) — both shipped under 0.0.69.

```kotlin
import org.drivine.query.dsl.property
import org.drivine.query.dsl.predicate
import org.drivine.query.dsl.query

// infix, ergonomic:
gom.loadMatching<ChunkNode>("graph databases", topK = 20) {
    where { query.property("metadata.source") eq "wiki" }     // → n.`metadata.source` = $param
}

// programmatic, for translating a runtime filter object:
gom.loadAll(ChunkNode::class.java, ChunkNodeQueryDsl.INSTANCE) {
    where { runtimeFilter.leaves.forEach { query.predicate(it.path, it.op, it.value) } }
}
```

This is the primitive that lets a consumer route **filtered** search (`loadMatching { where }` /
`loadNearest { where }`) through the object manager even when filter keys are arbitrary — no new
manager surface, since the filtered overloads already take a `where { }` block.

title: The two entry points
body:
The two entry points
Both are extensions on `NodeReference` (the interface every generated `…QueryDsl` implements), so
`query.property(...)` / `query.predicate(...)` work for a bare fragment (alias `n`) and, via
`query.<root>.property(...)`, for a view's root fragment.

- **`fun NodeReference.property(path: String): PropertyReference<Any?>`** — an untyped reference bound
  to the runtime property name. Composes with every **base** operator (`eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`,
  `lte`, `in`, `isNull`, `isNotNull`). Returns `PropertyReference<Any?>`, so it does **not** expose the
  string-only operators (`contains` / `startsWith` / `endsWith`) — use `predicate` for those.
- **`context(WhereBuilder<*>) fun NodeReference.predicate(path, operator: ComparisonOperator, value)`**
  — appends one `PropertyCondition` from a `(path, op, value)` triple. Covers the **full**
  `ComparisonOperator` set (incl. `CONTAINS` / `STARTS_WITH` / `ENDS_WITH`). `value` is ignored for
  `IS_NULL` / `IS_NOT_NULL` and should be a `List` for `IN`.

`ComparisonOperator` (public, `org.drivine.query.dsl`): `EQUALS`, `NOT_EQUALS`, `GREATER_THAN`,
`GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL`, `LESS_THAN`, `LESS_THAN_OR_EQUAL`, `IN`, `NOT_IN`, `CONTAINS`, `STARTS_WITH`,
`ENDS_WITH`, `MATCHES` (regex `=~`), `CONTAINS_IGNORE_CASE`, `EQUALS_IGNORE_CASE`, `IS_NULL`,
`IS_NOT_NULL`. The two `*_IGNORE_CASE` operators render `toLower(lhs) …` and lower-case the bound value.

Two conditions that aren't property comparisons get their own DSL entry points:

- **`not { … }`** — negates a sub-expression: `NOT (c1 AND c2 …)`. Compose with `anyOf { }` for
  `NOT ( … OR … )`. (`WhereCondition.NotCondition`.)
- **`query.hasAnyLabel("A", "B")`** — matches nodes carrying **any** of the labels:
  `ANY(l IN labels(alias) WHERE l IN $p)`. Contrast `instanceOf<T>()` (all of a type's labels).
  (`WhereCondition.AnyLabelCondition`.)

Ergonomic infix sugar mirrors the new operators for hand-written filters: `notIn`, `matches`,
`containsIgnoreCase`, `eqIgnoreCase` (the last three on `StringPropertyReference`).

title: Path resolution & safety
body:
Path resolution & safety
`path` is the **stored property name**. A `@PropertyBag(prefix = "metadata")` entry is stored as a flat
node property literally named `metadata.<key>`, so pass the full dotted name. Rendering (unchanged
`CypherGenerator.renderPropertyPath`, the same path `PropertyBagReference.key()` already uses):

- A path **with a dot** is backtick-quoted: `property("metadata.source")` → `` n.`metadata.source` ``
  (so it's a flat-property read, not Cypher nested-map access).
- A plain path is untouched: `property("owner")` → `n.owner`.
- **Values always bind** as `$param_*` — untrusted values can't inject. The generated param name is
  derived from the raw path (`param_n_metadata_source_0`), and `extractBindings` walks the same order so
  bindings stay aligned.
- **Backtick hardening (new):** a backtick inside a dotted path is doubled (`` a`b `` → `` a``b ``) so a
  runtime-supplied key can't break out of the quotes. Note this hardens the **key**; a caller passing a
  fully attacker-controlled *key* should still prefer keys that are property names or prefixed bag keys
  (before 0.1.0, a key with no dot was not quoted).

Since 0.1.0 any key that is not a plain identifier is quoted, with or without a dot, and a character
of the key that a parameter name cannot hold becomes an underscore in it
(`` metadata.a`b `` gives `param_n_metadata_a_b_0`). FalkorDB refuses a key that holds a backtick.

Prefer the generated typed accessors (`query.someField`, `query.metadata.key("k")`) when the key is
known at compile time; reach for `property` / `predicate` only for genuinely dynamic keys.

title: Why no new manager surface
body:
Why no new manager surface
The filtered `loadMatching(class, Q, …, spec)` / `loadNearest(class, Q, …, spec)` overloads (0.0.68 /
earlier) already accept a `where { }`. `property` / `predicate` just add new ways to populate that
block, feeding the existing `WhereCondition` → `CypherGenerator` parameterized-rendering pipeline. No
change to the search primitives, builders, or `CypherGenerator` rendering (only the backtick-escape
hardening).

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `query/dsl/DynamicPropertyPredicateTest` (unit) — `property` / `predicate` render the expected
  parameterized Cypher, dotted keys are backtick-quoted, `IN` binds a list, `IS_NULL` binds nothing, a
  backtick in a key is escaped, and `property("metadata.source")` renders identically to the typed
  `metadata.key("source")`. Plus the Phase B operators: `NOT_IN`, `MATCHES`, the `*_IGNORE_CASE` pair
  (LHS `toLower`-wrapped, value lower-cased), the infix sugar, `not { }` (incl. a **parameter-index
  alignment** case — a predicate before a `not { }` — and a negated `anyOf`), and `hasAnyLabel`.
- `manager/DynamicPropertyFilterCrossEngineTest` (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) — `loadAll` filtering a
  `@PropertyBag` fragment on dynamic `metadata.*` keys: eq, a numeric comparison, `CONTAINS`,
  composition with a typed accessor, equivalence with the typed `key()` form, and every Phase B
  operator (`NOT_IN`, `MATCHES` — gated off on FalkorDB, `*_IGNORE_CASE`, `not { }`, `hasAnyLabel`).
  Fixtures in `sample/dynamicfilter/`.

title: Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
body:
Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
This is the primitive that lets `textSearchWithFilter` / `vectorSearchWithFilter` move onto the object
manager. The consumer writes a small `PropertyFilter` → `where { }` translator (a `when` over the
sealed filter subtypes — embabel has no operator enum, the operator *is* the subtype) and drops
`CypherFilterConverter` + the regex `injectFilterIntoQuery` splicing:

```kotlin
// embabel side — path resolution owns the structural-vs-bagged split it already knows (STRUCTURAL_KEYS):
private fun ChunkNodeQueryDsl.pathFor(key: String) = if (key in ChunkNode.STRUCTURAL_KEYS) key else "metadata.$key"

context(WhereBuilder<*>)
private fun ChunkNodeQueryDsl.apply(f: PropertyFilter) { when (f) {
    is PropertyFilter.Eq                 -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.EQUALS, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Ne                 -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.NOT_EQUALS, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Gt                 -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.GREATER_THAN, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Gte                -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Lt                 -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.LESS_THAN, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Lte                -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.LESS_THAN_OR_EQUAL, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.In                 -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.IN, f.values)
    is PropertyFilter.Nin                -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.NOT_IN, f.values)
    is PropertyFilter.Contains           -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.CONTAINS, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.StartsWith         -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.STARTS_WITH, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.EndsWith           -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.ENDS_WITH, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.Like               -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.MATCHES, f.pattern)
    is PropertyFilter.ContainsIgnoreCase -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.CONTAINS_IGNORE_CASE, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.EqIgnoreCase       -> predicate(pathFor(f.key), ComparisonOperator.EQUALS_IGNORE_CASE, f.value)
    is PropertyFilter.And                -> f.filters.forEach { apply(it) }        // AND is implicit
    is PropertyFilter.Or                 -> anyOf { f.filters.forEach { apply(it) } }
    is PropertyFilter.Not                -> not { apply(f.filter) }
    is EntityFilter.HasAnyLabel          -> hasAnyLabel(*f.labels.toTypedArray())
} }
```

**This also fixes a latent bug.** `CypherFilterConverter` renders `chunk.<key>` unquoted, so a bagged
key like `metadata.source` becomes Cypher **nested-map access** (`chunk.metadata.source`), not the flat
`` chunk.`metadata.source` `` property — i.e. metadata filters on bagged keys are **currently broken**;
only promoted top-level fields work. Routing through drivine's `property`/`predicate` corrects it.

With the operators above, `CypherFilterConverter`, `injectFilterIntoQuery`, and the per-dialect filter
Cypher can all be deleted — filtered `textSearchWithFilter` / `vectorSearchWithFilter` run 100% through
`GraphObjectManager`.

### One engine caveat: FalkorDB has no regex

FalkorDB doesn't support the `=~` operator, so `MATCHES` (embabel's `Like`) throws there
("FalkorDB does not currently support =~"). Neo4j and Memgraph are fine. If a c

title: Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
1. **Java-friendly `predicate` / `hasAnyLabel`** — `PropertyConditionBuilder`-returning variants for the
   Java fluent `query(T).filterWith(...).where(...)` path (this bump is Kotlin-context-parameter only;
   the embabel consumer is Kotlin, so it wasn't needed yet).
2. **Model-aware key resolution** — optionally let drivine resolve a *logical* key to its stored path
   from the fragment's `@GraphProperty` / `@PropertyBag` annotations, so a consumer needn't know the bag
   prefix or the structural set. Not required (the consumer already owns `STRUCTURAL_KEYS`), but would
   remove the `pathFor` helper.
3. **A drivine-level guard for unsupported operators** — e.g. surface FalkorDB's regex gap as a typed
   `UnsupportedOperationException` at build time rather than a driver error at execution.

title: Model-aware key resolution — `field(key)` / `predicateOn(key, …)` — 0.0.70
body:
Model-aware key resolution — `field(key)` / `predicateOn(key, …)` — 0.0.70
Follow-up to the dynamic-predicate path (0.0.69). `property(path)` / `predicate(path, op, value)` take a
**stored** property name, which pushes the *logical-key → stored-path* mapping onto the caller. This adds
a resolving pair — `field(key)` / `predicateOn(key, op, value)` — that consults a mapping the generated
`<Fragment>QueryDsl` now carries, derived from the fragment's own `@GraphProperty` / `@PropertyBag`
annotations. The consumer stops re-encoding its model's structure.

```kotlin
// 0.0.69 — consumer owns the split:
where { query.predicate(if (key in STRUCTURAL_KEYS) key else "metadata.$key", op, value) }

// 0.0.70 — the QueryDsl already has the metadata:
where { query.field("containerSectionId") eq "s1" }   // @GraphProperty  → n.container_section_id
where { query.field("source") eq "wiki" }              // @PropertyBag    → n.`metadata.source`
where { query.predicateOn(key, op, value) }            // resolving, programmatic
```

title: The interface
body:
The interface
`ResolvableNodeReference : NodeReference` (`org.drivine.query.dsl`) carries the resolver:

```kotlin
interface ResolvableNodeReference : NodeReference {
    val fieldKeyPaths: Map<String, String>   // logical key (Kotlin name AND @GraphProperty on-disk name) → stored name
    val bagPrefixes: List<String>            // @PropertyBag stored prefixes (incl. delimiter), one per bag
}
```

Every generated `<Fragment>QueryDsl` now implements it (previously `NodeReference`). Because
`ResolvableNodeReference` extends `NodeReference`, this is source-compatible — all existing DSL usage
keeps working.

title: Resolution rules (`resolveKey`)
body:
Resolution rules (`resolveKey`)
Given a logical `key`:

1. **Declared field** — `fieldKeyPaths[key]` (populated with both the Kotlin/Java name *and* the
   `@GraphProperty` on-disk name, each → the on-disk name). `containerSectionId` and `container_section_id`
   both → `container_section_id`, rendering `n.container_section_id`.
2. **`@PropertyBag` key** — unmatched key + exactly one bag → `` `<prefix>key` `` (dotted, backtick-quoted
   by `CypherGenerator`). `source` → `` n.`metadata.source` ``.
3. **Unresolvable** — unmatched key with **zero** bags (no such field) or **more than one** bag
   (ambiguous) → throws `IllegalArgumentException` at build time with a clear message. Never guesses.

`field(key)` is the resolving counterpart of `property` (returns `PropertyReference<Any?>`, base
operators); `predicateOn(key, op, value)` is the resolving counterpart of `predicate` (full
`ComparisonOperator` set). The stored-path `property`/`predicate` remain for callers that already have an
on-disk path — this is additive.

title: Codegen
body:
Codegen
Both generators tap the exact point where the Kotlin/Java name and the computed on-disk name /
`@PropertyBag` prefix are already in scope (they're what the typed accessors are built from), and
accumulate the resolver as each reference is emitted:

- **KSP** (`drivine4j-codegen`): `generateFragmentDslClass` implements `ResolvableNodeReference`;
  `addPropertyReference` returns an `EmittedRef` (`Field(logicalName, onDiskName)` / `Bag(storedPrefix)`)
  that the loop folds into `fieldKeyPaths` + `bagPrefixes`, emitted as `override val` initializers.
- **APT** (`drivine4j-codegen-java`): `addPropertyGetters` gains optional out-collections it populates;
  `generateFragmentDsl` implements `ResolvableNodeReference` and emits `getFieldKeyPaths()` /
  `getBagPrefixes()` (a `LinkedHashMap`/`ArrayList` builder, or `Collections.empty*()`). The view
  `Properties` caller passes `null, null` (no resolver).

The `@PropertyBag` *field name* is deliberately **not** a `fieldKeyPaths` entry — free-form keys are
reached through the prefix, not by the bag field's own name.

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `query/dsl/KeyResolutionTest` (unit) — resolve by Kotlin name and on-disk name; unmatched → single bag
  prefix; **throws** for zero bags and for multiple bags; `field()`/`predicateOn()` render the resolved
  stored path (bag key backtick-quoted).
- `drivine4j-sample/GeneratedKeyResolverTest` (KSP) — a mixed `@GraphProperty` + `@PropertyBag` fragment
  (`SampleResolverNode`) generates `: ResolvableNodeReference` with `"sectionId" to "section_id"`,
  `"section_id" to "section_id"`, and `bagPrefixes = listOf("metadata.")`; the bag field is not a key.
- `drivine4j-codegen-java/PropertyBagCodegenTest#emitsModelAwareKeyResolverForMixedFragment` (APT) — the
  Java-generated DSL implements `ResolvableNodeReference` and emits the two getters with the same maps.
- `manager/DynamicPropertyFilterCrossEngineTest` (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) — `field("sectionId")` and
  `field("section_id")` both hit `section_id`; a free-form `field("source")` hits `metadata.source` and
  matches the explicit `property("metadata.source")` form; `predicateOn` resolves identically.

title: Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
body:
Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
Deletes `ChunkNode.STRUCTURAL_KEYS` + `storedPathFor` and the `pathFor` bridge in the `PropertyFilter →
where { }` translator: each `predicate(pathFor(f.key), …)` becomes `predicateOn(f.key, …)`. The translator
stops knowing the model's structure — drivine resolves it from the `@GraphProperty` / `@PropertyBag`
annotations that are the single source of truth.

title: Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
1. **Java-friendly `field` / `predicateOn`** — `PropertyConditionBuilder`-returning variants for the Java
   fluent path (this bump is Kotlin-context-parameter only).
2. **View-level resolution** — resolution is per-fragment; a `@GraphView`'s aggregate DSL resolves via
   its root reference (`query.<root>.field(key)`), which is itself resolvable.

title: Filtered fragment `loadNearest` — 0.0.71
body:
Filtered fragment `loadNearest` — 0.0.71
Maintainer handoff for follow-up #1 from 0.0.68. Filtered `loadNearest(class, Q, vector, topK, threshold)
{ where { } }` was `@GraphView`-only, while filtered `loadMatching` (0.0.68/0.0.69) and *unfiltered*
`loadNearest<Fragment>` already handle bare `@NodeFragment`s. A fragment hit the guard:

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException:
  loadNearest { where { } } currently supports @GraphView types; ChunkNode is not a @GraphView
```

This closes the asymmetry: **filtered `loadNearest` now accepts a `@NodeFragment`**, the exact vector
mirror of filtered `loadMatching`.

```kotlin
gom.loadNearest(ChunkNode::class.java, ChunkNodeQueryDsl.INSTANCE, vector, topK = 20, threshold = 0.7) {
    where { query.field("source") eq "wiki"; query.containerSectionId eq "sec-1" }
}   // → List<Scored<ChunkNode>>, polymorphic dispatch included
```

title: What changed (small — it's a mirror)
body:
What changed (small — it's a mirror)
The vector `CALL` + score-normalization head is unchanged; only the **root/index resolution +
where-rendering** needed to accept a fragment (`viewModel == null`), the way filtered `loadMatching`'s
planner already did.

- `VectorSearchPlanner.planFiltered` (`ScoredSearchPlanner.kt`) — dropped the `require(@GraphView)`
  guard and branched view-vs-fragment, identical in shape to `FullTextSearchPlanner.planFiltered`:
  - **view** → `buildWhereClause(…, viewModel, projectedCollectionMode = true)` + `GraphViewQueryBuilder.buildVectorQuery(…, whereClause)` (unchanged).
  - **fragment** → `buildWhereClause(conditions, null, grammar)` (renders against alias `n`) +
    `VectorIndexResolver.resolve(fragmentClass, …)` (the `{label}_{property}_vector` convention the
    unfiltered `loadNearest<Fragment>` already uses) + `FragmentVectorSearchBuilder.build(…, callerWhere)`.
- `FragmentVectorSearchBuilder.build` gained an optional `callerWhere: String?`, `AND`-ed with the
  threshold into the post-`CALL` `WHERE` (the same shape `FragmentFullTextSearchBuilder` already had).
  The unfiltered fragment path passes no `callerWhere`, so it is unchanged.

The `where` runs *after* the vector `CALL` binds the matched node to `n` — so `query.<field>` /
`property("metadata.key")` / `field("key")` all filter the vector-sourced node directly, no projection.
`topK` remains the index `k`; the post-filter can return fewer than `topK` rows (documented semantics).

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `manager/FilteredFragmentVectorSearchCrossEngineTest` (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) — filtered
  `loadNearest` over a `@VectorIndex` fragment (`VecDocNode`): a `where` on a promoted `@GraphProperty`
  field and on a `@PropertyBag` key (via both `property(...)` and the resolving `field(...)`), ranked
  closest-first, `topK`; **polymorphic dispatch** on a sealed `@VectorIndex` base (`VecContentNode` →
  `VecChunkNode` / `VecImageNode`); and a **regression** asserting the old "not a @GraphView" exception
  is gone for a fragment. Fixtures in `sample/vectorfilter/`.
  - Note: the sealed base declares a **property-target** `@VectorIndex val embedding` (not `@get:`), so
    `VectorIndexResolver` resolves it from the base type — confirmed working on all three engines.

title: Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
None specific — with this, both scored-search primitives (`loadNearest` / `loadMatching`) support the
full matrix: view/fragment × unfiltered/filtered, with the dynamic + model-aware key resolution from
0.0.69 / 0.0.70.

title: Dynamic list-membership — `ComparisonOperator.HAS_ELEMENT` — 0.0.72
body:
Dynamic list-membership — `ComparisonOperator.HAS_ELEMENT` — 0.0.72
Small follow-up to the dynamic-key path (0.0.69/0.0.70). Drivine has typed list-membership —
`infix fun <E> PropertyReference<List<E>>.hasItem(value: E)` → `value IN n.key` (0.0.56) — but the
dynamic-key path couldn't express it:

- `ComparisonOperator` had no reversed-membership entry (its `IN` is `n.key IN $list`, the opposite).
- `field(key)` / `property(key)` return `PropertyReference<Any?>`, which `hasItem` (needs `List<E>`) rejects.

`HAS_ELEMENT` closes that: reversed membership (`$value IN n.key`) reachable via `predicateOn` /
`predicate`, so a runtime/bagged list key works.

```kotlin
where { query.predicateOn("tags", ComparisonOperator.HAS_ELEMENT, "kotlin") }   // → $p IN n.tags
where { query.field("tags") hasElement "kotlin" }                                // infix twin, same render
where { query.property("metadata.tags") hasElement "graph" }                     // bagged → $p IN n.`metadata.tags`
```

title: What it is
body:
What it is
- **`ComparisonOperator.HAS_ELEMENT`** — renders `$param IN <lhs>` (bound value on the **left**, the
  list-valued property path on the right), the reverse of `IN` and the dynamic twin of the typed
  `hasItem` / `WhereCondition.ListMembershipCondition`. The value binds as `$param_*` (never spliced);
  the key resolves via the same model-aware path as any other `predicateOn` operator, so a dotted/bagged
  key is backtick-quoted (`$p IN n.`metadata.tags``).
- **`infix fun PropertyReference<Any?>.hasElement(value: Any?)`** — ergonomic hand-written form for an
  **untyped** reference (`property(path)` / `field(key)`), where the typed `hasItem` can't apply because
  the element type isn't known. Typed list fields keep using `hasItem`.

Rendering lives in `CypherGenerator.buildPropertyCondition` (and `buildPropertyConditionWithLhs`, which
also gained the previously-missing `NOT_IN` / `*_IGNORE_CASE` cases while I was there). No new
`WhereCondition` variant — it's a `PropertyCondition` with the new operator, so binding/`countParameters`/
`extractBindings` need no changes (it's a value-bearing, non-null op).

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `query/dsl/DynamicPropertyPredicateTest` (unit) — `HAS_ELEMENT` renders `$param IN n.<key>` (bound,
  not spliced), a dotted bag key is backtick-quoted on the right, and the `hasElement` infix renders
  identically to the operator form.
- `manager/DynamicPropertyFilterCrossEngineTest` (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) — a list-valued property
  filtered three ways returns the same rows: typed `hasItem`, dynamic `predicateOn(HAS_ELEMENT)`, and the
  `hasElement` infix.

title: Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
body:
Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
embabel 1.0 added `PropertyFilter.HasElement(key, value)` — the **only** untranslatable leaf left in the
`PropertyFilter → where { }` translator (all others already map to `predicateOn` / `anyOf` / `not` /
`hasAnyLabel`). It's now one line:

```kotlin
is PropertyFilter.HasElement -> predicateOn(filter.key, ComparisonOperator.HAS_ELEMENT, filter.value)
```

completing full `PropertyFilter` coverage — tag-filtered RAG included — with no remaining Cypher fallback
(the only residual engine caveat is FalkorDB's missing `=~` for `Like`, tracked upstream at
FalkorDB/FalkorDB#2237).

title: Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
None — with `HAS_ELEMENT`, the dynamic operator set covers embabel's entire `PropertyFilter` model.

title: Null-write policy — `NullPolicy` (IGNORE default) — 0.0.73
body:
Null-write policy — `NullPolicy` (IGNORE default) — 0.0.73
Maintainer handoff for making null-on-save a **single declared contract** instead of behaviour that was
emergent from implementation details. Previously "does a null field clear the stored property?" depended
on four hidden axes — single `save` vs `saveAll`, bagged vs bagless fragment, a vector-wrapping engine
(FalkorDB) vs not, and tracked vs detached — so a caller couldn't reason about it from the call site.
The acute case: a null `@VectorIndex` embedding on a partially-loaded object silently wiped a computed
vector.

title: The contract
body:
The contract
One policy, defined purely on **the object you pass**, applied identically across single/batch,
bagged/bagless, and every engine:

```kotlin
gom.save(chunk)                              // IGNORE (default): merge-patch — nulls left untouched
gom.save(chunk, nullPolicy = NullPolicy.CLEAR)   // full overwrite — nulls clear the property
gom.saveAll(chunks)                          // IGNORE (default)
gom.saveAll(chunks, nullPolicy = NullPolicy.CLEAR)
```

- **`IGNORE` (default):** only non-null fields are written; nothing is ever cleared. A partially-loaded
  object never destroys stored data.
- **`CLEAR`:** the object is authoritative — null fields clear the corresponding property.

**No field is special.** An embedding is treated like any other property: preserved under `IGNORE`,
cleared under `CLEAR`. The protection against wiping a computed vector comes from the **default being
`IGNORE`**, not a per-field exception — so `save(chunk)` is safe by construction, and there's no
carve-out to remember or reason around. (A null embedding under `CLEAR` clears with a plain `SET x =
null`; we only wrap *non-null* values in `vecf32(...)`, so there's no invalid `vecf32(null)`.)

title: The key design decision: null semantics are decoupled from dirty-tracking
body:
The key design decision: null semantics are decoupled from dirty-tracking
The footgun's root was that the snapshot/dirty system *decided* whether a null was written. Now:

- **The policy decides nulls**, independent of any snapshot: `IGNORE` always skips a null, `CLEAR`
  always clears one. So the observable result never depends on tracked-vs-detached, and there's no
  merge-patch snapshot-drift ("save a null, snapshot records null, DB still has the value, next CLEAR
  mis-diffs") — because CLEAR never consults the snapshot for nulls.
- **Dirty-tracking is now only an optimization:** it may skip re-writing an unchanged **non-null**
  field (a true no-op). It never gates a null. This means `saveAll` did **not** need to be made
  dirty-aware for the contract to be consistent — its UNWIND path drops nulls under `IGNORE` and keeps
  them (so `+= {x: null}` clears) under `CLEAR`, matching single `save` observably.

title: Behaviour changes (pre-1.0)
body:
Behaviour changes (pre-1.0)
- **Single `save` default flipped `CLEAR` → `IGNORE`.** Saving an object with a null field no longer
  clears that property by default; pass `NullPolicy.CLEAR` to clear. (Non-null fields are unchanged;
  dirty-tracked partial updates behaved this way already — confirmed by `PersonRepositoryTests`.)
- **`saveAll` is now consistent with `save`** (previously it silently ignored nulls in the UNWIND path
  but cleared them in the bagged/vector fallback).
- **Stale `@PropertyBag` key `REMOVE`** now only happens under `CLEAR` (removal is a clear); under
  `IGNORE` orphaned keys are left (merge-patch).
- **Vector null no longer clears under the default** — the original footgun, fixed by the `IGNORE`
  default rather than a hardcoded skip.

title: Code map
body:
Code map
- `manager/NullPolicy.kt` — the enum + the contract doc.
- `manager/GraphObjectManager.save` / `saveAll` — `@JvmOverloads`, `nullPolicy` param defaulting to
  `IGNORE`. (No `merge`/`mergeAll` aliases — with an `IGNORE` default, `save` *is* the merge-patch; the
  explicit destructive form is `save(obj, NullPolicy.CLEAR)`.)
- `query/FragmentMergeBuilder` — scalar loop: nulls handled by policy only (CLEAR emits `SET x = null`,
  IGNORE skips), non-nulls dirty-optimized; vectors wrap only when non-null; bag null values + stale-key
  `REMOVE` gated on `CLEAR`.
- `query/GraphObjectMergeBuilder` / `GraphViewMergeBuilder` — `nullPolicy` threaded (default `IGNORE`);
  it governs the root fragment of a view (relationship-target writes stay merge-patch — a follow-up if
  per-relationship tuning is ever wanted).
- `manager/BatchSaveOperations` — `nullPolicy` threaded; `unwindRootRow` drops nulls under `IGNORE`,
  keeps them under `CLEAR` (`+= {x: null}` clears; verified on Neo4j/Memgraph); the per-item fallback
  delegates to `FragmentMergeBuilder` with the policy.

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `query/NullPolicyMergeBuilderTest` (unit) — IGNORE skips null scalar+embedding; CLEAR clears both
  (embedding via plain `SET`, never `vecf32(null)`); non-null embedding wraps under either policy; bag
  null clears under CLEAR / skipped under IGNORE; default is IGNORE.
- `query/VectorMergeBuilderTest` — null embedding untouched by default, cleared (plain) under CLEAR.
- `manager/NullPolicyCrossEngineTest` (Neo4j / FalkorDB / Memgraph) — default `save`/`saveAll` never
  clear a null title or embedding; explicit `CLEAR` clears a null title (single: `SET`; batch:
  `+= {x:null}` on Neo4j/Memgraph, per-item on FalkorDB) and a null embedding.
- Regression: `PropertyBagMergeTest` stale-key tests opt into `CLEAR`; `SaveAllNeo4jTest`,
  `PersonRepositoryTests`, `GraphObjectManagerTests` all green under the new default.

title: Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
body:
Consumer impact (`embabel-agent-rag-graph`)
The store's save path becomes safe **by default**: `gom.save(chunkNode)` (or `saveAll`) is a merge-patch
— a chunk reconstructed or loaded without its embedding will never wipe the stored vector, and no
special API is needed. Only reach for `NullPolicy.CLEAR` when you deliberately want a full overwrite
(e.g. genuinely nulling a field). The store can also drop any defensive load-merge it added purely to
dodge the old footgun. (Recommendation still stands to keep whatever load-merge is needed for *other*
reasons; this only removes the null-clobber hazard.)

title: Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
- Per-relationship null policy inside a `@GraphView` save (root honours the policy today; nested targets
  are merge-patch).

title: Index-aware keyset pagination — `seek` + `IndexAdvicePolicy` — 0.0.75
body:
Index-aware keyset pagination — `seek` + `IndexAdvicePolicy` — 0.0.75
Maintainer handoff for two related changes: making the keyset predicate one a planner can actually
seek on, and telling callers when the index it needs isn't there. Also backfills the `0.0.74`
keyset-pagination feature, which shipped without a doc.

title: What shipped in 0.0.74
The contract: the index mirrors the cursor
body:
The contract: the index mirrors the cursor
A range index over **exactly** the ordered properties, in the same order:

```kotlin
@NodeFragment(labels = ["Session"])
@RangeIndex(properties = ["lastActivityAt", "sessionId"])
data class SessionNode(...)
```

One cursor key takes a single-property index. Same rule, one key.

title: Why partial coverage is worse than none
body:
Why partial coverage is worse than none
A Neo4j index excludes nodes that lack the property. So the planner will not answer from a composite
index unless the query provably excludes those same nodes — otherwise it could silently drop rows.
Given only `lastActivityAt <= $seek0`, a node missing `sessionId` might legitimately belong in the
result, so the planner refuses the index and falls back to a label scan.

`IS NOT NULL` on every cursor key is that proof. It is what makes the composite index usable at all.
Against an index that does *not* contain the property, the same conjunct is pure cost — a property
read per candidate row — which is why an index covering part of the cursor profiles worse than no
index at all.

Neo4j does this reasoning itself where it can; the pre-fix plan showed it synthesising
`sessionId IS NOT NULL` on the one union branch where it could establish it.

title: Measured
body:
Measured
Neo4j 25, 200k nodes, 20-row page from mid-relation:

| Index | Database accesses |
| --- | --- |
| Mirrors the cursor | **27** |
| Leading property only | 200,020 |
| None | 500,010 |

Good plan is `NodeIndexSeek` → `Limit` — no sort, stops when the page is full. For reference, the
0.0.74 predicate scored 600,010 against the mirroring index and 64 against a leading-property index;
no single predicate is good under both index shapes, which is why the contract picks one.

title: Engine differences, measured (0.0.76)
body:
Engine differences, measured (0.0.76)
0.0.75 emitted the `IS NOT NULL` conjuncts and gave index advice on every engine. Profiling the other
two showed that was a pessimisation, so 0.0.76 gates both on the grammar. Recorded here rather than
in a separate note, since it is the same contract.

Memgraph and FalkorDB **cannot satisfy an `ORDER BY` from an index**. Profiled in the simplest case —
one indexed property, no predicate, `LIMIT 20` — Memgraph ignores the index entirely (`ScanAll` over
200,001 rows, then `OrderBy`), and FalkorDB label-scans and sorts all 200,000. With a range predicate
FalkorDB will use `Node By Index Scan`, but still materialises all 100,009 candidates before sorting.
Both always have a blocking sort between scan and limit, and that operator is what makes early
termination impossible.

So there is no index setup that performs well across all three: Neo4j's fast plan exists precisely
because it has *no* sort. Consequences, both gated on `CypherGrammar`:

- `IS NOT NULL` is emitted only where `indexesExcludeNulls` — Neo4j. On Memgraph the conjuncts cost
  it the range bound: 200,001 index-scan hits with them against 100,010 without, for the same page.
  Shipping them everywhere in 0.0.75 was a ~2x pessimisation for Memgraph users.
- Index advice is given only where `supportsIndexBackedOrdering` — Neo4j. Elsewhere there is no index
  worth recommending, so advising one would be telling people to pay for something that cannot pay
  back. This also sidesteps FalkorDB index introspection, which reassembles every range-indexed
  property of a label into one item and would not have matched the advisor's exact-order rule.

Keyset pagination is therefore O(page) on Neo4j and O(remaining) on Memgraph and FalkorDB. `seek` is
still preferable to `skip` on those engines for stability — pages do not shift under concurrent
writes — but not for cost.

title: Index advice
body:
Index advice
Any root-level `orderBy`, with or without `seek`, is checked against the database's indexes:

```yaml
drivine:
  query:
    index-advice: FAIL      # WARN (default) | OFF
```

Ordering without an index is *correct*, just unindexed — reasonable on a small collection — so this
is advice, not validation. `WARN` logs once per label/property combination. `FAIL` is for development
and CI. Introspection failure degrades to silence rather than breaking a query that would otherwise
run.

**False positives are suppressed where they can be proven.** A query whose `where` pins a unique
property by equality at the top level selects at most one root, so its ordering is over a single row
and no index would change the plan — advising there is noise that erodes trust in the advice that is
accurate. Uniqueness comes from the fragment's `@NodeId` (unique by contract in Drivine, constraint
or not) and from single-property uniqueness constraints the database actually holds. Nested `anyOf`
equalities deliberately do not pin, because each constrains only one branch of the OR.

This is the reason `where` predicates are *not* index-advised in general: which index helps depends
on the predicate mix and on selectivity we cannot see, so a syntactic rule would produce false
positives at a rate that would push people to switch the whole thing off. The principled version is
to ask the planner via `EXPLAIN` rather than reimplement its rules — see follow-ups.

title: Behaviour changes (pre-1.0)
body:
Behaviour changes (pre-1.0)
- The emitted keyset predicate changed. Anyone who tuned indexes against `0.0.74`'s predicate — that
  is, created a single-property index on the leading sort key — should switch to an index mirroring
  the cursor, or they land on the 200,020 row above.
- `indexAdvice` defaults to `WARN`, so applications ordering without a matching index will start
  logging where they previously did not.
- README guidance from `5feebcb` ("index the leading sort property on its own") was measured against
  the old predicate and is superseded.

title: Code map
body:
Code map
- `query/grammar/CypherGrammar.kt` — `supportsIndexBackedOrdering` and `indexesExcludeNulls`, both
  false by default so a new engine is treated conservatively until measured.
- `query/dsl/KeysetPlanner.kt` — predicate construction; `IS NOT NULL` conjuncts and the leading
  range bound, with the rationale for both.
- `query/dsl/QueryIndexAdvisor.kt` — index introspection, per-manager cache, dedup, policy.
- `manager/GraphObjectManager.kt` — `indexAdvice` property; `adviseOnIndexes` at plan time.
- `manager/GraphObjectManagerFactory.kt` — carries the policy to every manager it creates.
- `autoconfigure/DrivineQueryProperties.kt` — the Spring property.

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `KeysetPlannerTest` — predicate shape for single-key, compound, and mixed-direction cursors.
- `QueryIndexAdvisorTest` — against a real Neo4j, so introspection is exercised rather than mocked.
  Covers the two cases that matter: an index over *part* of the ordering does not count, and neither
  does one with the right properties in the wrong order.
- `LimitSkipCrossEngineTest` — cursor walk and `where` + `seek` composition on all three engines.

title: Follow-ups
body:
Follow-ups
- An `EXPLAIN`-based advisor would cover `where` as well, and could not be wrong about the planner's
  rules because it *is* the planner's rules: a `NodeByLabelScan` on a query carrying predicates is
  ground truth, not a heuristic. Costs one round trip per distinct query shape, cacheable, dev-mode
  only. The work is per-engine plan parsing — Neo4j and Memgraph `EXPLAIN`, FalkorDB `GRAPH.EXPLAIN`.
- The starter module has no test source set, so `drivine.query.index-advice` binding is compile
  checked but untested.
- Null sort keys are documented, not enforced. Model nullability is the wrong hook — it describes the
  class, not the graph, and `NullPolicy.IGNORE` makes the gap routine. A property-existence
  constraint is the only place it could actually be guaranteed.
- The advisor caches the index list per manager; an application ensuring indexes lazily after the
  first ordered query will see a stale cache.

title: 0.0.79 — Pinning a vector index's physical configuration
body:
0.0.79 — Pinning a vector index's physical configuration
Vector DDL emitted only `dimensions` and `similarity_function`, leaving everything else to the server.
Neo4j 2026.04 fills in `vector.quantization.enabled: true`, `hnsw.m: 16`, `ef_construction: 100` — not
what earlier versions used. The same declaration therefore produced a **different physical index per
server**, silently, and the difference surfaced only as a recall or latency change nobody could
attribute to anything.

Pinning makes a declared schema reproducible across engine versions.

title: Two layers
body:
Two layers
**Portable** — `hnswM` and `hnswEfConstruction`. HNSW is genuinely the same algorithm in Neo4j and
FalkorDB, so these mean the same thing on both. This is not a lowest-common-denominator compromise; it
is the part that is actually common. They are the only tuning `@VectorIndex` expresses:

```kotlin
@NodeFragment(labels = ["Proposition"])
data class PropositionNode(
    @NodeId val id: String,
    @VectorIndex(similarity = SimilarityFunction.COSINE, hnswM = 32, hnswEfConstruction = 200)
    val embedding: List<Float>? = null,
)
```

Annotation attributes cannot be null, so `0` — the default — means "engine default".

**Engine-specific** — quantization is a Neo4j concept, `efRuntime` a FalkorDB one. Quantization trades
recall for memory: it shrinks the index substantially at the cost of approximate distances, which is a
reasonable default and a poor one to inherit unknowingly. Pretending otherwise
would either invent a lowest common denominator or leak one engine's vocabulary into every other. These
are declared only in a hand-written catalog spec:

```kotlin
SchemaCatalog.of(
    VectorIndexSpec("Proposition", "embedding", 1536,
        hnswM = 32,
        engineOptions = listOf(
            Neo4jVectorOptions(quantizationEnabled = false),
            FalkorDbVectorOptions(efRuntime = 10),
        )),
)
```

Each grammar reads only `optionsFor(its own engine)`. Options addressed elsewhere are ignored **without
warning** — declaring Neo4j options does not make a FalkorDB deployment incorrect, and warning about it
would train people to ignore the warning. One catalog therefore serves a mixed deployment with no
per-engine conditionals.

Where an engine option duplicates a portable one, the engine value wins **on that engine** and the
portable value still applies everywhere else — one declaration can say "m = 16 generally, 32 on Neo4j".

A portable pin an engine *cannot* express (Memgraph has no equivalent) is reported through
`SchemaGrammar.unsupportedVectorTuning` and logged, rather than dropped silently.

title: Declaring the same index twice
body:
Declaring the same index twice
An index that is both **queried** and **tuned** is necessarily declared twice: `@VectorIndex` must stay
on the fragment because `VectorIndexResolver` resolves vector queries from it, while engine options need
a catalog spec. The two meet in `SchemaCatalog.deduplicate`, which compares specs to each other with no
database involved — so drift cannot arbitrate, and plain equality would reject the pair as a conflict.

The rule:

- Declarations must agree on everything **portable** — dimensions, similarity, name, HNSW pins.
  Disagreement is a conflict and fails fast, as it always has.
- The declaration carrying **engine options wins whole**. No field-by-field merging.
- Two declarations that *both* pin engine options are a genuine conflict.

title: Drift, and what is deliberately not drift
body:
Drift, and what is deliberately not drift
**Unpinned is never drift.** With no declared value there is nothing for the database to differ from,
and the alternative would drift every index the moment a server changed its defaults — the exact failure
this feature exists to prevent, inverted.

A **pinned** value the engine contradicts *is* drift. `ensure` reports it and changes nothing; closing it
needs `recreate()`, which rebuilds the index — and rebuilding a vector index reindexes stored embeddings
without re-embedding them. Adding a pin to an existing index is therefore an operational decision, not a
config tweak.

**Drivine never substitutes its own defaults.** Hard-coding a "safe" `m` would freeze whatever this
version of Drivine believed the engine default was, which is the same class of bug one layer up.

title: The default is not cosmetic, and it moves
body:
The default is not cosmetic, and it moves
Quantization changes the score a search returns, not merely index size and build time. On a
four-dimensional vector whose exact normalized cosine is 0.8, a quantizing index reports **0.7998811**;
pin quantization off and the same nodes report exactly **0.8**.

And the unpinned behaviour is not stable. The same `neo4j:latest` tag, pulled two months apart, gave
those two different answers for an index Drivine created identically: approximate on the older image,
exact on the newer. A test that asserted the approximate result passed locally and failed in CI, which
pulls fresh — caught in this repo, on this feature, while writing this document.

That is the argument for pinning in one paragraph. Whether the shift is the default flipping or a
heuristic about small vectors does not matter; what matters is that an identical declaration produced
measurably different search behaviour on two builds of the same tag. The tests therefore assert what
pinning guarantees — quantization off yields exact scores, and the re-rank is exact regardless — and
deliberately assert nothing about the unpinned default.

title: Effective config is logged after every create
body:
Effective config is logged after every create
```
Vector index Proposition_embedding_vector on Proposition[embedding] effective config
  (engine defaults): dimensions=1536, similarity=COSINE, quantization.enabled=true,
  hnsw.m=16, hnsw.ef_construction=100
```

Pinned or not, this records what the server actually chose, so the value is attributable later instead
of becoming a suspect to be chased during an incident.

From Neo4j 2026.06 the server reports `vector.quantization.type` (`NONE`, `SCALAR` or `BINARY`) in place
of `vector.quantization.enabled`. Drivine reads it as `quantization.enabled=false` for `NONE` and `true`
otherwise, so a pinned value still reads back and drift is still detected. Drivine still writes
`vector.quantization.enabled`, which every Neo4j from 5.26 to 2026.10 accepts, where releases before
2026.06 refuse `vector.quantization.type`.

title: FalkorDB: verified by readback, not by a successful CREATE
body:
FalkorDB: verified by readback, not by a successful CREATE
FalkorDB spells the HNSW parameters `M` / `efConstruction` and adds `efRuntime`. Those names are
confirmed by reading the values back, because **FalkorDB silently accepts unknown `OPTIONS` keys** — an
index created with a made-up key is accepted and comes back carrying FalkorDB's defaults (`M=16`,
`efConstruction=200`, `efRuntime=10`) with no trace of the key and no error. "It applied cleanly" is
therefore not evidence of anything there.

It does report all three through `db.indexes()`, so pinned values are checkable and drift detection
works on FalkorDB as well as on Neo4j.

title: Upgrade note
body:
Upgrade note
`inventoryKey` embeds the effective name, so a spec that previously carried a blank name changes key
across this upgrade. Existing `_DrivineSchema` markers hold the old key and will produce a one-time
orphan warning on next boot. Non-destructive — orphans are reported, never dropped.

title: 0.0.79 — `partitionLabel`: targeting a vector index at runtime
body:
0.0.79 — `partitionLabel`: targeting a vector index at runtime
Previously the index a vector read searched was a **compile-time** function of the fragment:
`VectorIndexResolver` derived the label from `FragmentModel.labelsFor(fragmentClass)`, and the index
name derived from that. One vector index per partition — per corpus, tenant, or any other scope — needs
it to be a **runtime** function of the query, and nothing a caller could do reached below that.

title: Why partition at all
body:
Why partition at all
`where {}` predicates apply **after** the index yields, so a scoped caller receives roughly
`k × selectivity` rows. At 22% selectivity, asking for 40 returns about 9 — and those survivors are the
intersection of "globally nearest" with "in scope", which is not "nearest within scope".

[`searchK`](0.0.79-vector-search-k.md) mitigates that by searching wider. A per-partition index removes
it: the ANN search runs **inside** the partition, pre-filtered by construction, so `k` recovers its
intuitive meaning and every returned row already belongs to the scope.

The two fix different problems. Even with perfect HNSW recall, a `k` of 40 over a whole index filtered
to one scope still yields about `40 × selectivity` rows.

title: Usage
body:
Usage
Create the per-partition index — nothing new is needed, the imperative API already accepts an arbitrary
label at runtime:

```kotlin
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(VectorIndexSpec("Corpus_abc", "embedding", 1536))
```

Then name the partition on the read:

```kotlin
graphObjectManager.loadNearest(
    PropositionNode::class.java, null, queryVector,
    topK = 40, threshold = null, searchK = null, partitionLabel = "Corpus_abc",
)
```

Nodes carry both labels — `:Proposition:Corpus_abc` — so a node is stored once and indexed in both the
label-wide index and its partition's. Overlapping membership is free: a node in two partitions carries
both labels.

Composes with `searchK`: search wide *inside* a partition, then trim.

title: Three properties that matter
body:
Three properties that matter
**Targeting is not identity.** `partitionLabel` changes only which index is *located*. The yielded node
still carries the fragment's own label, so `where {}` and the projection are untouched, and
`:Proposition:Corpus_abc` projects as a `Proposition`. A test asserts the projection is byte-identical
with and without a partition, because the whole scheme rests on it.

**The label is the parameter, not the index name.** The name re-derives as
`${label}_${property}_vector`, which is exactly `VectorIndexSpec.defaultName()`. Letting callers pass a
name directly would break the create/read symmetry — the same symmetry the blank-index-name fix in
0.0.78 had to repair. Consequence: a fragment whose `@VectorIndex` pins an explicit name **cannot** be
partitioned, and throws saying so rather than quietly searching the wrong index.

**It is bound, not interpolated.** A literal would compile a distinct query string per partition, so the
plan cache would hold one plan per corpus instead of one in total, and a label derived from application
data would be concatenated straight into Cypher. Neo4j and Memgraph accept the bound form for the index
name; FalkorDB accepts it for the label it addresses indexes by. All three are verified end-to-end,
each asserting that **only the partition's members come back** — not merely that the query ran, which
is worthless evidence on FalkorDB given it silently accepts nonsense.

title: Where the policy lives
body:
Where the policy lives
Drivine targets the index it is told to target. It does not decide which corpora get their own index,
how large a partition must be to deserve one, or when to fall back to an exhaustive scan — those need a
selectivity estimate it does not have, and the same rule stops it substituting its own HNSW defaults.

A workable layout, for the consumer to own:

| Partition size | Physical layout | Read |
|---|---|---|
| small | shared bucket label | exhaustive `vector.similarity.cosine`, exact |
| medium | shared bucket label | ANN on the bucket, post-filter (dilution bounded by bucket size) |
| large | dedicated label | ANN on its own index, pre-filtered |

That gives a bounded number of HNSW graphs with an unbounded number of logical partitions, which is what
breaks under naive one-label-per-partition-forever. Note that only a **label** makes the routing
decision free: `MATCH (n:Corpus_abc) RETURN count(n)` is count-store metadata, O(1), while the same check
against a property is an index scan.

Creating a partition's index is a schema operation, and Neo4j rejects schema DDL inside an open data
transaction — so do it at ingest, not per request. Ingest is already doing chunking, embedding and bulk
insert, so it is a natural place for a schema event.

title: A coupling `partitionLabel` breaks
body:
A coupling `partitionLabel` breaks
A vector search never re-`MATCH`es the fragment's label — it projects whatever the index `CALL` yields.
That is safe by construction *without* a partition: the index name derives from the fragment's own
label, so membership of the index implies membership of the label.

`partitionLabel` breaks that coupling. If a partition index ever covers nodes of more than one fragment
type — the shared-bucket tier above is where that would happen — the index yields nodes that are no
node of the searched fragment.

Drivine therefore checks each node a partition's index yields for every one of the fragment's labels,
and drops the rest (#247). The check runs *after* the index yields, so it turns silent mis-projection
into visible under-delivery (which the short-read reporting then surfaces, and `searchK` offsets)
rather than making a heterogeneous bucket work: keep a bucket homogeneous. An unpartitioned search of
a one-label fragment needs no check, and its statement is unchanged.

title: Not yet supported
body:
Not yet supported
**Cross-partition search.** `partitionLabel` targets one partition. Searching several needs one call per
index, merged and re-ranked, which changes what `k` means (k per index, then a global top-k). Deferred
as its own design.

title: 0.0.79 — `searchK`: widening the vector search without widening the result
body:
0.0.79 — `searchK`: widening the vector search without widening the result
`k` handed to a vector index is the **HNSW search beam width**, not merely a row count. `searchK` lets a
caller widen the search and still get back the number of rows they asked for.

title: The evidence
body:
The evidence
On a ~9K-vector index (1536-dim, cosine), after bulk-ingesting ~2K tightly-clustered vectors: a vector
verified as true global rank 3 — by exhaustive `vector.similarity.cosine` — was **not returned at any
k ≤ 100**, and came back at rank 3 at **k = 200**. Reproduced across two full index rebuilds, with
quantization on and off, and across a database restart.

That result proves the mechanism rather than suggesting it. If `k` only limited rows, a vector at true
rank 3 would appear at k = 100 — it is comfortably inside 100. The only way k = 200 finds it and k = 100
does not is if `k` drives the candidate queue. In Lucene-backed HNSW the result queue *is* the candidate
queue, so `ef_search == k`, and Neo4j exposes no separate knob.

Two consequences:

- **Raising `k` is the only query-time lever on recall.** An "over-fetch multiplier" and "an
  effective-k knob" are therefore the same lever, not two options.
- **Under-recall here is a tunable tradeoff, not a defect.** Dense clusters saturate every neighbour
  list: with `M = 16`, near-duplicate vectors consume all sixteen links with intra-cluster neighbours,
  pruning the long-range links greedy descent needs to enter or leave the cluster. Low `ef` cannot then
  recover. Raising `hnswM` / `hnswEfConstruction` attacks that cause directly — see
  [0.0.79-vector-index-tuning.md](0.0.79-vector-index-tuning.md).

title: The compounding problem: post-filter dilution
body:
The compounding problem: post-filter dilution
`where {}` predicates apply **after** the index yields, so a scoped caller receives roughly
`k × selectivity` rows. At 22% selectivity, asking for 40 returns about **9** — and those survivors are
the intersection of "globally nearest" with "in scope", which is not "nearest within scope".

title: Usage
body:
Usage
```kotlin
// search with a beam of 200; return the best 40 that survive the filter
graphObjectManager.loadNearest<PropositionView>(dsl, queryVector, topK = 40, searchK = 200) {
    where { proposition.contextId eq ctx }
}
```

`searchK` is what the **index** is asked for. `topK` becomes a post-filter `LIMIT`.

This is the familiar fetch-200-trim-40 workaround, with the trim in the correct place: **after** the
`WHERE`. Trimming before the filter would discard exactly the rows over-fetching was meant to recover.

Emitted shape:

```cypher
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('Proposition_embedding_vector', $_vectorTopK, $_vectorQuery)
YIELD node, score
WITH node AS n, score AS _score
WHERE n.contextId = $p0
RETURN { value: {…}, score: _score } AS row
ORDER BY _score DESC
LIMIT $_vectorRowLimit
```

with `_vectorTopK = 200` and `_vectorRowLimit = 40`.

title: Over-fetching re-ranks (Neo4j)
body:
Over-fetching re-ranks (Neo4j)
Widening the beam only pays off if the trim that follows re-ranks by **exact** similarity. When
`searchK` is set, the Neo4j head yields `node` alone and recomputes the score with the index's own
similarity function:

```cypher
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('Doc_embedding_vector', $_vectorTopK, $_vectorQuery)
YIELD node
WITH node AS doc, vector.similarity.cosine(node.embedding, $_vectorQuery) AS _score
```

Because the index's yielded score can be **approximate**. When the index quantizes — which Neo4j has
done by default on some builds and not others — the score is computed against quantized vectors. The
effect is measurable even on a four-dimensional toy vector: a quantizing index reports 0.7998811 where
the exact normalized cosine is 0.8, and the same nodes under an index with quantization pinned off
report exactly 0.8 (`VectorSearchNeo4jTest`).

Whether *your* index quantizes depends on the engine build unless you pin it — see
[0.0.79-vector-index-tuning.md](0.0.79-vector-index-tuning.md), where the same `neo4j:latest` tag two
months apart produced both answers.

A beam ordered by that approximate score therefore does not reproduce exact-similarity order, and a
trailing `LIMIT` over it discards true matches the beam already found. Measured on a 9k-vector,
1536-dim cosine index with one dense cluster: the true top 40 were all present inside a beam of 200,
yet trimming by the yielded score returned only 38 — recall 0.95. Re-ranking the same beam returned all
40.

So the rescore is the load-bearing half of `searchK`: without it, over-fetching buys row *count* on the
filtered path but not row *correctness*.

Two consequences to know:

- **Scores differ slightly between a tuned and an untuned call** for the same node — approximate versus
  exact. Verified to be the same normalization, not merely the same ballpark, so `threshold` keeps its
  meaning in general.

  **The exception matters if your threshold is a round number.** A node whose true similarity is exactly
  0.8 is reported by a quantizing index as 0.7998811, so `threshold = 0.8` *excludes* it without
  `searchK` and *includes* it with. Any node whose true similarity lies within roughly 1e-4 of the threshold can flip.
  A threshold of exactly 0.8 is a common default, so this is worth knowing before attributing the
  difference to recall.

  The gating is the reason: the exact re-rank is tied to `rowLimitParam`, i.e. to `searchK`, but the
  *cause* of the approximation is quantization, not over-fetching. So exact scores currently cannot be
  had without also paying for a wider beam. Decoupling them — always re-ranking on Neo4j, or a separate
  opt-in — is a live design question; it would cost a property read per row on every vector query and
  would end the byte-identical-when-off guarantee.
- **Neo4j only.** FalkorDB and Memgraph over-fetch and trim by their own engine score. `searchK` still
  widens the beam and still recovers rows on the filtered path there; it does not re-rank.

title: Properties worth knowing
body:
Properties worth knowing
- **Off by default is a genuine no-op.** Omit `searchK` and the emitted Cypher is byte-identical to what
  an untuned search has always produced — no stray `LIMIT`, no extra binding. Pinned by a test, because
  "we added a knob and every existing query changed shape" is its own risk.
- **`searchK < topK` throws.** It would ask the index for fewer rows than the caller wants back, which
  can only lose results — a mistake rather than a tuning choice.
- **Available everywhere the search is.** Manager API, reified extensions, and the codegen'd per-view
  wrapper — a filtered view search is the case that needs it most, and a knob unreachable from the
  generated extension is not a knob.

title: Seeing a diluted result
body:
Seeing a diluted result
A short result is otherwise silent — the caller gets a short list and cannot tell dilution from a
genuinely small result. A vector search returning fewer rows than requested now logs, at DEBUG:

```
Vector search on PropositionView returned 9 of 40 requested rows; the index was asked for 200.
Filters apply after the index yields, so a scoped search thins the result — raise searchK to
widen the search, or search a partition's own index.
```

Turn up `org.drivine.manager.GraphObjectManager` when recall looks wrong.

**DEBUG rather than WARN, deliberately.** A view with required relationships routinely returns fewer
than `topK` — documented, intended behaviour — so warning would be noise that teaches people to ignore
the warning. Gating it behind a "shortfall greater than X" heuristic would mean picking X from a
selectivity estimate Drivine does not have.

One number is deliberately absent: how many rows the index yielded **before** the filter. Observing it
means restructuring the query to aggregate pre-filter, changing the plan shape and costing every caller
on every query — and it is redundant in the only case that matters. When the result is short of `topK`
the trailing `LIMIT` never bound, so the rows returned *are* the post-filter survivors.

title: What Drivine deliberately does not do
body:
What Drivine deliberately does not do
No automatic over-fetch multiplier, no adaptive top-up loop that retries with a larger `k`, no
exact-scan fallback threshold. Each would have Drivine choosing a cost/correctness tradeoff from a
selectivity estimate it does not have — the same rule that stops it substituting its own HNSW defaults.
The knob is explicit; the policy is the caller's.

title: If recall is poor, in order
body:
If recall is poor, in order
1. **Measure.** Exhaustive `vector.similarity.cosine` for ground truth, then compare against the ANN
   result at a range of `k`. Everything else is guesswork without this.
2. **Raise `searchK`.** Free to try, no rebuild.
3. **Raise `hnswM` / `hnswEfConstruction`** and rebuild — attacks the cluster-navigation cause rather
   than the symptom, at the cost of index size and build time.

Steps 2–3 address under-recall. They do **not** address dilution: even with perfect recall, a `k` of 40
over a whole index filtered to one scope still yields about `40 × selectivity` rows.
