title: Breaking: the Java query DSL has its own method names
body:
Breaking: the Java query DSL has its own method names
Every DSL operator used to exist twice on `PropertyReference`, under one name: a plain member for Java
(`asc(): OrderSpec`, `eq(v): PropertyConditionBuilder`) and a context-parameter member for Kotlin that
registers itself inside `where` / `orderBy` / `seek`. Kotlin 2.2 resolved the tie in favour of the
context one. Kotlin 2.3 does not, so a consumer on 2.3 could not write `orderBy { query.id.asc() }`.

The Kotlin DSL is unchanged. The Java methods are renamed:

| Kotlin | Java, before | Java, from 0.0.87 |
|---|---|---|
| `eq` / `neq` | `eq` / `neq` | `isEqualTo` / `isNotEqualTo` |
| `gt` / `gte` | `gt` / `gte` | `isGreaterThan` / `isAtLeast` |
| `lt` / `lte` | `lt` / `lte` | `isLessThan` / `isAtMost` |
| `isNull` / `isNotNull` | `isNull` / `isNotNull` | `isAbsent` / `isPresent` |
| `contains` / `startsWith` / `endsWith` | same | `hasSubstring` / `hasPrefix` / `hasSuffix` |
| `asc` / `desc` | `asc` / `desc` | `ascending` / `descending` |
| `after` | `after` | `cursorAfter` |

```java
JavaQueryBuilderKt
    .query(graphObjectManager, RaisedAndAssignedIssue.class)
    .filterWith(RaisedAndAssignedIssueQueryDsl.class)
    .where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getState().isEqualTo("open"))
    .orderBy(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().descending())
    .loadAll();
```

Kotlin code that built an order spec and registered it by hand, `this(query.issue.id.asc())`, now
writes `this(query.issue.id.ascending())`, or simply `query.issue.id.asc()`.

`OneNamePerLanguageTest` keeps the two sets apart. Drivine itself builds on Kotlin 2.2, where the
compiler still breaks the tie, so the rule is checked by the test rather than the compiler.

title: Fixed: ordering a `@PropertyBag` or polymorphic fragment
body:
Fixed: ordering a `@PropertyBag` or polymorphic fragment
These fragments return through `WITH properties(n) AS props, labels(n) AS lbls`, which dropped `n`, so
the `ORDER BY n.<field>` after the `RETURN` referred to nothing: every ordered or keyset-paged load of
one failed with `Variable n not defined`, on every engine. The `WITH` now carries `n` through (#20).

title: Node labels as a field, a flat property bag, and runtime-typed relationships — 0.0.91
body:
Node labels as a field, a flat property bag, and runtime-typed relationships — 0.0.91
Three additions for nodes whose labels, properties or relationship types are not known when the
model is written. Nothing existing changes behaviour.

title: `@NodeLabels`
body:
`@NodeLabels`
A set-valued field on a `@NodeFragment` whose contents are the node's labels, beyond the fragment's
own. Loaded from the node's labels; saved as real labels.

Saving follows `NullPolicy`: `IGNORE` adds the field's labels and removes none; `CLEAR` also removes
the labels that are the field's and are no longer in it.

- `Set<SomeEnum>`: the field's labels are the enum's members. It reads only those. An enum that names
  one of the fragment's own labels is rejected when the model is built.
- `Set<String>`: the field's labels are the ones it has written, recorded on the node in the list
  property `__drivine.labels.<fieldName>`. A default save adds to the record; a `CLEAR` save removes
  what the record holds and the field does not, then sets the record to the field. The record is read
  from the database, so the outcome does not depend on a session snapshot. It reads every label on
  the node.

Under `CLEAR` the labels are written even when the field is unchanged since the last snapshot: the
snapshot records what the object said, not what the node carries.

Limits:

- one `@NodeLabels` field per fragment;
- `saveAll` saves a fragment with one per object, not in an `UNWIND`, because labels are part of the
  statement text;
- on a relationship target in a `@GraphView`, a `Set<String>` field adds under both policies and
  removes under neither.

title: `@PropertyBag(flat = true)`
body:
`@PropertyBag(flat = true)`
A bag with no prefix. Each entry is stored under its bare key; on load the bag holds every node
property that no declared field and no other bag accounts for. One per fragment. An entry whose key
is a declared field's property, or falls under another bag's prefix, is rejected at save. In the
query DSL, `field(key)` / `predicateOn(key, …)` resolve an undeclared key to itself.

title: `GraphObjectManager.edges`
body:
`GraphObjectManager.edges`
`relate(from, to, type, properties, mode)` joins two stored nodes with a relationship whose type is a
runtime value. `loadRelated(from, type, direction, targetClass)` loads the nodes so joined.

The nodes are named by `NodeRef` (fragment class, id, and any further labels the node must carry)
and are matched, never created. `relate` returns whether both were found. `RelateMode.MERGE` keeps at
most one such relationship and sets its properties; `RelateMode.CREATE` makes another each time.
`loadRelated` returns each related node once on every engine.

title: Reserved property names
body:
Reserved property names
Property names beginning `__drivine.` belong to Drivine. A flat bag never claims one, and a fragment
that declares a field or a bag prefix beginning with it is rejected when the model is built.

title: Code generation
body:
Code generation
Both generators skip a `@NodeLabels` field (it is not a property) and give a flat bag an empty stored
prefix.

title: A stateless object manager, a checked stamp, and read-only view fields — 0.1.0
body:
A stateless object manager, a checked stamp, and read-only view fields — 0.1.0
`GraphObjectManager` keeps a snapshot of every object it loads or saves, and a save writes only what
differs from it. The snapshot is what that manager last saw, not what the store holds. When anything
else changes or deletes the node (plain Cypher, another manager, another process), the next save is
partial.

0.1.0 adds a manager that keeps no snapshot, and a way to refuse a save when the node has changed.

This page is the release's record: what changed, how to upgrade, and the tools that repair data saved
before it. How to use the new manager is in the docs, under
[Saving Data](06-object-manager.md#saving-data) and
[@NodeStamp](06-object-manager.md#nodestamp-refusing-a-save-when-the-node-changed).

title: What changed
body:
What changed
### Breaking

- **Recompile.** Code compiled against 0.0.x must be compiled again. The loading and query methods
  of `GraphObjectManager` are now declared on `GraphObjectOperations`, and a caller compiled against
  the old class does not link. The same holds for Java callers of `JavaQueryBuilder` and the query
  starter, whose constructors now take a `GraphObjectOperations`.
- **Every node a manager saves carries `__drivine.stamp`**, and so does the node at each end of a
  relationship a manager or `edges` writes or removes, whether or not its type declares a
  `@NodeStamp` field. A node that has no stamp is given one by the first save that writes it, even
  when nothing else about it differs. It cannot be turned off. Drivine's own mapping ignores the
  property. Cypher that returns all of a node's properties, such as `properties(n)`, now returns it
  too: a test that compares a whole property map, Cypher that copies one node's properties to
  another, an export, or a class of your own that refuses unknown properties will see it. Property
  names beginning `__drivine.` are Drivine's own (`NodeLabelsModel.RESERVED_PREFIX`), should your
  code need to tell them from its own.
- **Relationships saved through an `INCOMING` field point the wrong way in the store.** A view save
  now writes a relationship in the direction its field declares. Before, it wrote every one as
  outgoing, and the view did not load an `INCOMING` field back. What is stored needs turning round:
  see [Repairing data saved before 0.1.0](#repairing-data-saved-before-010).
- **A `@GraphPath`, `@Count` or `@Aggregate` field, and a list of fragments read over several hops
  (`maxDepth` above 1), is read-only**, with either manager. A view the manager had not loaded used
  to write a path field as a direct relationship of the first hop's type, and a several-hop list as
  a direct relationship from the root to each item. Neither is written now, and what was written
  stays in the store until removed: see
  [`PathRelationshipReport`](#pathrelationshipreport).
- **A cascading delete no longer follows a read-only field.** Before,
  `delete(id, View::class.java, CascadeType.DELETE_ALL)` deleted the nodes of a `@ReadOnly` field,
  and for a `@GraphPath` field the nodes a direct relationship of the first hop's type led to.
- **A view cannot be ordered, paged by keyset, or filtered in a scored search on a root property it
  does not project.** A property that is not a declared field of the root fragment used to be read
  from the projected root as null, so the order was arbitrary and a keyset cursor skipped or
  repeated rows. It is now refused with `IllegalArgumentException`. Declare the field.
- **A recursive collection cannot be sorted in the query.** It emitted Cypher that did not run; it
  is now refused with `UnsupportedOperationException`. Use `@SortedBy`.
- **`OrderSpec` and `SeekValueSpec` paths are not rendered verbatim.** What follows the first dot
  is a property name, and is quoted unless it is a plain identifier.
- **Generated query DSL extensions have the receiver `GraphObjectOperations`**, which both managers
  implement. Calls on a `GraphObjectManager` compile as before; generate the DSL again with the
  0.1.0 generator.
- **On Memgraph, `edges.unrelate`, and `edges.relate` when it makes or changes a relationship, now
  write to both nodes**, to mark them, so two calls on the same node at the same moment can conflict
  where before they did not. `edges

title: Upgrading from 0.0.x
body:
Upgrading from 0.0.x
1. Move the core library and the code generator to 0.1.0 together, and compile again.
2. Suppress the deprecation where the old manager is still used, if warnings fail your build.
3. Deploy 0.1.0 to everything that writes to the store. A writer still on 0.0.x writes
   `INCOMING` relationships the wrong way, and path fields as relationships, again.
4. Back the store up.
5. Repair what the old saves left, as [below](#repairing-data-saved-before-010). This matters only
   for a model that has an `INCOMING` relationship field, a `@GraphPath` field or a list read over
   several hops, in a view that was ever saved.
6. Replace `factory.get()` with `factory.stateless()` and change the saves, as the
   [table](#moving-from-graphobjectmanager) says.
7. Add a `@NodeStamp` field to each type that is loaded, changed and saved. Nodes that have no
   stamp yet are covered in the docs, under
   [Existing data](06-object-manager.md#existing-data).

Between steps 3 and 5 an `INCOMING` field does not load the relationships that were stored the
wrong way, and a save through it writes a new one the right way beside the old. The repair makes
one relationship of such a pair, and counts them beforehand as `collisions`.

title: `StatelessGraphObjectManager`
body:
`StatelessGraphObjectManager`
It remembers nothing. What a save does depends on the object and the arguments, never on what was
loaded earlier. Get one from `GraphObjectManagerFactory.stateless()`.

```kotlin
stateless.save(view)                                              // add only, every non-null field
stateless.save(view, Replace(PropositionView::mentions))          // this field's list is the whole list
stateless.save(view, Replace.all())                               // every relationship field's list is the whole list
stateless.save(chunk, except = setOf(Chunk::embedding))           // write everything but these
stateless.save(person, only = setOf(Person::name))                // write just these
stateless.update<Person>(id) { it.copy(name = "Ada") }            // load, change, save what differs
stateless.edges.unrelate(from, to, "MENTIONS")
```

Loading, querying and deleting are the same on both managers: both implement
`GraphObjectOperations`. Saving is not on that interface: `save`, `saveAll` and `update` are on
`StatelessGraphObjectManager` itself, so code that saves depends on the class.

The docs describe it in full. In outline:

- **A save is one Cypher statement**: the root, the relationships it drops, each related node and
  the relationship to it. It is applied whole or not at all, with or without a transaction, on
  Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph. A save that is refused as stale has written nothing.
- **The statement's text does not grow with a list**: the related nodes of a field are the rows of
  one `UNWIND`. A related view, a fragment with a `@PropertyBag` or a `@NodeLabels` field, and on
  FalkorDB a fragment with a `@VectorIndex` field, still has a part of the statement to itself.
- **`save` adds relationships and removes none.** `Replace(View::field)` makes a field's list the
  whole list, and `Replace.all()` covers every relationship field of the view itself.
  `RemovedTargets.DELETE_UNREFERENCED` also deletes a removed target that nothing else refers to.
  See [Relationships](06-object-manager.md#relationships).
- **`only` and `except`** choose the root fields written.
- **`update`** is a load and a save, two statements, and writes what the change altered. It makes
  no node: if the node is gone, it returns null. See
  [Load, Change and Save](06-object-manager.md#load-change-and-save-update).
- **`saveAll`** is several statements in one transaction, or in the transaction it is called in.
  On FalkorDB, which has none, each statement is atomic and the batch is not. See
  [Batch Save](06-object-manager.md#batch-save-saveall).
- **Under `NullPolicy.CLEAR`**, a root with a `@PropertyBag` or an open `@NodeLabels` field is read
  first, for the keys and labels it holds: one more statement, which writes nothing. `update` knows
  the keys from its load. The policy governs the root; a related node is written as under `IGNORE`.
- **From Java**, fields are named as strings: see
  [Saving from Java](06-object-manager.md#saving-from-java).

title: `@NodeStamp`
body:
`@NodeStamp`
```kotlin
@NodeFragment(labels = ["Person"])
data class Person(
    @NodeId val id: String,
    val name: String,
    @NodeStamp val stamp: String? = null,
)
```

The field is optional and strongly recommended: without it a save is never checked. It plays the
role of JPA's `@Version`: optimistic locking, with a random value in place of a counter.

The stamp is two random tokens in one property, `__drivine.stamp`. The **data token** is replaced
when a save changes the node's properties or labels, and every save of an object that carries a
stamp compares it. The **relationship token** is replaced, at both ends, when a relationship is
added or removed or its properties change, and only a save with `Replace` compares it, because only
that save overwrites a relationship list. A save that finds what it would overwrite changed is
refused with `StaleObjectException`, and writes nothing.

The docs have the whole of it: [the stamp](06-object-manager.md#the-stamp),
[when a save is refused](06-object-manager.md#when-a-save-is-refused),
[the stamp a save hands back](06-object-manager.md#the-stamp-a-save-hands-back),
[existing data](06-object-manager.md#existing-data),
[Cypher you write yourself](06-object-manager.md#cypher-you-write-yourself) and
[what a stamp does not cover](06-object-manager.md#what-a-stamp-does-not-cover).

### Cost

- The stamp is 33 characters a node.
- Replacing a stamp only when the node changes, against writing one on every save, was measured on
  Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph before the stamp had two tokens: no measurable difference on a single
  save, embeddings included, and at most about 4 microseconds a node in a batch. It has not been
  measured since.
- A save of a view with a list of related nodes, on Neo4j with an index on their id, in one run:
  19 ms for 100 nodes, 64 ms for 1,000 and 136 ms for 5,000.
- Marking both ends of a relationship costs nothing measurable on Neo4j. On Memgraph, of 2,000
  statements from 8 writers at once that each joined a new node to the same node and marked both,
  about 700 were turned away and had to be run again; without the marks, none.
- Every write takes the node's lock before it reads the node, by setting and removing a property.
  On each engine: no difference on a single save, and 3 to 5 ms more for a batch of 5,000 nodes that
  took about 40 ms.

These are single runs on one machine, and the repository holds no benchmark that reproduces them.

title: `@ReadOnly`
body:
`@ReadOnly`
A view field that is loaded and never written.

```kotlin
@ReadOnly @GraphRelationship(type = "REVIEWED_BY")
val reviewers: List<Person>

@ReadOnly @GraphPath([Hop("MENTIONS", OUTGOING, label = "Person"), Hop("WORKS_AT", OUTGOING)])
val employers: List<Organization>
```

- Every save skips it, on both managers: no relationship is written and the nodes it holds are not
  saved.
- Naming it in `Replace` is an error, and `Replace.all()` leaves it alone.
- It is a choice on a `@GraphRelationship` field. A `@GraphPath`, `@Count` or `@Aggregate` field,
  and a list of fragments read over several hops (`maxDepth` above 1), is read-only whether or not
  it is declared so.
- To write along a path: `edges.relate`, Cypher, or a view rooted where the hop starts.

title: Repairing data saved before 0.1.0
body:
Repairing data saved before 0.1.0
Three things a view save before 0.1.0 wrote are wrong in the store:

| What the old save did | What is in the store | The tool |
|---|---|---|
| wrote a relationship of an `INCOMING` field from the root to the target | a relationship pointing the wrong way, which the field does not load | `RelationshipDirectionRepair` |
| wrote a `@GraphPath` field, of a view the manager had not loaded, as a direct relationship | a relationship of the first hop's type from the root to each node the path ended at | `PathRelationshipReport.report` |
| wrote a list read over several hops as direct relationships | a relationship from the root to each node of the list, however far away | `PathRelationshipReport.reportSeveralHopLists` |

The tools go by label and relationship type. They cannot tell a relationship a save wrote from one
made some other way between the same kinds of node, so read each report before acting on it.

Both tools are written in Cypher, for the graph engines. They do not run on Oracle, and have nothing
to repair there: the Oracle backend came after 0.1.0.

### The procedure

1. Upgrade every writer to 0.1.0, then back the store up.
2. Run `PathRelationshipReport.report` and `reportSeveralHopLists` over every view of the model.
   Review the findings. Run a finding's `removalStatement` where it gives one and every
   relationship counted is one to remove; deal with the rest by hand.
3. Run `RelationshipDirectionRepair.report` over every view of the model, and check that
   `unexamined` is empty.
4. Review each finding's `ambiguity`, `collisions` and `eitherWay`.
5. Run `repair` for each finding you have decided to repair. This is a step of its own, after the
   review, not something to chain to the report.
6. Report again, and expect `wrongWay` to be 0.

The path report comes first because a relationship the old save wrote for a path field also points
away from the root: turned round, it would be loaded by an `INCOMING` field of the same type.

### `RelationshipDirectionRepair`

```kotlin
val repair = RelationshipDirectionRepair(persistenceManager)

// Changes nothing. Give every view of the model.
val findings = repair.report(PersonView::class.java, IssueView::class.java)
findings.forEach {
    println("${it.view.simpleName}.${it.field}: ${it.wrongWay} wrong way, ${it.rightWay} right way, " +
        "${it.eitherWay} either way, ${it.collisions} collisions. ${it.ambiguity ?: ""}")
}
repair.unexamined(PersonView::class.java, IssueView::class.java).forEach(::println)
```

```kotlin
// Later, for a finding you have read and decided on:
val turned = repair.repair(finding)
```

**The report**

- `report` gives one finding for each `INCOMING` relationship field, in the views you pass, the
  views nested in them, and the subtype views a sealed class or `@JsonSubTypes` names. A field you
  have since declared `@ReadOnly` has one too, because the old save wrote it as it wrote every
  other. A list read over several hops has none.
- `wrongWay` counts the relationships pointing from a root to a target, which is what the old save
  wrote. `rightWay` counts those the field reads.
- `eitherWay` counts a relationship between two nodes that each carry the labels of both the root
  and the target. Either node can be the root, so it may already point the right way; it is counted
  in neither `wrongWay` nor `rightWay`. Where a view rooted at `Organization` reads `PART_OF` from a
  `Company`, a relationship between two no

title: Moving from `GraphObjectManager`
body:
Moving from `GraphObjectManager`
The reasons are in the docs, under
[Migrating from GraphObjectManager](15-migrating-from-graphobjectmanager.md#migrating-from-graphobjectmanager).

| With `GraphObjectManager` | With `StatelessGraphObjectManager` |
|---|---|
| `factory.get()` | `factory.stateless()` |
| `save(obj)` of a new object | `save(obj)` |
| load, change a field, `save` | `update(id) { it.copy(...) }`, or `save` of the loaded object |
| load, drop an item from a list, `save` | `update(id) { ... }`, or `save(obj, Replace(View::field))` |
| `save(obj, CascadeType.DELETE_ORPHAN)` | `save(obj, Replace(View::field, removedTargets = RemovedTargets.DELETE_UNREFERENCED))` |
| `save(obj, CascadeType.PRESERVE)` | `save(obj)` |
| `save(obj, CascadeType.DELETE_ALL)` | no equivalent: `Replace` the field, then `delete` each node dropped |
| `clearSession()` | not needed |

- `DELETE_UNREFERENCED` deletes a removed target that nothing else refers to the way the field did.
  `DELETE_ORPHAN` deletes one with no relationship in either direction. A removed target that
  nothing points at, and that points at something itself, is deleted by the first through an
  outgoing field and kept by the second.
- A stateless `save` leaves a relationship's property alone where the relationship fragment's is
  null, as it leaves a null field of a related node; `update` clears one the change set to null.
  `GraphObjectManager` clears it.
- `GraphObjectManager` marks the stamp of each node it changes, and of both ends of each
  relationship it makes, removes or changes the properties of. A relationship it finds as it would
  write it is left unmarked. It neither checks a stamp nor hands one back.
- Every test of `GraphObjectManager` in this repository has a mirror that runs on the stateless
  manager, but for four that save with `CascadeType.DELETE_ALL`, which has no equivalent, and a
  comparison test runs the same scenarios through both and compares the graphs.

title: Engines
body:
Engines
Everything here is verified on Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph. `CascadeType.DELETE_ORPHAN` on
`GraphObjectManager` remains unavailable on Memgraph; `DELETE_UNREFERENCED` is available there.
Nothing here has been run against Neptune.

- **Contention.** On Neo4j and Memgraph a stateless `save`, `update` or `saveAll` that the engine
  turns away, because another writer was changing the same node at that moment, is run again: six
  attempts in all. A checked save is then refused as stale. `edges` runs its statement again too;
  `GraphObjectManager` does not, and the engine's error reaches the caller. Only such a conflict is
  run again: a lost connection is not, since the save may have been applied.
- **A save turned away every time.** A checked save the engine turns away on every attempt throws
  `StaleObjectException`, with the engine's error as its cause and no found stamp. The contended
  node can be one the save reaches through a relationship, so the exception says the save was turned
  away and that the node may have changed, not that it did. Memgraph does this inside a transaction
  that read the node before another writer changed it; that transaction has failed, and is to be
  run again from its start.
- **The lock.** Every write sets and removes a property `__drivine.lock` on the node, within its
  statement, to hold the node's write lock before it reads the node: a checked save to compare the
  stamp, an unchecked one to say truly whether it changes a node another writer is changing at the
  same moment. `edges.relate` takes the lock of both nodes. Without it, on Neo4j, two writers saving
  a node at once were handed the same token for two different texts.
- **FalkorDB** runs one write at a time and turns none away. It has no transactions: a save is one
  statement and atomic, an `update` is two statements, and a `saveAll` is several, of which those
  that ran before a failure or a refusal stay applied. With `falkorDbTransactionMode` set to
  `STRICT` a batch is refused, as any transaction is.
- **Oracle**, added after this release, holds the stateless manager to the same contracts: `save`,
  `update`, `saveAll`, `Replace`, `edges`, the stamp and `StaleObjectException` behave as above. What
  differs is how. A save is one PL/SQL block and not a Cypher statement. The stamp is a column of
  the node's row, loaded as `__drivine.stamp`. A node is locked by its row (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`),
  so no `__drivine.lock` property is written. A deadlock (`ORA-00060`) or a serialization failure
  (`ORA-08177`) is what is run again. `Stamps.setClause` and `Stamps.linksClause` are Cypher and do
  not apply; neither does `GraphObjectManager.save`, which throws `UnsupportedOperationException`
  there. See the docs, under [Oracle](09-supported-engines.md#oracle).

title: A `saveAll` of several labels as one statement, and a batch FalkorDB cannot apply whole — 0.1.7
body:
A `saveAll` of several labels as one statement, and a batch FalkorDB cannot apply whole — 0.1.7
A store sometimes has to write nodes of two labels as one unit. Recording a processed chunk in
[embabel/dice#162](https://github.com/embabel/dice/pull/162) merges a hash node and moves a bookmark
node: if the hash is written and the bookmark is not, the chunk is skipped as processed while its
bookmark never moves.

Before 0.1.7, `StatelessGraphObjectManager.saveAll` wrote fragments of one class as one `UNWIND`
statement, and fragments of two classes as two statements, run by `queryBatch` in one transaction.
FalkorDB has no multi-statement transactions. In the default `WARN` mode a transaction there is a
pass-through: each statement commits as it runs, and a rollback only logs. A batch whose second
statement failed left the first one's writes, and nothing in the API said so.

title: What changed
body:
What changed
### Fragments of several classes are one statement

On Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph, a `saveAll` of fragments alone, of any number of classes, is one
statement, where:

- each fragment can be written as a row of an `UNWIND`: not one with a `@PropertyBag` or a
  `@NodeLabels` field, nor on FalkorDB one with a `@VectorIndex` field; and
- there are no more than 1,000 of them, the rows one statement of a batch takes.

One statement is applied whole or not at all on every engine, FalkorDB included. A fragment that
cannot be written as a row is saved by statements of its own, stamped or not, and the fragments of
the batch that can are still one statement where they are of two classes or more. A batch of more
than 1,000 such fragments is written as before: a statement or more for each class.

In that statement the classes go in the order of their names, unstamped classes first, and the rows
of each in the order of their ids, so two batches over the same nodes take their locks in the same
order whatever order the caller gave them in.

Oracle is unchanged: it already wrote a batch of fragments, of any classes, as one block for each
500 of them, and runs the blocks of a batch in one transaction.

Each class is written by the `UNWIND` it has on its own, and the stamps a stamped fragment is handed
back are the same as before. A batch is not checked, as before: a stale stamp on a fragment is
written over, and the object handed back keeps a token the store's node does not vouch for.

A view is a statement of its own, as it was. A batch that holds a view is more than one statement.

### A batch FalkorDB cannot apply whole is reported, or refused

`PersistenceManager.atomicBatches` says whether a batch of more than one statement is applied whole.
It is true on Neo4j, Memgraph and Oracle, and false on FalkorDB. It is a capability to ask, as
`supportsSchemaManagement` is, rather than an engine to match. A `ConnectionProvider` declares it;
one of your own that commits each statement as it runs should say `false`.

On a store where it is false:

- **A batch of one statement runs with no transaction.** It is applied whole on its own, and a
  transaction would add nothing to that. Before, `STRICT` mode refused it, as any transaction is
  refused, so every `saveAll` and `patchAll` failed in that mode.
- **In `WARN` mode (the default), a batch of more runs statement by statement**, as before: a
  failure midway leaves the statements before it written, and nothing is undone. The first such
  batch on a manager logs a warning saying the batch is not applied whole; each later one is logged
  at debug. Nothing else tells the caller: a batch that succeeds returns as it does on any engine,
  and one that fails throws the failing statement's error with the statements before it still
  applied.
- **In `STRICT` mode, a batch of more is refused with `NonAtomicBatchException`** before any of it
  runs, and before a connection is taken. Nothing is written. `statements` says how many statements the batch would have run.

Inside a caller's transaction (`@Transactional`), the transaction is what runs the batch:

- **In `WARN` mode** a batch of more runs statement by statement on the transaction's connection,
  and is reported as above. A rollback of the caller's transaction undoes none of it.
- **In `STRICT` mode** the store refuses to start the transaction, at the first statement the
  transaction runs. A `saveAll` there is refused with the store's `Unsupported

title: Upgrading
body:
Upgrading
- **Nothing to change** for a `saveAll` that worked before. A batch of fragments of several classes
  now sends one statement where it sent one for each class.
- **On FalkorDB in `STRICT` mode**, a `saveAll` or `patchAll` of one statement is now written where
  it was refused. One of more statements is refused with `NonAtomicBatchException` where it was
  refused with a plain `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- **A `PersistenceManager` of your own** gets `atomicBatches` from the interface, as true. Override
  it if its store cannot roll back.
- **A `ConnectionProvider` of your own** gets `atomicBatches` as true and `refusesNonAtomicBatches`
  as false. A provider whose store cannot roll back says `atomicBatches = false`, and says
  `refusesNonAtomicBatches = true` where a batch of more than one statement is to be refused rather
  than run statement by statement.

title: Engine notes
body:
Engine notes
FalkorDB 6 needs the statement written a particular way. Each class's `UNWIND` is folded to one row
before the next class begins, and two things that would be natural in Cypher make FalkorDB bind the
wrong node:

- carrying a count from one fold through two more fails the statement ("Type mismatch: … but was
  Integer"), so only the stamps a class hands back are carried on
  ([FalkorDB#3369](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3369));
- a `MERGE` after two folds, of which the later follows a `WITH`, binds the node of the `MERGE`
  before it and writes the row to that node. The rows are projected (`WITH row`) before each
  `MERGE` after the first, which FalkorDB then reads correctly
  ([FalkorDB#3368](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/issues/3368)).

Either workaround can be removed once FalkorDB fixes its issue.

The tests that hold these are in `StatelessSaveAllAtomicCrossEngineTest`, which runs on Neo4j,
FalkorDB and Memgraph.

title: 0.1.7 — `create`: make a node only if it is not there
body:
0.1.7 — `create`: make a node only if it is not there
A store that keeps an aggregate per id needs "make it if it is not there, otherwise merge into it",
and the first write of an id must not overwrite a concurrent first write of the same id.
`StatelessGraphObjectManager` had no way to say the first half. `update(id) { }` merges into a node
that is there, and makes none. A `save` of an object with no stamp is not checked, so two writers
that each load null and each save write the same node, and the second overwrites the first.

`create(obj)` makes the node only if no node has its id, in one statement. If one does, it writes
nothing and returns null, and the caller falls back to `update`:

```kotlin
val stored = sgom.create(p) ?: sgom.update<Proposition>(p.id) { it.merge(p) }
```

How to use it is in the docs, under
[Create If Absent](06-object-manager.md#create-if-absent-create).

title: The API
body:
The API
```kotlin
fun <T : Any> create(obj: T): T?
```

- It returns the object carrying the whole stamp the save left, as `save` does, or null when a node
  has the id.
- When the node is there, nothing is written: not the root, not a related node, not a relationship,
  not the stamp.
- A view is made as `save` makes it. A related node is written unchecked, as `save` writes it.
- An object that carries a stamp is refused with `IllegalArgumentException` before anything is
  written. A stamp comes from a node that was loaded, and `create` makes one that is not there.

### Why null, and not an exception or a flag on `save`

The other choices were `save(obj, ifAbsent = true)`, and a named exception for a node that is
there. `create` returning `T?` was chosen because:

- It composes with `update`, which already returns `T?` for "no such node": the two halves of the
  upsert are each a call that answers null when its case does not hold, joined by `?:`. A Java
  caller tests for null, as for `update`.
- A node that is there is the expected answer half the time, not a failure. An exception would
  make the upsert a `try`/`catch`.
- A flag on `save` would sit beside `relationships`, `nullPolicy`, `only` and `except`, most of which
  mean nothing for a node that is made: `Replace` removes nothing from a new node, `CLEAR` clears
  nothing on it, and `only` would make a node holding part of an object. And `save` returns `T`, not
  `T?`, so the flag would change its return type.

title: How each backend makes the node only if it is absent
body:
How each backend makes the node only if it is absent
The root's part of the save statement is what changes; the rest of the statement is the save's.

**Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph** (Cypher). The root is merged, marked if the statement made it, and
the statement goes on only from a node it made:

```cypher
MERGE (n:Claim {id: $p0_id})
ON CREATE SET n.`__drivine.made` = true
WITH n WHERE n.`__drivine.made` IS NOT NULL
...
REMOVE n.`__drivine.made`
```

The mark is the one a save already uses to tell a node it made from one it found, for the stamp it
hands back. It is set and removed in the same statement. A node that was there gives no row, so no
later part of the statement runs and nothing is written.

**Oracle** (one PL/SQL block). The root's `node` step carries `absent`. A node the step finds,
locked, raises the block's refusal before anything is written, and the block gives no row, as it
does for a stale checked save. Where a uniqueness constraint refuses the insert because another
writer made the node at the same moment, the step finds that writer's node, as a save does, and so
refuses too.

**No row, or a refusal.** The manager reads no row from a statement that only makes its root as "the
node is there", and returns null. If the statement fails, it has written nothing, and the manager
reads the node: if it is there now, another writer made it at the same moment and a uniqueness
constraint refused this one (on Memgraph, "Unable to commit due to unique constraint violation"), so
it returns null. The engine's error is not read, since it differs from engine to engine. Where the
node is not there, or cannot be read, the failure is thrown.

title: Two writers at the same moment
body:
Two writers at the same moment
Both find the node absent, as two `MERGE`s do. Whether the second makes it again depends on the
engine:

| Engine | Without a uniqueness constraint on the id | With one |
|---|---|---|
| Neo4j | both can make a node | the second waits for the first, finds its node, returns null |
| Memgraph | both can make a node | the second is refused at commit, finds the first's node, returns null |
| Oracle | both can make a node | the second is refused at insert, finds the first's node, returns null |
| FalkorDB | the second finds the first's node: writes run one at a time | the same |

So, on every engine, declare one:

```kotlin
persistenceManager.constraints.ensure(UniquenessConstraintSpec("Proposition", "id"))
```

The test `concurrent first writes of one id all end up in the one node` runs four writers of one id
at once, ten rounds, each `create(f) ?: update(f.id) { it.merge(f) }`, on all four engines with the
constraint, and checks that every writer's data is in the one node. The same test with the
load-then-`save` the issue describes fails on all four.

On Memgraph inside a caller's transaction the constraint is checked when the transaction commits,
so the second of two transactions that each made the node fails at its commit and not at its
`create`. Running that transaction again, its `create` returns null. The test `a create in a
transaction that began before another writer made the node makes no second node` shows this on
Memgraph, and on the other engines that the `create` finds the other writer's node and returns null.

title: What a save statement says about its root
body:
What a save statement says about its root
A save, an update and a create differ only in which root the statement writes. That is one value,
`RootMode`, carried from the request to the statement and, on Cypher engines, to the stamping the
root's part is built with:

| `RootMode` | Root not there | Root there | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EITHER` | made | written | `save` |
| `FOUND` | no row | written | `update` |
| `ABSENT` | made | no row | `create` |

The nodes a view reaches through a relationship are always `EITHER`, unchecked, whatever the root
is held to.

title: Upgrading
body:
Upgrading
Nothing changes for existing callers. `create` is new, on `StatelessGraphObjectManager` alone.

title: Order by an expression over the root's properties — 0.1.7
body:
Order by an expression over the root's properties — 0.1.7
`orderBy` took property references only. It now also takes an expression built from the root's
properties, arithmetic, a few functions and values the caller binds, so a ranking computed from
several properties stays in the database with its `LIMIT`: a top-k read does not load every
candidate. No existing order changes behaviour. Issue #79; the motivating case is the effective
confidence of embabel/dice#162.

title: The DSL
body:
The DSL
```kotlin
val asOf = Instant.now()

graphObjectManager.loadAll<PropositionView> {
    where { proposition.status eq "active" }
    orderBy {
        case(
            (proposition.validFrom above asOf) or (proposition.validTo atMost asOf) then 0.0,
            otherwise = proposition.confidence * coalesce(proposition.boost, 1.0) *
                exp(-proposition.decay * floor((epochSeconds(asOf) - proposition.lastAccessedSeconds) / 86400)),
        ).desc()
        proposition.id.asc()    // breaks the ties of the score, as after a property
    }
    limit(20)
}
```

The building blocks, all in `org.drivine.query.dsl`:

| Kotlin | Java (`OrderExpressions.*`) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b`, `a / b`, `-a` | `plus`, `minus`, `times`, `div`, `unaryMinus` | arithmetic; an operand is a property reference, an expression, or a number |
| `exp(x)` | `exp` | `e` raised to `x` |
| `floor(x)` | `floor` | the largest whole number no greater than `x` |
| `coalesce(x, y, …)` | `coalesce` | the first that has a value |
| `epochSeconds(instant)` | `epochSeconds` | a moment of the caller's as seconds, bound as a number |
| `case(c1 then v1, …, otherwise = v)` | `caseOf(new CaseBranch[]{…}, v)`, `c.then(v).otherwise(w)` | the value of the first branch whose condition holds |
| `a above b`, `below`, `atLeast`, `atMost`, `equalTo`, `notEqualTo` | the same names | comparisons in a case; `b` is an operand or a value, bound |
| `x.hasValue()`, `x.hasNoValue()` | the same names | tests for a value |
| `c and d`, `c or d`, `!c` | `c.and(d)`, `c.or(d)`, `c.not()` | combinations of conditions |
| `param(value)` | `param` | any value, bound; a node reference, a condition or an order is refused |

A stored moment read as seconds, `epochSeconds(property)`, is not among them: not every backend can
write it (see [Backend-specific functions](#backend-specific-functions)).

An expression orders with `asc()` / `desc()` inside an `orderBy` block, which take
`nullsFirst()` / `nullsLast()` after them as a property order does. From Java,
`expression.descending()` gives an `ExpressionOrder` for `JavaQueryBuilder.orderBy`, and a generated
property reference is an operand as it stands:

```java
gom.query(PropositionView.class).filterWith(PropositionViewQueryDsl.class)
    .orderBy(q -> times(q.proposition().confidence(), exp(unaryMinus(q.proposition().decay()))).descending())
    .orderBy(q -> q.proposition().id().ascending())
    .limit(20)
    .loadAll();
```

title: Backend-specific functions
body:
Backend-specific functions
A function every backend writes lives in `org.drivine.query.dsl`. One that some backends cannot
write lives in a package named for its capability, never for a backend, so a function that works on
several backends but not all has one home. There is one such capability:

| Package | Opt-in | Functions | Java |
|---|---|---|---|
| `org.drivine.query.dsl.temporal` | `@OptIn(TemporalOrder::class)` | `epochSeconds(property)`: a stored moment as seconds since the epoch, with the fraction | `TemporalOrderExpressions.epochSeconds` |

The opt-in is a Kotlin `@RequiresOptIn` marker at the error level: a call without it does not
compile, so a caller states that it has checked its backend. The KDoc of `TemporalOrder` lists the
backends that support it (the table in [Each backend](#each-backend) below). Java does not see an
opt-in; there the capability's functions are the statics of their own class, apart from
`OrderExpressions`.

The opt-in is read at compile time and knows nothing of the backend. The backstop is at run time:
a backend that cannot write the function refuses the load with an `UnsupportedOrderFunctionException`
as the statement is built, before anything is sent to the store.

`epochSeconds(property)` takes a reference to a temporal property (`PropertyReference<out Temporal>`),
so a reference to a text or a number does not compile. It still takes a local date-time's
property, which names no instant; the property should hold an `Instant`, `OffsetDateTime` or
`ZonedDateTime`.

```kotlin
import org.drivine.query.dsl.temporal.TemporalOrder
import org.drivine.query.dsl.temporal.epochSeconds

@OptIn(TemporalOrder::class)
fun recentFirst() = graphObjectManager.loadAll<PropositionView> {
    orderBy {
        (proposition.confidence * exp(-proposition.decay * floor((epochSeconds(asOf) - epochSeconds(proposition.lastAccessed)) / 86400))).desc()
        proposition.id.asc()
    }
    limit(20)
}
```

`epochSeconds(asOf)`, a moment of the caller's, is folded on the caller's side and bound as a number,
so it needs no opt-in and every backend takes it; the import of `temporal.epochSeconds` adds the
overload for a property beside it.

title: What it guarantees
body:
What it guarantees
- **Values are bound.** Every value in an expression that is not a property — an `asOf`, a number
  written in the expression — is a parameter (`$_order_0`, … on Cypher; `$_p…` on Oracle). None is
  written into the statement, so its text is the same for every `asOf`.
- **Division is of real numbers** on every backend: Cypher divides two integers as integers, so the
  Cypher form is `toFloat(a) / b`. Division by zero is not the same on each: Oracle refuses the
  statement (`ORA-01476`), and so does Neo4j where the divisor is a whole number; FalkorDB and
  Memgraph run it, and where such a row sorts is theirs to say. Guard a divisor that can be zero
  with a `case`.
- **Ties fall to the next term.** An expression is one term of the `ORDER BY`; the terms after it
  order the rows it ties.
- **A null is not a crash.** A property with no value makes the arithmetic it is in null, as in
  Cypher and SQL; a comparison with no value holds for no row, so such a row takes a case's next
  branch. `coalesce` supplies a default.
- **Only the root's properties.** An expression is one value per root, so a property of a related
  node is refused (`IllegalArgumentException`). On a view the expression reads the root by the keys
  of the view's projection, as a property order does.
- **No seek.** A keyset cursor holds property values; an order by an expression under `seek` is
  refused (`IllegalArgumentException`). Use `skip` / `limit`.
- **No index advice.** No index holds an expression's value, so no index is advised for an order
  that has one.

title: Each backend
body:
Each backend
| | arithmetic, `exp`, `floor`, `coalesce`, case | `epochSeconds(property)` |
|---|---|---|
| Neo4j 5 | yes | `(p.x.epochMillis / 1000.0)` |
| Neo4j 4 | yes | `(p.x.epochMillis / 1000.0)` |
| Memgraph | yes | `(timestamp(p.x) / 1000000.0)` |
| FalkorDB | yes | **refused**: FalkorDB holds a moment as its ISO-8601 text and has no function that reads one as a number |
| Oracle | yes, as SQL (`EXP`, `FLOOR`, `COALESCE`, `CASE`) | from the interval since the epoch, for a property a field declares as a moment; refused for any other |

A grammar not in the table refuses `epochSeconds(property)` the same way: its
`CypherGrammar.epochSeconds` is the interface's default, which refuses. A refusal is an
`UnsupportedOrderFunctionException`, naming the function and the engine, thrown while the statement
is built: nothing is sent to the store. On FalkorDB, store the moment's seconds
since the epoch in a property of its own and order by that — the comparisons of a validity window
still work on the moments themselves, since FalkorDB compares their fixed-width text in time order.

On Oracle a property is read as the type of the field that declares it, as an order by it is. A
property no field declares is read as a number in arithmetic, in a comparison as the kind of the
value it is compared with, and as text in `hasValue()` / `hasNoValue()`, so a text counts as a value.

title: What changes in the API
body:
What changes in the API
`OrderSpec` and the new `ExpressionOrder` are both an `OrderTerm`. `OrderClauseResult.rootOrders` and
`JavaQueryBuilder.orderBy` now carry `OrderTerm` where they carried `OrderSpec`, and
`OrderClauseResult` has the expression's `bindings`. A caller that reads `rootOrders` as property
orders narrows them with `filterIsInstance<OrderSpec>()`.

`CypherGenerator.processOrders` has a form of four arguments,
`processOrders(orders, relationshipNames, viewModel, grammar)`, whose `grammar` is required: it says
how the engine reads a moment as a number, or that it cannot. The forms that were there before,
`processOrders(orders, relationshipNames)` and `processOrders(orders, relationshipNames, viewModel)`,
keep their signatures and write for Neo4j 5, as they did; a caller that knows its engine passes the
grammar.

`CypherGrammar`, which a custom grammar implements, has one new member:

```kotlin
fun epochSeconds(moment: String): TemporalOrderSupport
```

given the expression that reads a moment as the engine holds it, it answers
`TemporalOrderSupport.Written(expression)`, the moment as seconds since the epoch with their fraction,
or `TemporalOrderSupport.Refused(engine, reason)`, which the load throws as an
`UnsupportedOrderFunctionException`. The default refuses, so a custom grammar compiles unchanged and
refuses `epochSeconds(property)` until it overrides this.

title: `loadAll(class, where)`
body:
`loadAll(class, where)`
The raw `loadAll(class, whereClause)` still takes no order. It has no need to: a store that ranks
moves its read onto the DSL — `where`, `orderBy` with the expression, and `limit` — rather than
keeping a hand-written statement beside it.

title: 00-introduction
body:
00-introduction
[![CI](https://github.com/liberation-data/drivine4j/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/liberation-data/drivine4j/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)

**Docs: [drivine.org](https://drivine.org/jvm/)**, for Kotlin & Java, TypeScript, and Python.

A graph database client library for Java and Kotlin supporting **Neo4j**, **FalkorDB**, **Amazon Neptune**, **Memgraph**, **Oracle** (SQL/PGQ), **Postgres** (plain SQL, with pgvector for vector search) and **SQLite** (a file, no server) with two approaches to graph mapping:

1. **PersistenceManager** - Low-level API with manual Cypher queries (classic Drivine approach). Cypher runs on every
   engine, compiled to SQL on Oracle, Postgres and SQLite: see [Cypher on a relational database](05-cypher-on-a-relational-database.md#cypher-on-a-relational-database).
2. **Object manager** (`StatelessGraphObjectManager`) - High-level API with annotated models and type-safe DSL.

Drivine4j is the graph database client library for [Embabel](https://hub.embabel.com) - Agentic AI for the JVM. 

> **On Node.js or Python?** [Drivine](https://github.com/liberation-data/drivine) (`npm install @liberation-data/drivine`)
> and [drivine-python](https://github.com/liberation-data/drivine-python) (`pip install drivine`) are drivine4j's
> TypeScript and Python twins, with the same object manager, query DSL, schema management and engines. The three share
> a storage format: a store written from any of them is read, stamped and checked alike by the others.

title: Philosophy
body:
Philosophy
### Composition Over Inheritance

A typical ORM defines a reusable object model. From this model, statements are generated to hydrate to and from the model to the database. This addresses the so-called impedance mismatch between the object model and the database. However, there are drawbacks:

* Generated queries work well for simple cases, but can get out of hand and degrade performance when it's more complex. Debugging these generated statements can be painful.
* One model for many use cases is a big ask - the original CRUD cases work well, but more complex cases mean the model gets in the way more than it helps.

These trade-offs might be acceptable for relational databases, but with graph databases this mismatch doesn't really exist.

Just as we favor composition over inheritance in software development, we prefer composition when mapping results from complex queries. A person can play many roles: sometimes we're here to help them have a great holiday, other times to manage a team, in others they're a person of interest. With Drivine, you compose views as needed:

```kotlin
@GraphView
data class HolidayingPerson(
    @Root val person: Person,
    @GraphRelationship(type = "BOOKED_HOLIDAY")
    val holidays: List<Holiday>
)
```

Behind the scenes, Drivine generates efficient Cypher:

```cypher
MATCH (person:Person {firstName: $firstName})
WITH person, [(person)-[:BOOKED_HOLIDAY]->(holiday:Holiday) | holiday {.*}] AS holidays
RETURN {
         person:   properties(person),
         holidays: holidays
       }
```

Composition lets us mix and match as needed.

title: Requirements
body:
Requirements
- **Java 21+**
- **Kotlin:**
  - For PersistenceManager API: Any Kotlin version
  - For the object manager API: **Kotlin 2.2.0+** (requires context parameters feature)

title: Installation
body:
Installation
### Spring Boot Starter

Drivine4j works hand in hand with Spring. For a Spring Boot application, add the starter: it brings the core library,
Drivine's transaction manager and the auto-configuration (see [Configuration](04-quick-start.md#1-configuration)). `@Transactional` and
`TransactionTemplate` run Drivine's transactions, alongside your other Spring transactions.

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("org.drivine:drivine4j-spring-boot-starter:0.4.1")
}
```

Spring without Boot takes `drivine4j-spring` instead: the core library and `DrivineTransactionManager`, Drivine's
`PlatformTransactionManager`, for `@Transactional` and `TransactionTemplate`, with no auto-configuration. The starter
is built on it.

### Core Library

The core library depends only on what it uses: the drivers, Jackson and HikariCP. The Spring artifacts above bring it,
and it can be used on its own too, with another framework or none (see [Other frameworks, or none](04-quick-start.md#4-other-frameworks-or-none)).

#### Gradle (Kotlin DSL)
```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation("org.drivine:drivine4j:0.4.1")
}
```

#### Gradle (Groovy)
```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation 'org.drivine:drivine4j:0.4.1'
}
```

#### Maven
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.drivine</groupId>
    <artifactId>drivine4j</artifactId>
    <version>0.4.1</version>
</dependency>
```

| Artifact | Holds | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| `drivine4j-spring-boot-starter` | the auto-configuration, `@EnableDrivine`, `@EnableDrivinePropertiesConfig`, `@EnableDrivineTestConfig` | `drivine4j-spring`, Spring Boot |
| `drivine4j-spring` | `DrivineTransactionManager`, for `@Transactional` and `TransactionTemplate`; `FalkorDbCleanupListener` | `drivine4j`, Spring Framework (`spring-tx`) |
| `drivine4j` | the engines, the managers, the query DSL, schema management, `Transactions` and `Drivine` | the drivers, Jackson, HikariCP |
| `drivine4j-coroutines` | `transactionSuspending { }`, a transaction block for Kotlin coroutines: see [Transactions in coroutines](07-core-features.md#transactions-in-coroutines-drivine4j-coroutines) | `drivine4j`, `kotlinx-coroutines-core` |

### Code Generation (For the Type-Safe Query DSL)

If you want to use the object manager with the type-safe query DSL, you need to add the code generation processor.

> **Note for Java Projects:** Both Java and Kotlin are fully supported at runtime. The code generator (KSP) produces Kotlin DSL extensions, but a Java-friendly query builder API is also available. Define your `@GraphView` and `@NodeFragment` classes in either language. See the [Java Interoperability](14-java-interoperability.md#java-interoperability) section for details.

title: Quick Start
Cypher on a relational database
body:
Cypher on a relational database
Write a statement in Cypher once, and run it on any store Drivine supports. Neo4j, FalkorDB, Memgraph and Neptune run
it as written. On Postgres, Oracle and SQLite, Drivine compiles it to SQL over the node and edge tables it keeps the
graph in, and it gives the rows a graph engine gives.

### Configuration

SQLite is the quickest to try: the graph is a file, with no server to run. Add `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` and name the
file:

```yaml
database:
  datasources:
    graph:
      type: SQLITE
      database-name: /var/data/app.db  # the file, made if it is not there
```

On Postgres, add `org.postgresql:postgresql`:

```yaml
database:
  datasources:
    graph:
      type: POSTGRES
      host: localhost
      port: 5432
      database-name: app
      user-name: app
      password: secret
```

Oracle takes `type: ORACLE` and the properties in [Oracle](09-supported-engines.md#oracle). Without Spring, give `Drivine` the same
properties:

```kotlin
val drivine = Drivine(DataSourceMap(mapOf(
    "graph" to ConnectionProperties(type = DatabaseType.SQLITE, databaseName = "/var/data/app.db")
)))
val manager = drivine.persistenceManager("graph")
```

The graph's tables are made, where they are not there yet, before the datasource's first connection, so the first
statement sent to a new store finds them, with no object manager made first. A user who may read the tables but not
make them works with a store where they are there. The tables are made committing each statement, also on a datasource
whose connections start with `autoCommit = false`. A graph name that can't name tables, such as `my-graph`, makes no
tables: plain SQL still works, a Cypher statement fails with a `DrivineException`, naming the graph and saying why, and
an object manager over the graph is refused with an `IllegalArgumentException` that says the same. A schema catalog for
every database skips the datasource, and one that names it fails.

### A write and a read

Wrap the text in a `CypherStatement`. A plain string is Cypher to a graph engine but SQL to Postgres, Oracle and
SQLite, so the `CypherStatement` is what lets one statement run on every store.

```kotlin
data class Person(val name: String, val city: String)

manager.execute(
    QuerySpecification
        .withStatement(CypherStatement(
            "MERGE (p:Person {name: \$name}) SET p.city = \$city " +
            "MERGE (c:City {name: \$city}) " +
            "MERGE (p)-[:LIVES_IN]->(c)"
        ))
        .bind(mapOf("name" to "Ada", "city" to "London"))
)

val londoners: List<Person> = manager.query(
    QuerySpecification
        .withStatement(CypherStatement(
            "MATCH (p:Person)-[:LIVES_IN]->(:City {name: \$city}) " +
            "RETURN properties(p) AS person ORDER BY person.name"
        ))
        .bind(mapOf("city" to "London"))
        .transform(Person::class.java)
)   // [Person(name=Ada, city=London)]
```

The write is applied whole or not at all on each SQL store. The same read from Java:

```java

title: Object Manager - Type-Safe Graph Mapping
body:
Object Manager - Type-Safe Graph Mapping
`StatelessGraphObjectManager` is a high-level API for working with graph-mapped objects using annotated models. It generates efficient Cypher queries automatically and provides a type-safe DSL for filtering and ordering.

It keeps no state between calls. What a load returns is what the store holds, and what a save writes depends only on the object and the arguments you pass.

Get one from the `GraphObjectManagerFactory`, which the Spring Boot starter provides:

```kotlin
@Bean
fun graphObjectManager(factory: GraphObjectManagerFactory): StatelessGraphObjectManager = factory.stateless()
```

> Earlier releases documented `GraphObjectManager`, which tracks what it loads in a session. It is deprecated: see [Migrating from GraphObjectManager](15-migrating-from-graphobjectmanager.md#migrating-from-graphobjectmanager).
>
> Upgrading from 0.0.x? [docs/0.1.0-stateless-object-manager.md](../docs/0.1.0-stateless-object-manager.md) lists what changed and what to do about data saved before it.

### Key Concepts

#### 1. NodeFragment - Mapping Nodes

A `@NodeFragment` represents a single node in the graph:

```kotlin
@NodeFragment
data class Person(
    @NodeId val uuid: String,
    val name: String,
    val bio: String?
)

@NodeFragment
data class Organization(
    @NodeId val uuid: String,
    val name: String
)
```

**Defaults for missing properties.** When a node is missing a property, the value loads as `null` — which fails for a non-nullable type. Two annotations handle that without any Jackson knowledge:

```kotlin
@NodeFragment(labels = ["User"])
data class UserNode(
    @NodeId val id: String,
    @Default val roles: List<String> = emptyList(),  // missing/null → the declared default []
    @Default val status: String = "active",          // missing/null → "active"
    @EmptyWhenAbsent val tags: List<String>,         // missing/null → [] (no default needed)
)
```

- **`@Default`** falls back to the property's declared default (a Kotlin constructor default, or a Java field initializer). Works for any type; a provided value always wins.
- **`@EmptyWhenAbsent`** maps an absent/null collection or map to empty, with no declared default required — the right choice for **Java records**, whose components have no field initializer:
  ```java
  public record UserNode(@NodeId String id, @EmptyWhenAbsent List<String> roles) {}
  ```

#### 2. RelationshipFragment - Capturing Relationship Properties

A `@RelationshipFragment` captures properties on relationship edges, not just the target node:

```kotlin
@RelationshipFragment
data class WorkHistory(
    val startDate: LocalDate,  // Property on the edge
    val role: String,           // Property on the edge
    val target: Organization    // Target node
)
```

This is useful for modeling:
- Employment history (start date, role, organization)
- Transaction records (timestamp, amount, target account)
- Audit trails (timestamp, action, target entity)
- Any relationship with metadata

#### 3. GraphView - Composing Views

A `@GraphView` composes multiple fragments and relationships into a single query result:

```kotlin
@GraphView
data class PersonCareer(
    @Root val person: Person,  // Root fragment

    @GraphRelationship(type = "WORKS_FOR")
    val employmentHistory: List<WorkHistory>  // Relationship with properties
)
```

The `@Root` annotation marks which fragment is the query's starting point.

Core Features (PersistenceManager)
### Fluent Query Building

```kotlin
val activeAdults = manager.query(
    QuerySpecification
        .withStatement("MATCH (p:Person) RETURN properties(p)")
        .transform(Person::class.java)
        .filter { it.age >= 18 }           // Client-side filtering
        .filter { it.email != null }
        .map { it.firstName }              // Transform to String
        .limit(10)
)
```

### Chainable Transformations

```kotlin
val fullNames: List<String> = manager.query(
    QuerySpecification
        .withStatement("MATCH (p:Person) RETURN properties(p)")
        .transform(Person::class.java)    // Map to Person
        .filter { it.age > 25 }            // Filter
        .map { "${it.firstName} ${it.lastName}" }  // Transform to String
)
```

### Transaction Management

```kotlin
@Component
class UserService @Autowired constructor(
    private val personRepo: PersonRepository,
    private val emailService: EmailService
) {
    @Transactional  // Spring's @Transactional works
    fun registerUser(person: Person) {
        val created = personRepo.create(person)
        emailService.sendWelcome(created.email)
        // Auto-commits on success, rolls back on exception
    }

    @DrivineTransactional  // Or use Drivine's annotation
    fun updateUserProfile(uuid: String, updates: Partial<Person>) {
        personRepo.update(uuid, updates)
    }
}
```

`DrivineTransactionManager` is a Spring `PlatformTransactionManager`, so everything Spring does with transactions
works with Drivine: `@Transactional` with any propagation but `NESTED`, `TransactionTemplate`, `@Rollback` in tests,
and other transaction managers in the same application (name Drivine's with `@Transactional("drivineTransactionManager")`
where there are several). The starter registers it, and so does `@EnableDrivine`.

Object-manager saves join these transactions: see [Saves and transactions](06-object-manager.md#saves-and-transactions) for what a refused save does to one.

#### Transactions in code (`Transactions`)

To run a block in a transaction without an annotated method, inject `Transactions` (the starter makes the bean; outside
Spring, `drivine.transactions`). Its blocks and `@Transactional` methods share one transaction, either way round: a
`@Transactional` method called from a block joins the block's transaction, and a block run in a `@Transactional`
method joins Spring's.

```kotlin
@Component
class Onboarding(private val transactions: Transactions, private val gom: StatelessGraphObjectManager) {

    fun onboard(person: Person, hire: Hire) = transactions.transaction {
        gom.save(person)
        gom.save(hire)
    } // both commit here; a throw out of the block rolls both back

    fun audit(hire: Hire) = transactions.transaction(Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) { gom.save(hire) } // commits whatever the caller does
}
```

`transaction { }` returns what the block returns, and takes a propagation, with the meaning Spring gives it:

| `propagation` | With a transaction in progress | Without one |
|---|---|---|
| `REQUIRED` (the default) | joins it | begins one |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | sets it aside, and begins one | begins one |
| `SUPPORTS` | joins it | runs without one |
| `MANDATORY` | joins it | refuses: `IllegalTransactionStateException` |
| `NEVER` | refuses: `IllegalTransactionStateException` | runs without one |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED` | sets it aside, and runs without one | runs without one |

title: API Reference
body:
API Reference
### PersistenceManager

```kotlin
interface PersistenceManager {
    fun <T> query(spec: QuerySpecification<T>): List<T>
    fun <T> getOne(spec: QuerySpecification<T>): T
    fun <T> maybeGetOne(spec: QuerySpecification<T>): T?
    fun <T> execute(spec: QuerySpecification<T>)
    fun executeBatch(specs: List<QuerySpecification<*>>)                      // several statements, one transaction
    fun queryBatch(specs: List<QuerySpecification<*>>): List<List<Any?>>      // the same, returning each statement's rows
    val atomicBatches: Boolean                                                // whether a batch of several statements is applied whole
}
```

`executeBatch` and `queryBatch` run their statements in one transaction on the managers Drivine provides, or in the transaction they are called in. FalkorDB has no transactions: there each statement commits by itself, `atomicBatches` is false, a batch of one statement runs with no transaction, and a batch of more runs statement by statement (`WARN`) or is refused with `NonAtomicBatchException` before any of it runs (`STRICT`). The interface's own defaults run each statement on its own, so a `PersistenceManager` you implement must override both to make a batch atomic; `saveAll` calls `queryBatch`.

### QuerySpecification

```kotlin
QuerySpecification
    .withStatement(cypherQuery)       // Start with Cypher query
    .bind(params)                        // Bind parameters
    .transform(TargetClass::class.java)  // Map to target type
    .filter { predicate }                // Client-side filtering
    .map { transformation }              // Transform results
    .limit(n)                            // Limit results
    .skip(n)                             // Skip first n results
```

### ConnectionProperties

```kotlin
data class ConnectionProperties(
    val type: DatabaseType,                  // NEO4J, FALKORDB, NEPTUNE, MEMGRAPH, ORACLE, POSTGRES, SQLITE
    val host: String = "",                   // not read on SQLite, a file
    val port: Int? = null,                   // the engine's own when null: 1521 on Oracle, 5432 on Postgres
    val userName: String? = null,
    val password: String? = null,
    val idleTimeout: Int? = null,
    val connectionTimeout: Int? = null,
    val poolMax: Int? = null,
    val databaseName: String? = null,        // on Oracle, the service to connect to; on Postgres, the database; on SQLite, the file's path
    val defaultGraphPath: String? = null,    // on Oracle, Postgres and SQLite, the name of the graph and its tables
    val protocol: String? = null,
    val cypherDialect: CypherDialect? = null,
    val falkorDbTransactionMode: FalkorDbTransactionMode? = null,
    val region: String? = null,
    val neptuneAuth: NeptuneAuthMode? = null,
)
```

title: Supported Engines
body:
Supported Engines
Drivine4j supports multiple graph database engines from the same codebase. Switch engines with a one-line YAML change — your models, queries, and DSL code stay the same.

| Engine | Type | Transactions | Collection Sort | Auth |
|--------|------|-------------|----------------|------|
| Neo4j 5.x | `NEO4J` | Full ACID | APOC (default) or CALL subquery | Basic (user/pass) |
| Neo4j 4.x | `NEO4J` | Full ACID | APOC (required) | Basic (user/pass) |
| FalkorDB | `FALKORDB` | Passthrough (no multi-statement) | CALL subquery | None |
| Amazon Neptune | `NEPTUNE` | Full ACID | CALL subquery | IAM SigV4 or None (tunnel) |
| Memgraph | `MEMGRAPH` | Full ACID | CALL subquery | Basic (user/pass) or None |
| Oracle 23.9+ | `ORACLE` | Full ACID | In the statement | User and password |
| Postgres 14+ | `POSTGRES` | Full ACID | In the statement | User and password |
| SQLite 3.45+ | `SQLITE` | Full ACID, one writer at a time | In the statement | None (a file) |

### Neo4j

The default engine. Works out of the box with Testcontainers or a local instance:

```yaml
database:
  datasources:
    graph:
      type: NEO4J
      host: localhost
      port: 7687
      user-name: neo4j
      password: your-password
      database-name: neo4j
```

### FalkorDB

FalkorDB is an in-memory graph database built on Redis. It offers extremely fast query execution but does not support multi-statement transactions.

```yaml
database:
  datasources:
    graph:
      type: FALKORDB
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      database-name: mygraph
```

**Transactions:** FalkorDB does not support multi-statement transactions. `@Transactional` methods work but each query executes and commits independently. An object-manager `save` is one statement and so still atomic, and so is a `saveAll` of fragments alone that fits in one; an `update` is two and a `saveAll` that holds a view several, and what ran before a failure or a refused save stays applied. By default, `startTransaction()` logs a debug message, `rollbackTransaction()` logs a warning, and the first batch of more than one statement logs a warning that it is not applied whole. To enforce strict no-transaction usage (throw on `@Transactional`, and refuse a batch of more than one statement with `NonAtomicBatchException` before any of it runs), set:

```yaml
      falkor-db-transaction-mode: STRICT   # default: WARN
```

**Jedis:** the FalkorDB client needs Jedis 8. Spring Boot's dependency management sets an older one (6.0.0 on Boot 3.5, 7.4.1 on Boot 4.1), and a managed version in your build wins over the one Drivine declares, so a FalkorDB datasource fails at start-up with `NoSuchMethodError` on `DefaultJedisClientConfig.Builder.autoNegotiateProtocol`. Set it yourself:

```xml

<properties>
    <jedis.version>8.0.1</jedis.version>
</properties>

<!-- Maven, importing a BOM: declare it BEFORE the import -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>redis.clients</groupId>
            <artifactId>jedis</artifactId>
            <version>8.0.1</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

```groovy
// Gradle, with the Spring Boot plugin
ext['jedis.version'] = '8.0.1'
```

body:
Schema Management (Indexes & Constraints)
Drivine manages vector indexes, full-text indexes, range indexes, Neo4j's TEXT indexes, and uniqueness constraints across Neo4j, Memgraph, FalkorDB, Oracle and Postgres — with idempotent, drift-aware `ensure` semantics and engine differences (DDL syntax, introspection, FalkorDB's Redis-command constraints) handled for you. Opt-in: declare nothing, pay nothing.

### Imperative API

Every `PersistenceManager` exposes `indexes` and `constraints` managers. Operations always run in auto-commit mode (schema DDL cannot run inside a data transaction):

```kotlin
// Idempotent — call on every startup
val result = persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(
    VectorIndexSpec(label = "Proposition", property = "embedding", dimensions = 1536)
)
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(RangeIndexSpec("Proposition", "contextId"))
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(RangeIndexSpec("Message", listOf("sessionId", "createdAt")))  // composite
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(FullTextIndexSpec("Chunk", "text"))                            // full-text (single property)
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(FullTextIndexSpec("Entity", listOf("name", "description")))    // full-text (multi-property)
persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(TextIndexSpec("Chunk", "title"))                               // Neo4j TEXT index

persistenceManager.constraints.ensure(UniquenessConstraintSpec("ChatSession", "sessionId"))
persistenceManager.constraints.ensure(UniquenessConstraintSpec("Membership", listOf("tenantId", "userId")))
```

`ensure` returns an `EnsureResult`:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Created` | Nothing existed and the item was created, or it existed without part of what the engine makes for it (on Oracle, a range index without its index over the label's nodes) and that part was made |
| `AlreadyMatching` | A matching item exists; nothing changed |
| `Drift` | An item exists with a **different shape** (e.g. vector dimensions changed). Nothing changed — call `recreate(spec)` to replace it (destructive) |
| `Violation` | Constraint only: existing data violates it — a key the constraint covers repeats. Includes a bounded sample of the conflicting values, each with the nodes that hold it: their engine id (`elementId`), and their `@NodeId` when the constraint is declared on a fragment, as many nodes per value as `violationSampleSize`. A refusal the data does not bear out (no key repeats) is thrown, not reported as a `Violation` |
| `BlockedByIndex` | Constraint only: a plain range index over the same label and properties is in the way of it, and is named. Neo4j alone refuses a constraint for one, since its constraint brings its own index. Nothing changed — drop the index, or ensure with `replaceBlockingIndex = true` (`drivine.schema.replace-blocking-index=true`), which drops it and makes the constraint |
| `Recreated` | From an explicit `recreate(spec)` — old item dropped, new one created |

**An item that ignores case** (`ignoreCase = true`) is made over the lowercased copy a `@CaseInsensitive` field keeps, and `ensure` fills the copy in first: see [@CaseInsensitive](09-supported-engines.md#caseinsensitive-lookups-that-ignore-case). The object managers keep the copy in step, but Cypher you send yourself does not: set the copy in the same statement, or `recreate` the item afterwards to fill it in again ([how](09-supported-engines.md#cypher-of-your-own)).

Java Query DSL
Drivine4j provides a fluent, type-safe query API for Java that mirrors the Kotlin DSL capabilities.

### Basic Usage

```java
import org.drivine.query.dsl.JavaQueryBuilderKt;

List<RaisedAndAssignedIssue> results = JavaQueryBuilderKt
    .query(graphObjectManager, RaisedAndAssignedIssue.class)
    .filterWith(RaisedAndAssignedIssueQueryDsl.class)
    .where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getState().isEqualTo("open"))
    .loadAll();
```

The pattern is:
1. `query(graphObjectManager, GraphViewClass)` - Start a query
2. `filterWith(QueryDslClass)` - Specify the generated DSL for type-safe filtering
3. Chain `where()`, `whereAny()`, `orderBy()` as needed
4. Terminate with `loadAll()`, `loadFirst()`, or `deleteAll()`

### Available Operators

**Comparison:**
```java
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isEqualTo(100L))      // equals
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isNotEqualTo(100L))   // not equals
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isGreaterThan(100L))  // greater than
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isAtLeast(100L))      // greater than or equal
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isLessThan(100L))     // less than
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getId().isAtMost(100L))       // less than or equal
```

**String Operations:**
```java

.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getTitle().hasPrefix("Feature"))
.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getTitle().hasSuffix("needed"))
```

**Null Checks:**
```java

.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getBody().isPresent())
```

**Collections:**

.where(dsl -> dsl.getIssue().getState().isIn(Arrays.asList("open", "reopened")))

```java

```

```java

body:
Migrating from GraphObjectManager
`GraphObjectManager` is deprecated in favour of `StatelessGraphObjectManager`. It still works, with the fixes and the stamping that 0.1.0 brought to both managers, and is described in [docs/legacy-graph-object-manager.md](../docs/legacy-graph-object-manager.md). Everything 0.1.0 changed is listed once, in [docs/0.1.0-stateless-object-manager.md](../docs/0.1.0-stateless-object-manager.md#what-changed).

### Why

`GraphObjectManager` keeps a snapshot of every object it loads or saves, and a save writes only what differs from the snapshot. Whether a save was correct therefore depended on things you could not see from the call: whether this manager had loaded the object, whether it was still in the session, and whether anything else had written to the node since. Each of those produced a real bug:

- A node deleted by plain Cypher and saved again came back with only some of its properties.
- A relationship dropped from a list was removed or kept depending on whether the object had been evicted from the session.
- A view the manager had not loaded wrote a path field as a direct relationship.

A library should make the graph easier to work with, not require forensics to save an object safely. A `StatelessGraphObjectManager` save depends only on the object and the arguments you pass, and with a `@NodeStamp` field it is refused when another writer got there first.

### Upgrade steps

1. Move the core library and the code generator to 0.1.0 together, and compile again. Code compiled against 0.0.x does not link: the loading and query methods of `GraphObjectManager` are now declared on `GraphObjectOperations`.
2. A build that treats warnings as errors now fails on `GraphObjectManager` and `GraphObjectManagerFactory.get()`, which are deprecated. Injecting a `GraphObjectManager` by type warns too. Until the code has moved, suppress it where it is used: `@Suppress("DEPRECATION")` in Kotlin, `@SuppressWarnings("deprecation")` in Java.
3. Deploy 0.1.0 to everything that writes to the store.
4. If any view has an `INCOMING` relationship field, a `@GraphPath` field or a list read over several hops, and was ever saved, repair what the old saves left: see [Data saved before 0.1.0](#data-saved-before-010). Do it after step 3, since a writer still on 0.0.x writes the same mistakes again.
5. Replace `factory.get()` with `factory.stateless()`, and change the saves as the table below says.
6. Add a `@NodeStamp` field to each type you load, change and save. See [Existing data](06-object-manager.md#existing-data) for nodes that have no stamp yet.

### What you give up

- **Dirty-only writes are no longer automatic.** Ask for them with `update { }`, `only` or `except`.
- **Saving with `CascadeType.DELETE_ALL` has no equivalent.** Remove the relationships with `Replace`, then delete the nodes:

  ```kotlin
  val dropped = loaded.attachments - kept
  graphObjectManager.save(loaded.copy(attachments = kept), Replace(MessageView::attachments))
  dropped.forEach { graphObjectManager.delete<Attachment>(it.id) }
  ```
- **Saves have no interface.** `save`, `saveAll`, `patch`, `patchAll` and `update` are on `StatelessGraphObjectManager` itself. `GraphObjectOperations` covers loading, querying and deleting, so code that saves depends on the class.
- **The session.** There is none, so nothing to clear, and nothing that remembers what was loaded.

### What changes in your code
