title: `GraphObjectManager` (deprecated)
body:
`GraphObjectManager` (deprecated)
`GraphObjectManager` is deprecated in favour of `StatelessGraphObjectManager`. Apart from the fixes below it behaves as it
always did, and this page keeps its documentation. For why it was replaced and how to move, see
[Migrating from GraphObjectManager](15-migrating-from-graphobjectmanager.md#migrating-from-graphobjectmanager).

Loading, querying and deleting are the same on both managers and are described in the [docs](README.md). This
page covers what differs: saving, the cascade on save, and the session.

The fixes 0.1.0 made to saving apply to this manager too, and are listed under
[What changed](0.1.0-stateless-object-manager.md#what-changed). The ones that alter what a save
writes: a relationship field declared `INCOMING` is written towards the root; a `@GraphPath`,
`@Count` or `@Aggregate` field, and a list of fragments read over several hops, is never written;
an `UNDIRECTED` field does not add a relationship beside one stored towards the root.

It also stamps what it changes, without checking a stamp: see [Stamps](#stamps) below.

Its `save` and `saveAll` are written in Cypher alone. On Oracle they throw
`UnsupportedOperationException`; this manager's loads, queries and deletes work there, and saving is
`StatelessGraphObjectManager`'s.

```kotlin
@Suppress("DEPRECATION")
@Bean
fun graphObjectManager(factory: GraphObjectManagerFactory): GraphObjectManager = factory.get()
```

title: Saving
body:
Saving
### Simple Save (Dirty Tracking)

GraphObjectManager tracks loaded objects and only saves changed fields:

```kotlin
// Load an object
val person = graphObjectManager.loadOrThrow<PersonCareer>(uuid)

// Modify it
val updated = person.copy(
    person = person.person.copy(bio = "Updated bio")
)

// Save - only dirty fields are written!
graphObjectManager.save(updated)
```

### Save with Relationship Changes

```kotlin
val person = graphObjectManager.loadOrThrow<PersonCareer>(uuid)

// Remove all employment history
val updated = person.copy(employmentHistory = emptyList())

graphObjectManager.save(updated, CascadeType.NONE)
```

### Batch Save (`saveAll`)

Persist a collection in **one atomic round-trip group**, with `save`'s per-item semantics unchanged
(cascade, dirty tracking, MERGE identity). Within an ambient `@Transactional` the statements join it;
otherwise they run together in a single transaction — a failure on any item rolls the whole call back.
On FalkorDB, which has no transactions, each statement is atomic and the batch is not.

```kotlin
val saved = graphObjectManager.saveAll(views, CascadeType.DELETE_ORPHAN)
```

Homogeneous root upserts collapse into chunked `UNWIND … MERGE … SET n += row.props` statements
(sub-linear round trips); relationship/cascade statements stay per-item. Heterogeneous collections are
grouped by runtime class; the returned list preserves input order. Roots with a `@PropertyBag` fall
back to the per-item path. Null handling follows [`NullPolicy`](06-object-manager.md#null-write-policy-nullpolicy)
uniformly with `save` — `IGNORE` (default) leaves nulls, `CLEAR` clears them —
via `saveAll(objs, nullPolicy = …)`.

### Null handling

Null handling is independent of dirty tracking: the `NullPolicy` alone decides, so the result never
depends on whether the object is tracked by the session.

### Stamps

`GraphObjectManager` does not check a `@NodeStamp`, and does not hand one back. It marks what it
changes, so a `StatelessGraphObjectManager` save notices its writes:

- the data token of each node whose properties or labels it changes;
- the relationship token at both ends of each relationship it makes or removes, or whose properties
  it changes. A relationship it finds as it would write it is left unmarked, so saving a view again
  with nothing changed does not refuse another writer's `Replace`.

It does not run a statement again when the engine turns it away because another writer was changing
the same node. The engine's error reaches the caller.

### What it does not notice

It does not notice a node that anything else changed or deleted. Its snapshot is what it last saw,
not what the store holds.

title: Cascade on save
body:
Cascade on save
When saving `@GraphView` objects with modified relationships, `CascadeType` determines what happens to target nodes:

### CascadeType.NONE (Default - Safest)

Only deletes the relationship, leaves target nodes intact:

```kotlin
graphObjectManager.save(updated, CascadeType.NONE)
```

Use when: Target nodes are shared or should persist independently.

### CascadeType.DELETE_ORPHAN (Safe Deletion)

Deletes relationship and target only if no other relationships exist to the target:

```kotlin
graphObjectManager.save(updated, CascadeType.DELETE_ORPHAN)
```

The relationship list you save is authoritative: every relationship of that type to a target not in
the list is removed, whether or not the view was loaded first, and including relationships another
writer added after it was loaded.

Use when: You want to clean up orphaned nodes but preserve shared ones.

**Example:** Removing a person's employment at a solo startup deletes the startup (orphaned), but removing employment at a company with other employees keeps the company.

### CascadeType.DELETE_ALL (Destructive)

Always deletes both the relationship and target nodes:

```kotlin
graphObjectManager.save(updated, CascadeType.DELETE_ALL)
```

⚠️ **Warning:** Permanently deletes data. Use with caution.

Use when: Target nodes are exclusively owned and should be deleted with the relationship.

### CascadeType.PRESERVE

Skips removals: relationships are added and none is removed.

```kotlin
graphObjectManager.save(updated, CascadeType.PRESERVE)
```

### Engines

`DELETE_ORPHAN` is not available on Memgraph.

title: Session and dirty tracking
body:
Session and dirty tracking
`GraphObjectManager` maintains a session that tracks loaded objects:

1. **On Load**: Takes a snapshot of the object's state
2. **On Save**: Compares current state to snapshot
3. **Optimization**: Only writes changed fields (dirty checking)

This means:
- **Loaded objects**: Optimized saves (only dirty fields)
- **New objects**: Full saves (all fields written)

The session outlives transactions, so an object loaded in one request and saved in another still
writes only what changed. It is kept small and bounded:

- **Compact snapshots**: a snapshot keeps the object's shape and ids and replaces large values (long
  strings, embeddings) with a 64-bit hash, so a tracked object costs bytes per field, not a copy of
  its data.
- **Bounded**: at most `drivine.query.session-max-entries` objects (default 100,000) per
  `GraphObjectManager`; past that the least recently used is evicted. An evicted object is untracked,
  and its next save writes all fields. `DELETE_ORPHAN` and `NullPolicy.CLEAR` do not depend on
  tracking, so an evicted object saves correctly under both.
- **Thread-safe**: one manager can be shared by concurrent requests.
- **Scoping**: call `graphObjectManager.clearSession()` to end tracking for a unit of work, such as a
  request or a job.

title: next-feature
body:
next-feature
Three Drivine-relevant findings from RAG benchmarking this week

1. Vector index DDL inherits server defaults that changed under us. Neo4jSchemaGrammar's CREATE VECTOR INDEX sets only vector.dimensions and vector.similarity_function. Neo4j fills in the rest at creation time — on 2026.04 that means vector.quantization.enabled: true, hnsw.m: 16, ef_construction: 100. So the same schema declaration produces different physical indexes across Neo4j versions, silently. Suggestion: let VectorIndexSpec optionally pin quantization and HNSW parameters (and perhaps log the effective config after creation), so a declared schema is reproducible. We chased quantization as a suspect during an incident precisely because nobody had chosen it.

2. Filtered ANN reads have a sharp small-k recall failure mode worth documenting or defending against. On a ~9K-vector index (1536-dim cosine), after a bulk insert of ~2K tightly-clustered vectors, db.index.vector.queryNodes failed to return a vector we verified as true global rank 3 (by exhaustive vector.similarity.cosine) at every k ≤ 100 — while k=200 returned it at rank 3. This reproduced across two full index rebuilds, with quantization on and off, and across a database restart, so it looks like genuine HNSW navigation failure on clustered data rather than transient state. Two compounding effects hit Drivine-style filtered queries (loadNearest + where{}): the ANN read itself under-recalls at practical k, and the filter applies after the index yield, so a tenant-scoped caller can receive far fewer than k rows, all from the wrong region. Our workaround is caller-side over-fetch (fetch 200, trim to 40). If Drivine wants to own this, options are an over-fetch multiplier on filtered loadNearest, or exposing the effective-k knob so callers can reason about it.

3. Thanks for the fast turnarounds — the HAS_ELEMENT/predicateOn support in 0.0.73 fixed a class of UnsupportedOperationExceptions across our corpus suites (everything green after), and the blank-index-name fix (PR #9 + your whitespace follow-up in 0.0.78) closes a real boot failure on fresh databases.

Repro details for #2 available on request: exact queries, index configs, and the exhaustive-vs-ANN comparison script.

title: Oracle: JSON_QUERY of a string past 32 KB, over two rows, corrupts the session's memory
body:
Oracle: JSON_QUERY of a string past 32 KB, over two rows, corrupts the session's memory
A standalone repro of an Oracle server bug, in plain SQL, for an Oracle service request or a forum post. Drivine works
around it (liberation-data/drivine4j#255; see `OracleCypherCompiler.itemProperty`), and the workaround can go once a
release of Oracle no longer fails this repro.

title: Summary
body:
Summary
Selecting a string value longer than about 32 KB out of a `JSON` column with `JSON_QUERY(… RETURNING JSON)`, over two
or more rows, corrupts the server process's memory. The server process dies, during that statement or a few statements
later, and the client gets ORA-03113; where it survives the statement, the alert log already has ORA-00600 `[17114]`.
The ORA-07445 that kills it faults at an address such as `0x78787878787878`: the bytes of the string, `xxxxxxx`, read as a
pointer, so the long value has been written over the heap.

- **Seen on:** Oracle AI Database 26ai Free, Release 23.26.3.0.0 (container image `gvenzl/oracle-free:23-faststart`,
  Oracle Linux 8.10, on an aarch64 host under Docker). Not tried on other versions or platforms.
- **Needs:** a string value past 32 KB (33,000 characters fail; 30,000 don't), read from two or more rows in one
  statement. It fails returned straight to the client and fed on through a subquery, an `ORDER BY` or a `JSON_ARRAY`.
- **Doesn't fail:** the same statement over one row; a list of 60 KB, or a map holding a 40 KB string, read the same
  way; and the same value read through its text instead (see [Workaround](#workaround)).

title: Repro
Expected
body:
Expected
Each `SELECT` returns the two strings, the session stays open, and the alert log has no internal error.

title: Actual
body:
Actual
The server process dies, and the alert log has internal errors. Where it dies varies from run to run. In a fresh
container, one run of this script lost the session on the first `SELECT`:

```
Table created.
2 rows created.
Commit complete.
ERROR:
ORA-03113: end-of-file on communication channel
Process ID: 265
Session ID: 57 Serial number: 38176
```

```
ORA-07445: exception encountered: core dump [kghsrch_new()+148] [SIGSEGV] [ADDR:0x78787878787868] [PC:0xFC738C4] [Address not mapped to object] []
ORA-07445: exception encountered: core dump [kghsrch_new()+148] [SIGSEGV] [ADDR:0x78787878787868] [PC:0xFC738C4] [Address not mapped to object] []
ORA-07445: exception encountered: core dump [kghxhal()+40] [SIGSEGV] [ADDR:0x78787878787878] [PC:0xFC94D78] [Address not mapped to object] []
```

Two other runs, each in a fresh container, returned the rows of all three selects, logged ORA-00600 `[17114]` twice,
and lost the session at `EXIT`, with ORA-07445 in `kxsFreePages` at `ADDR:0x78787878787878`. Other runs, through JDBC
and in statements that feed the value on through a subquery and an `ORDER BY`, logged ORA-00600 `[kghfrh1]`, `[17147]`
or `[17182]`, and ORA-07445 in `kghalo` or `kgscFreeCachedCursor`. Each ORA-07445 faults at an address made of the
string's bytes.

With 30,000 characters in place of 40,000, or `CONNECT BY level <= 1` in place of `2`, the same script runs clean.

title: Workaround
body:
Workaround
Read the value through its text: keep only the key, serialize it to a CLOB, and read it back from that text. This runs
clean over any number of rows, and keeps the value's type, a float that is a whole number among them:

```sql
SELECT JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(JSON_TRANSFORM(props, KEEP '$.a') RETURNING CLOB EXTENDED),
                       '$.a' RETURNING CLOB) EXTENDED) AS a
FROM repro_node;
```

It costs about 2.4 to 3.8 times the plain `JSON_QUERY` on short values (100,000 rows: 493 ms against 147 ms).

title: In a PL/SQL block, from a `JSON` variable
body:
In a PL/SQL block, from a `JSON` variable
The workaround above doesn't hold where the JSON is a PL/SQL `JSON` variable that a block sets once for each row it
loops over (liberation-data/drivine4j#309). Drivine's block for `UNWIND $rows AS r MATCH (n {id: r.id}) SET n.a = r.a`
loops over the rows, sets a `JSON` variable to each, and reads `r.a` from it in a `SELECT … INTO` of its own. Over three
rows of 40,000 characters, on the image above, each of these crashed the session (ORA-03113, with ORA-00600 `[17114]`
and ORA-07445 faulting at the string's bytes in the alert log):

```sql
SELECT JSON_QUERY(JSON_QUERY(row_, '$.v1' RETURNING JSON), '$.a' RETURNING JSON) INTO value_ FROM dual;
SELECT JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(JSON_TRANSFORM(row_, KEEP '$.v1.a') RETURNING CLOB EXTENDED),
                       '$.v1.a' RETURNING CLOB) EXTENDED) INTO value_ FROM dual;
```

Serializing the whole variable, and reading the value from that text, ran clean in each of a few fresh containers:

```sql
SELECT JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(row_ RETURNING CLOB), '$.v1.a' RETURNING CLOB)) INTO value_ FROM dual;
```

So did serializing it with `EXTENDED` and reading it back as extended JSON. Drivine reads a text so, and a value of any
other type with the plain `JSON_QUERY`, which didn't crash for a list or a map that holds a long text (see
`OracleCypherCompiler.rowValue`). Unlike the repro above, these were seen only through Drivine's blocks, not in a
standalone script.

title: An item of a list, read by its place
body:
An item of a list, read by its place
The same crash comes from a text past 32 KB taken out of a list as JSON (liberation-data/drivine4j#388): an item of a
list that `split` makes, of a stored list, or of one a `WITH` passes on, read with `JSON_QUERY(list, '$[0]' RETURNING
JSON)`, over two or more rows, closed the session from the second run of the statement on. Reading it from the list's
text ran clean in fresh containers, three runs each, and so did `JSON_VALUE(list, '$[0]' RETURNING CLOB)`:

```sql
JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(list RETURNING CLOB), '$[0]' RETURNING CLOB))
```

Drivine reads an item so where it is a text, and an item of any other type with the plain `JSON_QUERY` (see
`OracleCypherCompiler.listItem`). An unwound item, which `JSON_TABLE` takes out, ran clean as it was. A list made of a
long property, `JSON_ARRAY(JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a' RETURNING JSON), 'y')`, crashes in its making, and isn't worked around.

title: Two texts, compared
body:
Two texts, compared
The same crash comes from a text past 32 KB compared as JSON (liberation-data/drivine4j#389): `<`, `>`, `<=` or `>=` of
a property read with `JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a' RETURNING JSON)`, over two or more rows, closed the session from the first
run of the statement or a later one. `=` of such JSON is refused instead (ORA-40180), and the session stays open. Read
by the property's own path, `JSON_VALUE(props, '$.a' RETURNING CLOB)`, and compared with `DBMS_LOB.COMPARE`, it ran
clean in a fresh container, three runs:

```sql
DBMS_LOB.COMPARE(JSON_VALUE(n1.props, '$.a' RETURNING CLOB), JSON_VALUE(n2.props, '$.a' RETURNING CLOB))
```

Drivine compares two texts so where either is past 4,000 bytes, and as `VARCHAR2`s where neither is (see
`OracleCypherCompiler.jsonEquals` and `OracleCypherCompiler.ordered`). A list or a map that holds a long text is still
compared as JSON, and refused. So is a text in a statement that writes, or in the step of a `reduce()`, which run as
PL/SQL: there a CLOB read from an unwound row's JSON, `UNWIND $items AS t MERGE (n {a: t.a})`, closed the session,
where the JSON is refused (ORA-40180).

The same crash came back with `n.t IN $l` where `$l` held a short item and a null (liberation-data/drivine4j#475): where no
item was equal, the property was read for the nulls it holds, written out with `JSON_SERIALIZE(JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a'
RETURNING JSON) …)`, and compared with each item again by the graph's `nulls_equal` function, so a text past 32 KB was
taken out as JSON over two rows. Items the statement writes or is given, none a list or a map, are equal to no value that holds a null,
and a comparison with one is null only where the item is null, so Drivine decides between null and false when it compiles
the statement and doesn't read the property again (see `SqlCypherCompiler.givenItemsDecided`).

title: An argument of `coalesce()`
body:
An argument of `coalesce()`
The same crash comes from a text past 32 KB that is an argument of `coalesce()` (liberation-data/drivine4j#459):
`coalesce($p.q, n.a)` took the property out as JSON, and tested it for JSON's null, with
`CASE WHEN JSON_VALUE(JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a' RETURNING JSON), '$.type()') <> 'null' THEN JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a'
RETURNING JSON) END`. Over two or more rows, it closed the session on the first run of the statement or a later one:
returned whole, passed on by a `WITH`, measured, read by `trim` or `toLower`, of a node or a relationship, beside a
variable-length walk, and in a write (there with ORA-00600 `[kghfrempty:ds]`). Read by its kind, each by the property's
own path, it ran clean in a fresh container, three runs:

```sql
CASE JSON_VALUE(props, '$.a.type()')
  WHEN 'string' THEN COALESCE(JSON_SCALAR(JSON_VALUE(props, '$.a')),
                              JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(JSON_TRANSFORM(props, KEEP '$.a') RETURNING CLOB EXTENDED),
                                              '$.a' RETURNING CLOB) EXTENDED))
  WHEN 'null' THEN NULL
  ELSE JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a' RETURNING JSON)
END
```

A text of at most 4,000 bytes is read as a `VARCHAR2`, and only a longer one (or an empty one, which a `VARCHAR2` holds
as null) through its text, which alone cost about twice the plain read on short texts. Read so, 20,000 rows of
`coalesce($p.q, n.name)` took as long as before, 72 ms. Drivine reads an argument of `coalesce()` so where it is a
property of a node or a relationship (see `OracleCypherCompiler.coalescedProperty`); one of a map is read as the next
section has it.

title: A property of a value a statement works out
body:
A property of a value a statement works out
The same crash comes from a text past 32 KB that is a property of a node or a relationship a function or an index gives,
or of a map (liberation-data/drivine4j#531): `head([n]).a`, `last(collect(n)).a`, `[r][0].a` or `properties(n).a` took
the property out of the value as JSON, `JSON_QUERY(value, '$.a' RETURNING JSON)`. Over two or more rows, it closed the
session (ORA-03113, once ORA-00600 `[17114]`) on the first run of the statement or a later one: returned, passed on,
measured, searched, compared with `<`, and in a `WHERE` and an `ORDER BY`. Read as JSON by a path whose filter leaves
out a text past 4,000 characters, and such a text through its text, it ran clean in a fresh container, three runs each;
where the value is long, Drivine binds it in a subquery and reads the property there:

```sql
COALESCE(JSON_QUERY(value, '$.a?(@.type() != "string" || @.length() <= 4000)' RETURNING JSON),
         JSON(JSON_QUERY(JSON_SERIALIZE(JSON_TRANSFORM(value, KEEP '$.a') RETURNING CLOB EXTENDED),
                         '$.a' RETURNING CLOB) EXTENDED))
```

Read by its kind instead, as an argument of `coalesce()` is above, it ran clean too, but cost about 1.5 times the
plain read where the value is a map a `WITH` passes on: the map was worked out again for each read of it. Read by the
filtered path, 20,000 rows of `WITH properties(n) AS m RETURN m.t` take as long as before. See
`OracleCypherCompiler.valueProperty`. A property of a node or a relationship a pattern binds is read as before, and so
is one of an unwound item, which `JSON_TABLE` takes out and which ran clean. Three shapes still crash and aren't worked
around: a map made of a long property and then read (`head([n {.a}]).a`, `WITH n {.a} AS m RETURN size(m.a)`); `=`
of a long property with a value that may hold a null (`head([n]).a = n.a`, `UNWIND [{a: 'x'}, {a: null}] AS r MATCH
(n) WHERE r.a = n.a`), which takes the stored property out as JSON to compare it; and a long text in a map that is
itself a property, returned as it is (`RETURN n.m.a`), which is taken out of the map as JSON. Measured, searched or
compared (`size(n.m.a)`, `n.m.a ENDS WITH 'x'`), that one is read from the map as text and runs clean.

title: A text reversed
body:
A text reversed
The same crash comes from `reverse()` of a text past 32 KB (liberation-data/drivine4j#538), in two places. A text past
4,000 bytes is reversed in pieces, put together as a JSON list of one text, and that text was taken out of the list as
JSON, `JSON_QUERY(list, '$[0]' RETURNING JSON)`, as an item of a list was above. And the kind of a property `reverse()`
is given, a text or a list, was read from the property taken out as JSON, `JSON_VALUE(JSON_QUERY(props, '$.a' RETURNING
JSON), '$.type()')`. Over two or more rows, each closed the session (ORA-03113, or ORA-00600 `[kghfrh:ds]`) on the first
run of the statement or a later one: returned, passed on, measured, searched, collected, in a `WHERE` and an `ORDER BY`,
and of a stored text, of a property of a value a function gives, of a map, of an item of a list, and of a text made
from a long one. A given text, bound once, ran clean. Taken out through its text, as an item of a list is, and with the
property's kind read by its own path, each ran clean in a fresh container, three runs:

```sql
CASE JSON_VALUE(props, '$.a.type()')
  WHEN 'string' THEN ... JSON(JSON_QUERY(list_text, '$[0]' RETURNING CLOB ASCII)) ...
  WHEN 'array' THEN ...
END
```

The list's text is written in ASCII, so a character past U+FFFF stays whole. See `OracleCypherCompiler.reversedPieces`
and `OracleCypherCompiler.reversedKind`. A text of at most 4,000 bytes is reversed as a `VARCHAR2`, as before.

title: Oracle: a join `ON TRUE` in a scalar subquery is refused, or crashes the session
body:
Oracle: a join `ON TRUE` in a scalar subquery is refused, or crashes the session
A standalone repro of an Oracle server bug, in plain SQL, for an Oracle service request or a forum post. Drivine works
around it (liberation-data/drivine4j#338; see `OracleCypherCompiler.lateral`), and the workaround can go once a release
of Oracle no longer fails this repro.

title: Summary
body:
Summary
A join whose condition is the literal `TRUE` (`LEFT JOIN … ON TRUE`, `JOIN … ON TRUE`), inside a scalar subquery, is
mis-parsed. Followed by a `WHERE` with an `AND`, the statement is refused with ORA-00907 (missing right parenthesis).
Without one, the server process dies while compiling the statement (ORA-07445 in `qcsjccqb`), and the client gets
ORA-03113.

- **Seen on:** Oracle AI Database 26ai Free, Release 23.26.3.0.0 (container image `gvenzl/oracle-free:23-faststart`, on
  an arm64 host under Docker). Not tried on other versions or platforms.
- **Needs:** the join on `TRUE` (also `ON (TRUE)`) in a scalar subquery: a subquery in the select list, as
  `SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM …) FROM dual`.
- **Doesn't fail:** the same query at the top of a statement or as an inline view; the same scalar subquery joined
  `ON 1 = 1`, or by `OUTER APPLY`; a `CROSS JOIN … WHERE TRUE`; and the join on `TRUE` in an `EXISTS (…)`.

title: Repro
body:
Repro
Run in one SQL*Plus session as any user (`sqlplus user/password@FREEPDB1 @repro.sql`). No table is needed:

```sql
SET FEEDBACK ON
-- Refused: ORA-00907 at the AND.
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dual d LEFT JOIN dual e ON TRUE WHERE 1 = 1 AND 2 = 2) AS c FROM dual;
-- Runs: 1.
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dual d LEFT JOIN dual e ON 1 = 1 WHERE 1 = 1 AND 2 = 2) AS c FROM dual;
SELECT 'session alive' AS status FROM dual;
-- Crashes the server process: ORA-03113.
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dual d LEFT JOIN dual e ON TRUE) AS c FROM dual;
SELECT 'session alive' AS status FROM dual;
EXIT
```

Then look at the alert log (on the image above, `/opt/oracle/diag/rdbms/free/FREE/trace/alert_FREE.log`):

```sh
grep -E 'ORA-00600|ORA-07445' /opt/oracle/diag/rdbms/free/FREE/trace/alert_FREE.log
```

title: Expected
body:
Expected
Each `SELECT` returns 1, the session stays open, and the alert log has no internal error.

title: Actual
body:
Actual
```
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dual d LEFT JOIN dual e ON TRUE WHERE 1 = 1 AND 2 = 2) AS c FROM dual
                                                                         *
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-00907: missing right parenthesis
```

The query joined `ON 1 = 1` returns 1. The last query loses the session:

```
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-03113: end-of-file on communication channel
```

and the alert log has:

```
ORA-07445: exception encountered: core dump [qcsjccqb()+160] [SIGSEGV] [ADDR:0x20000] [PC:0x13534640] [Address not mapped to object] []
```

title: Workaround
body:
Workaround
Join on a condition other than the literal: Drivine's Oracle compiler writes an optional lateral join (an `OPTIONAL CALL`
or an `OPTIONAL MATCH`) as `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) cN ON 1 = 1`, where the other stores write `ON TRUE`. A Cypher
`COUNT { … }` is compiled to a scalar subquery, so such a join in one met this bug, in a read and in a write alike.

title: Plan: `StatelessGraphObjectManager` on Oracle (SQL/PGQ)
body:
Plan: `StatelessGraphObjectManager` on Oracle (SQL/PGQ)
Status: **phases 1 to 7 done** on `feat/oracle-sql-pgq`; 8 and part of 9 remain. Target: Oracle Database 23ai / 26ai.
What was built, and what it showed, is under [Outcome](#outcome) at the end. How to use it is in the
docs, under [Oracle](09-supported-engines.md#oracle).

The phases below are the plan as it was written. Where a class was built under another name, or a
step turned out otherwise, the phase says so in italics.

Target API: everything on `GraphObjectOperations`, plus `save`, `saveAll`, `update` and `edges` on
`StatelessGraphObjectManager`. The deprecated `GraphObjectManager.save` (session diffing,
`CascadeType`) stays Cypher-only.

This supersedes the generation half of [postgres-sql-backend-plan.md](postgres-sql-backend-plan.md)
for Oracle. Its Phase 0 (a JDBC substrate) is Phase 1 here and is shared: `JdbcConnection` is not
Oracle-specific.

title: What was established before any of this was written
body:
What was established before any of this was written
Two spikes ran against Oracle AI Database 26ai Free (23.26.3). Both are kept as tests.

- **Writes work.** `OracleWriteSpikeTest` holds a hand-written PL/SQL save to 17 scenarios from the
  stateless save contracts: checked and unchecked saves, both stamp tokens, relationship replace,
  whole-or-nothing without a transaction, read-your-writes through `GRAPH_TABLE`, eight concurrent
  writers. Removing `FOR UPDATE` fails two of them.
- **Hydration is reused.** `OracleConnectionIntegrationTest` hydrates a real `@GraphView` from one
  JSON column through `persistenceManager.getOne(spec.transform(MemoView::class.java))`.

Facts about Oracle that shape the design, each observed and not assumed:

| Fact | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` on `GRAPH_TABLE` is refused (`ORA-40968`) | Writes are DML on the tables under the graph |
| A PL/SQL block that fails is rolled back to where it began | A save can be one statement, as it is in Cypher |
| A block hands rows back with `DBMS_SQL.RETURN_RESULT` | A save returns its `stamps` row with no out-parameter plumbing |
| A nested `GRAPH_TABLE` cannot name the outer row in its `MATCH … WHERE` (`ORA-40996`) | A nested collection exposes the root's key in `COLUMNS` and is joined outside |
| A `MATCH … WHERE` holds no subquery (`ORA-40988`) | A test against a list, and a query of another pattern, are asked of the rows a pattern gives |
| A correlated `EXISTS` over a `GRAPH_TABLE` that tests, on its rows, a property with an index for equality ends the server process (`ORA-07445` in `kkosjt`, `ORA-03113` to the client; Free 23.26). `<>`, the tests of a text, a regular expression, a list, and an `OR` of an equality with a list did not | A condition on a related node is tested in the pattern that reaches it, and one written with a subquery on the pattern's rows |
| A node joined by a foreign key, of which nothing is read but a test of a property with a range index over it, is dropped from the plan with its test (Free 23.26). The statement answers for every node, or ends the server process (`ORA-07445` in `kkocfbMarkBindFroCB` with the value bound, `kkosjt` with it written in; `ORA-03113` to the client). It was not seen with the index of a uniqueness constraint, which is over a `CASE`, with a test of the node's labels beside it, or at the far end of a correlated `EXISTS` | The node a load of related nodes starts from is found first, from the node table, and the relationship is tested against it |
| A `MERGE` may not update a column its `ON` reads (`ORA-38104`), unless an index over the expression stands in for the column | The schema marker is found by a query and matched by its id |
| Labels belong to a table, not a row; `!Label` is refused as a "complex label expression" | Labels that are data cannot be SQL/PGQ labels |
| JSON columns are graph properties, usable in `MATCH … WHERE` with `JSON_EXISTS`/`JSON_VALUE` | Labels and properties that are data can be JSON |
| A quantified path takes a predicate on its edge: `-[e IS edge WHERE e.type = 'KNOWS']->{1,2}` | Variable-length and `@GraphPath` reads map directly |
| Multivalue index on a JSON array; function-based and conditional unique indexes on JSON | `@RangeIndex` and `@Unique` have an implementation |
| A property graph can be defined over views, and a property can be an expression | Typed labels can be layered over generic storage later |

title: Decision 1: how a graph is stored
body:
Decision 1: how a graph is stored
**Chosen: one node table and one edge table per graph, with labels and properties as JSON.**

```sql
CREATE TABLE <graph>_node (
    nid    NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    labels JSON NOT NULL,          -- ["Person", "Musician"]
    props  JSON NOT NULL,          -- {"id": "ada", "name": "Ada", "metadata.source": "x"}
    stamp  VARCHAR2(33)
);
CREATE TABLE <graph>_edge (
    eid   NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    src   NUMBER NOT NULL REFERENCES <graph>_node (nid),
    dst   NUMBER NOT NULL REFERENCES <graph>_node (nid),
    type  VARCHAR2(128) NOT NULL,
    props JSON
);
CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH <graph>
    VERTEX TABLES (<graph>_node KEY (nid) LABEL node PROPERTIES (nid, labels, props, stamp))
    EDGE TABLES (<graph>_edge KEY (eid)
        SOURCE KEY (src) REFERENCES <graph>_node (nid)
        DESTINATION KEY (dst) REFERENCES <graph>_node (nid)
        LABEL edge PROPERTIES (eid, type, props));
```

Reads are SQL/PGQ over that graph. A Cypher label becomes a predicate on `labels`, a relationship
type a predicate on `type`.

*As built (`OracleGraph`): the edge table's `src` and `dst` cascade on delete, so a node's
relationships go with its row, and its `props` is never null; `src` and `dst` are properties of the
edge label too; the vertex label has one more property, `doc`, the node as the map a load returns; and
a third table, `<graph>_schema`, records the indexes and constraints Drivine made.*

Why this and not a table per fragment class:

- It is the only layout that carries the whole model. `@NodeLabels`, an open `@PropertyBag`,
  `edges.relate` with a type known at run time, a node read as two classes with overlapping labels,
  and several relationships of one type between two nodes all need labels, keys and types to be
  data. `EntityNode` in `embabel-agent-rag-graph` uses three of those.
- Polymorphism is unchanged: hydration picks the concrete class from the `labels` list of each node
  map, exactly as it does today.
- A save is data, not generated code. With two tables, one fixed PL/SQL block can interpret a save
  described as JSON, where typed tables would need a block generated per model.
- The existing cross-engine contracts can be held against it without carving out exceptions.

What it costs:

- An outside reader of the graph sees one label, `node`, and filters on JSON. Phase 8 adds typed
  labels as generated views, which the probe showed Oracle accepts as vertex tables.
- Every lookup is a JSON predicate, so it is only fast with the indexes of Phase 6. Phase 9 measures.
- An embedding cannot be indexed inside JSON; Phase 7 gives each vector index a side table.

This is the decision to revisit first if the direction is wrong. Phases 1 and 2 do not depend on it.

title: Decision 2: where the second backend plugs in
body:
Decision 2: where the second backend plugs in
`CypherGrammar` abstracts differences within Cypher and is not the seam. The managers pass Cypher
text between layers (`WHERE` fragments, prologs, bridge variables), so replacing the builders alone
does not work. The cut is one level up: what `GraphObjectManager` and `StatelessGraphObjectManager`
ask of a store, expressed as operations that return a ready `QuerySpecification`.

```
GraphObjectManager / StatelessGraphObjectManager      model, hydration, stamps handed back, retries
        │
   GraphBackend                                        load, count, delete, search, save, edges, bookkeeping
    ├── CypherBackend   the present builders, moved behind the interface, behaviour unchanged
    └── OracleBackend   SQL/PGQ reads, PL/SQL writes
```

The condition AST (`WhereCondition`, `OrderSpec`) is already nearly free of Cypher and is what the
managers hand to the backend. The raw `whereClause: String` overloads stay, and mean "a predicate in
the store's own language".

title: Phases
body:
Phases
Each phase ends green on the existing suites, and on Oracle with `ORACLE_TESTS=true`.

### Phase 1 — SQL through `PersistenceManager` ✅

- `JdbcConnection`, `JdbcConnectionProvider` (application `DataSource` or its own pool),
  `JdbcResultMapper`, `DatabaseType.ORACLE`, `ConnectionProviderBuilder` wiring.
- `$name` parameters translated to positional markers; `skip`/`limit` as `OFFSET … FETCH`.
- Collections bound as JSON; a JSON column read as a document; `VECTOR` read as a list.
- Transactions, batches, and a block that returns rows.

*As built: the translation is `SqlParameters`, and what is bound is reshaped by
`JdbcParameterCoercer`. A string whose bytes run past 32,767 is bound as a `CLOB`. A pool Drivine
makes is HikariCP, with the driver's statement cache on.*

### Phase 2 — The backend seam (no behaviour change) ✅

- `GraphBackend` and `CypherBackend`; both managers, `EdgeOperations`, `BatchSaveOperations` and the
  scored-search planners go through it.
- Retry is asked of the backend ("was this turned away by another writer?"), not of
  `org.neo4j.driver.exceptions.TransientException`.
- The inline Cypher of `SaveExecutor.staleObject`, `storedKeys`, `StoreIdentityResolver` and

- `PersistenceManager` and `ConnectionProvider` expose the backend; `grammar` remains for Cypher.
- Proof: the full existing suite, unchanged, on Neo4j, FalkorDB and Memgraph.

### Phase 3 — Storage and reads ✅

- `OracleGraphStore`: creates the two tables, their base indexes and the property graph when absent.
  *Built as `OracleGraph`.*
- Load of a fragment and of a view: root, to-one and to-many relationships, nested views,
  `@RelationshipFragment`, `@Count`/`@Aggregate`, `@GraphPath`, recursive and variable-length
  fields, `depth()` overrides. One JSON document per root.
- `SqlConditionGenerator` over the condition AST: property, relationship (`any`/`none`), label,
  list membership, ignore-case, bag keys; ordering, collection sorts, keyset paging, `count`.
  *Built as `OraclePredicates`, with the statement itself written by `OracleSelect` and a raw
  `whereClause` read by `CypherShorthand`.*
- Proof: the read-side cross-engine contracts, their seed data supplied per engine.

### Phase 4 — Writes ✅

- The save block: root (checked or unchecked), dropped relationships, related nodes and their
  relationships, nested views, relationship properties, `NullPolicy`, `only`/`except`, `update`

- `saveAll`, `edges.relate`/`unrelate`/`unrelateAll`/`loadRelated`, `delete` and cascade delete.
- Deadlocks: nodes are locked in a fixed order; `ORA-00060` and `ORA-08177` are reported as
  contention and retried.
- Proof: `StatelessSaveContract`, `StatelessSaveSoundnessContract`,

### Phase 5 — Bookkeeping ✅

- Store identity, schema version store, `TestCleanup`, and the migration tools that apply.

- `OracleSchemaGrammar`: `@RangeIndex` as a function-based index, `@Unique` as a conditional unique

title: Known limits, by design
body:
Known limits, by design
- A statement written by hand in Cypher does not run on Oracle. The 14 `.cypher` files and
  `CypherFilterConverter` in `embabel-agent-rag-graph` need SQL counterparts or a move to the DSL.
- Temporals are stored in JSON as ISO-8601 text, as on FalkorDB.
- The deprecated manager's own `save` is not ported.
- Oracle stores an empty string as null.

title: Risks
body:
Risks
1. **Read performance on JSON predicates.** Mitigated by Phase 6, measured in Phase 9. If it is not
   good enough, hot properties can be promoted to virtual columns without changing the layout.
2. **The save block is the largest single piece.** Its contract is already written down as four
   cross-engine suites, and the spike covers its core.
3. **Size limits.** A save's description and a node's properties must be bound as `CLOB` past 32K.
4. **Full-text scoring.** Oracle Text scores are not BM25; normalising them to the existing
   threshold semantics needs its own check.

title: Outcome
body:
Outcome
Every stateless contract that has engine subclasses has an Oracle one: the four save contracts, and
the read, search, label, bag, null-policy, relate, temporal, property-name and store-identity suites.
That includes the contract the review of the stateless manager added, and its read-path tests.
With `ORACLE_TESTS=true`: 563 tests in 57 classes, none failing. The nine skipped are the deprecated
manager's own save, one Memgraph-only case and the benchmark.

What differed from the plan:

- **A save is a plan, not generated code.** One PL/SQL block interprets a JSON array of steps. Its
  text depends only on the kinds of node a save names, so it is compiled once for a view class.
- **Fixtures.** The contracts seed and read back in Cypher. A small interpreter (`MiniCypher`)
  works such a statement out over the graph, so the contracts run unchanged. It ships with the test
  support, in `org.drivine.test`, and is reached through `OracleCypherFixtures`. It reads a statement
  once, into a tree, and refuses what it does not know before it reads the graph.
- **A read is written to be read beside its Cypher.** A row is called what the model calls it, the
  node of a `MATCH` has its row's name, `COLUMNS` names only what the statement reads, and every query
  in a statement is laid out the same way (`Query`, `GraphTable`). The README shows one.
- **An index is a table beside the nodes.** Oracle indexes a `VECTOR` column, not a list inside JSON,
  so a vector index is a table of embeddings that a trigger keeps in step, with the index (neighbour
  partitions) over it. A full-text index is the same with an Oracle Text index. Without an index, or
  without Oracle Text (the slim image), a search reads every node of the label.

What the work found that the plan did not foresee:

- **A lock taken through a function-based index can hang.** `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` through the index
  over a node's id waited for a row lock while holding a page of that index; the lock's holder, whose
  update keeps the index, waited for the page. Oracle reports no deadlock. A node is now found without
  a lock and locked by its key.
- **The multivalue index over labels is chosen too eagerly.** With a label and an id in one
  predicate, Oracle read every node of the label. Labels are tested in a form that index cannot
  answer wherever a node is found another way.
- **An Oracle Text index must not be on the node table.** It holds what has been committed, and once
  it is there Oracle answers ordinary tests of a JSON property from it. A save could not find a node it
  had made a moment before in the same statement, and made it again.
- **A bound JSON array named twice in one statement gave wrong counts** from `JSON_TABLE` on 23.26.
  Full-text terms are bound one by one.
- **A node reached through a relationship fragment was loaded without its stamp.** Oracle returns a
  node as it is stored, and the stored names were mapped back to field names for every shape but that
  one. The contracts did not assert the loaded stamp there; one does now.

What holds on Oracle and not on the graph engines:

- **An empty string is null.** A stamp stored as `''` is no stamp. A property saved as `""` is kept
  in the node's JSON, and `JSON_VALUE` reads it as null: the query DSL writes a comparison with `""`
  as a JSON path test, so that it still finds one.
- **A load reads the node as stored**, so a view can be filtered and ordered by a property no field
  declares, where a graph engine

title: Plan: the object manager on plain Postgres
body:
Plan: the object manager on plain Postgres
Status: **done** in drivine4j; Drivine (TypeScript) and drivine-python to follow · Replaces the July proposal (a table per label, join tables, one label per
node), which was written before the Oracle backend and its layout existed.

title: Goal
body:
Goal
`GraphObjectManager` and the stateless manager work on plain Postgres, with pgvector for vector
search, as they work on Oracle: the same annotations, the same query DSL, the same results. No
Apache AGE, no extension beyond pgvector, and nothing new for a caller to declare.

title: The layout: Oracle's, so a store is one store
body:
The layout: Oracle's, so a store is one store
A graph is kept as Oracle keeps it (`OracleGraph`):

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `<graph>_node` | `nid` identity key, `labels` (array), `props` (JSON object keyed by stored name), `stamp` |
| `<graph>_edge` | `eid` identity key, `src` and `dst` (cascading to the nodes), `type`, `props` |
| `<graph>_schema` | what Drivine made of indexes and constraints |

On Postgres, `labels` and `props` are `jsonb`, the labels a JSON array under a GIN index, as they are
JSON on Oracle: a list is bound as JSON, and a node's map is made of the two with no conversion. So:

- **A node has as many labels as it likes**, and a label is found through the index
  (`labels @> '["Person"]'`). This is the mistake of AGE, a label being a table, not made again.
- **Nothing new to declare.** No table, column or join annotations: a fragment is a set of labels,
  as everywhere else.
- **One store format across Oracle and Postgres, and across drivine4j, Drivine and drivine-python**,
  as Oracle already is. A store written from the JVM reads the same from Node or Python.
- **Indexes are partial**, which suits the layout better than Oracle's `CASE` expressions: a range
  index on `Person.email` is `CREATE INDEX … ((props->>'email')) WHERE labels @> '["Person"]'`, a
  uniqueness constraint the same index made `UNIQUE`.

Mapping onto hand-made relational tables is a different feature, a mode of its own if it is ever
wanted, and out of scope here.

title: Shape of the work: two SQL backends, one family
body:
Shape of the work: two SQL backends, one family
Oracle's backend is about 4,000 lines in `backend/oracle`. Much of it is not about Oracle: the
model walk that turns a view into nested JSON, the predicates of the query DSL, the plan a save is
written as, the scope of a statement's names and parameters, the catalog of what was made. What is
Oracle's own is the dialect: `GRAPH_TABLE`, `JSON_VALUE`, `JSON_OBJECT`, PL/SQL.

The work pulls the shared part into `backend/sql`, behind seams, with Oracle and Postgres each
implementing them:

| Seam | Shared (in `backend/sql`) | Oracle | Postgres |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SqlDialect` (from `OracleSql`) | the vocabulary: property, label test, JSON object/array, literal, page | `JSON_VALUE`, `JSON_EXISTS`, `JSON_OBJECT`, `JSON_ARRAYAGG` | `->>`, `?`, `@>`, `jsonb_build_object`, `jsonb_agg` |
| `SqlGraph` (from `OracleGraph`) | table names, `objectName`, the catalog, `ensure` | 128-character names, PL/SQL ensuring block, property graph | 63-character names, `CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS` |
| `RowSources` (from `OracleRowSources`) | `Step`, `Query`, `RowSource`, `StatementScope` | `GRAPH_TABLE` patterns | joins over the edge table; recursive CTEs for depth |
| `SqlSelect`, `SqlPredicates` (from `OracleSelect`, `OraclePredicates`) | the whole model walk, written against the dialect and row sources | | |
| `WriteBlock` (from `OracleWriteBlock`) | `WritePlan`, `NodeShape`, `SqlSavePlan`: a save as a JSON plan of steps | the PL/SQL block | a PL/pgSQL function the store is given (see below) |
| `SqlSchemaGrammar` (from `OracleSchemaGrammar`) | the catalog, `recorded`/`forgotten`, listing and parsing | JSON expression indexes, Oracle Text, vector side tables | partial btree indexes, `tsvector` GIN indexes, pgvector HNSW |
| `SqlBackend` (from `OracleBackend`) | almost all of `GraphBackend` | contention codes, cascading delete in PL/SQL | contention codes (`40001`, `40P01`), cascading delete in a CTE |

As built, fewer seams were drawn than this table plans: there is no `SqlDialect`, `SqlSelect`,
`SqlPredicates`, `SqlSchemaGrammar` or `SqlBackend`, and each backend keeps its own select,
predicates, grammar and backend over what `backend/sql` shares (see "More shared code" below).

**Each seam is pulled out when Postgres first needs it, not ahead of it.** A step is a refactor
commit, which leaves Oracle's behaviour and statements as they were (its tests are the proof), then
a commit that adds the Postgres side. A seam drawn with both sides in view is a better seam than
one guessed at with only Oracle's.

### Writes on Postgres

A save on Oracle is a plan, a JSON array of steps (`node`, `ref`, `link`, `unlink`, `cut`, `patch`),
carried out by one PL/SQL block whose text depends only on the node shapes it names. The plan is not
Oracle's and is kept (`WritePlan`, `SqlSavePlan`, with their tests). On Postgres the interpreter
is a PL/pgSQL function, `<graph>_write(plan jsonb, shapes jsonb, mark text, returns text, patched_if text)`
returning the rows a block returns, installed by `ensure` beside the tables; the node shapes the plan
names are data beside it, so the function's text is the same for every plan. A `DO` block cannot
return rows, so a function it is. The `patch` step's predicate, which is SQL and cannot be data, is
passed as text the function runs with `EXECUTE … USING` the node it found, with its values written into
it as literals. Drivine writes that text itself, from the query DSL, so no caller's text reaches

title: Steps
body:
Steps
Each step is a commit or two on `postgres-backend`, with the gate green:
`./gradlew :test` and `ORACLE_TESTS=true ./gradlew :test --tests '*Oracle*'`, plus
`POSTGRES_TESTS=true ./gradlew :test --tests '*Postgres*'` once there are Postgres tests.

1. **Substrate.** `DatabaseType.POSTGRES` through `JdbcConnectionProvider`: URL, pool, the driver
   as an optional dependency (as `ojdbc11` is), `$name` parameters bound positionally, `jsonb` and
   `text[]` values bound and read. `PostgresTestContainer` (`pgvector/pgvector`), `PostgresTestDatabase`,
   `@PostgresTests`. A connection test: queries, parameters, transactions commit and roll back.
2. **The graph.** Pull out `SqlDialect` and `SqlGraph`, move the dialect-free pieces (`Query`,
   `RowSource`, `StatementScope`, `Step`, `CypherShorthand`, `TextQuery`) to `backend/sql`.
   `PostgresGraph` and `PostgresDialect`; `ensure` makes the tables. `OracleCypherFixtures` becomes
   `SqlCypherFixtures`, so the cross-engine contracts seed Postgres as they seed Oracle.
3. **Reads.** Pull out `RowSources`, then `SqlSelect` and `SqlPredicates`. `PostgresRowSources`.
   `PostgresBackend`, reading only: `load`, `loadAll` (raw `where` and the DSL, orders, pages, keyset
   seeks), `count`, `related`, views with nested views, paths, depths and recursion, collection sorts.
   The read contracts gain a Postgres subclass each.
4. **Writes.** Pull out `WriteBlock`, `SqlSavePlan`. The PL/pgSQL write function. `save`,
   `saveTogether`, `patch`, `patchAll`, `relate`, `unrelate`, `unrelateAll`, `foundStamp`, stamps and
   stale checks, `contended`. The save, patch, null-policy, property-bag and edge contracts.
5. **Deletes.** `delete`, `deleteAll`, cascades (`DELETE_ALL`, `DELETE_ORPHAN`) and the depth checks,
   as one statement of CTEs. Pull out `SqlBackend` here, when both backends are whole.
6. **Groups.** `groups`, against the groups contract.
7. **Schema.** `SqlSchemaGrammar`; `PostgresSchemaGrammar` for range indexes and uniqueness
   constraints (partial indexes), the labelled-index catalog that filters are read through, the
   version marker and store stamp. The schema-management contract.
8. **Search.** Vector search through pgvector (an HNSW index over a partial expression, or a side
   table as on Oracle, whichever the planner serves; `searchK` as `hnsw.ef_search`), full-text search
   through `tsvector` and `ts_rank_cd`, read with `TextQuery`. The search contracts.
9. **Finish.** README (a Postgres section beside Oracle's, the engine table), `TEST_CONTAINERS.md`,
   Spring Boot starter properties, the benchmark run against Postgres.

Then the same for Drivine (TypeScript) and drivine-python, guided by statements that match.

title: Open questions
body:
Open questions
- **Postgres tests by default, or behind `POSTGRES_TESTS=true`?** The image is small and starts in
  seconds, unlike Oracle's, so they could run in the default suite. Gated for now, with a CI job of
  their own, as Oracle's are.
- **Lowest Postgres version.** 14: nothing used is newer (`jsonb`, GIN, partial indexes, identity
  columns, `ON CONFLICT`, `starts_with`, `regexp_matches`; no `MERGE`, `any_value` or `regexp_count`).
  Tests run on 17 only.
- **Comparisons across types.** Postgres compares a number only with a number stored as one, as the
  graph engines do: `'7'` is not `7`. Oracle, through `JSON_VALUE … RETURNING NUMBER`, reads the text
  `'7'` as 7. Whether Oracle should change to match is a question for Oracle's backend.
- **More shared code.** What the two SQL backends share is in `backend/sql`: the tables and names
  (`SqlGraph`), a statement's parts (`Query`, `RowSource`, `Step`, `StatementScope`, `SqlKind`), the
  plan a save is written as (`WritePlan`, `SqlSavePlan`, `WriteBlocks`), what a cascade follows
  (`Cascade`), how conditions and sorts are read against a view (`RelationshipConditions`), the keyset
  predicate (`KeysetPredicate`), `TextQuery` and `CypherShorthand`. What is left in each backend is
  the SQL it writes: Oracle's `GRAPH_TABLE` patterns, PL/SQL and workarounds, Postgres's joins,
  recursive queries and PL/pgSQL. A base select over a dialect of expressions is the next step if a
  third SQL store comes.

title: Handoff: corpus partitioning for filtered vector search (embabel-agent-rag-graph)
body:
Handoff: corpus partitioning for filtered vector search (embabel-agent-rag-graph)
Status: design agreed, not started. Drivine4j side tracked separately — see "What Drivine must supply" below.

title: Why this exists
body:
Why this exists
A filtered ANN read (`loadNearest` + `where {}`) has two compounding failure modes, observed live on a
~9K-vector index (1536-dim, cosine) after bulk-ingesting ~2K tightly-clustered vectors:

1. **Under-recall at practical k.** A vector verified as true global rank 3 (by exhaustive
   `vector.similarity.cosine`) was not returned at any k ≤ 100. At k = 200 it came back at rank 3.
   Reproduced across two full index rebuilds, with quantization on and off, and across a database
   restart.
2. **Post-filter dilution.** Drivine emits `CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes(name, $k, $vec)` and applies
   the `where {}` predicates *after* the index yields. A corpus-scoped caller therefore receives roughly
   `k × selectivity` rows, and those survivors are the intersection of "globally nearest" with "in my
   corpus" — which is not "my corpus's nearest".

### The mechanism (established, not hypothesised)

The rank-3 result proves `k` is the **search beam width**, not merely a row count. If `k` only limited
rows, a vector at true rank 3 would appear at k = 100 — it is comfortably inside 100. The only way k =
200 finds it and k = 100 does not is if k drives the candidate queue. That is Lucene-backed HNSW:
`ef_search == k`, and Neo4j exposes no separate knob.

Two consequences:

- "Over-fetch multiplier" and "expose the effective-k knob" are the same lever. The existing workaround
  (fetch 200, trim to 40) *is* running the search at ef = 200, and is correct rather than a hack.
- Under-recall is a tunable tradeoff, not a defect. Dense clusters saturate every neighbour list: with
  `M = 16`, near-duplicate vectors consume all 16 links with intra-cluster neighbours, pruning the
  long-range links greedy descent needs to enter or leave the cluster. Low ef then cannot recover.

**Run this experiment before building anything.** As of drivine4j 0.0.78+, `M` and `ef_construction` are
pinnable:

```kotlin
VectorIndexSpec("Proposition", "embedding", 1536, hnswM = 64, hnswEfConstruction = 400)
```

Rebuild and retest recall at k = 40. If recall returns, the original symptom has an index-level fix and
the cost/benefit of everything below changes materially.

title: The design
body:
The design
Separate **logical** from **physical** partitions.

- **Logical partition = corpus.** Domain meaning, set by the application, unbounded. Not reorganisable
  for index-efficiency reasons — merging two corpora changes what a query means.
- **Physical partition = the Neo4j label carrying the vector index.** Bounded, chosen for layout.

The mapping between them is the tunable part:

| Corpus size | Physical layout | Read strategy |
|---|---|---|
| below exact-scan threshold | shared bucket label | exhaustive `vector.similarity.cosine`, exact |
| medium | shared bucket label | ANN on bucket index, post-filter by `corpusId` (dilution bounded by bucket size) |
| large | dedicated label | ANN on the corpus's own index — pre-filtered by construction, `k` recovers its intuitive meaning |

This gives a bounded number of HNSW graphs with an unbounded number of corpora, which is what breaks
under naive one-label-per-corpus-forever.

Nodes take multiple labels, so overlapping membership is free: a proposition in two corpora carries both
labels. Stored once, indexed twice.

### Why label-per-partition and not property-per-partition

Only a **label** makes the routing decision free. `MATCH (n:Corpus_abc) RETURN count(n)` is count-store
metadata, O(1). The same check against a property — `MATCH (n:Proposition {corpusId: $c})` — is an index
scan, proportional to the partition. Labels also give per-partition vector indexes, which is what
converts post-filtering into pre-filtering. Both benefits come from the same change.

### Why ingest time is the right moment

A new physical partition means a new label and a new vector index — a schema operation, and Neo4j
rejects schema DDL inside an open data transaction (Drivine already routes schema ops through the
auto-commit path). Per-request partition creation would make that fatal. Corpus ingestion already does
chunking, embedding and bulk insert, so adding an index creation there is a rounding error and a natural
place for a schema event.

Note the symmetry: bulk-ingesting one semantically coherent corpus is exactly what *creates* the dense
cluster that breaks navigation, and is also the natural partition boundary that dissolves it.

title: Work items (this repo)
body:
Work items (this repo)
1. **Corpus → physical label mapping.** Bucketing policy: which corpora share a label, which get their
   own. Persist the mapping; it must survive restarts and be authoritative for both read and write paths.
2. **Ingest-time index creation.** Call `persistenceManager.indexes.ensure(VectorIndexSpec(label, ...))`
   when a physical partition first appears. No new Drivine feature needed — the imperative API already
   accepts an arbitrary label at runtime.
3. **Read routing.** Count the partition (count-store, O(1)) → below threshold, exhaustive scan; above,
   ANN against that partition's index.
4. **Promotion.** Moving a corpus out of a shared bucket into its own label: add label, create index,
   backfill, drop from bucket. Physical migration only — query semantics must not change.
5. **Recall harness.** Given an index and a sample of query vectors: exhaustive ground truth via
   `vector.similarity.cosine`, ANN at a range of k, report recall@k. Optionally sweep `M` /
   `ef_construction` across rebuilds. This is what turns tuning into measurement, and it is what would
   have answered "is quantization the suspect?" in minutes rather than two rebuilds.

title: What Drivine must supply
body:
What Drivine must supply
- **Runtime label targeting for vector reads.** Today `VectorIndexResolver.kt:63` derives the label from
  `FragmentModel.labelsFor(fragmentClass)`, and codegen emits `loadNearest(vector, topK, threshold, spec)`
  keyed on the view type — the index is a compile-time function of the fragment. Per-partition indexes
  need it to be a runtime function of the query. This cannot be worked around from here; it is below the
  API surface. Design in progress.
- **Yield observability** — requested `k`, index yield, post-filter count, so dilution stops being silent.
- **Documentation** that `k` is the beam width.
- Index creation — already available, no work.

title: Deliberately not in Drivine
body:
Deliberately not in Drivine
Every policy decision stays here: bucket sizes, the exact-scan threshold, when to promote a corpus.
Drivine emits faithfully what it is told and does not invent strategies from selectivity estimates it
does not have — the same rule that stopped it substituting its own HNSW defaults.

title: Open questions
body:
Open questions
- **Corpus cardinality per deployment**, and whether it is bounded. Dozens to low hundreds makes
  dedicated indexes attractive; thousands and growing makes bucketing mandatory.
- **The exact-scan crossover**, which must be measured rather than assumed. Expect it lower than a
  raw-FLOPS estimate suggests: `vector.similarity.cosine` reads a 1536-float property off each node, so
  the scan pays property-store access per vector rather than walking a packed array.
- **Cross-partition queries.** Searching several corpora at once needs one ANN call per index, merged and
  re-ranked. Affects the Drivine API signature — see the design note.

title: Vector search on `@GraphView` items (`loadNearest`)
body:
Vector search on `@GraphView` items (`loadNearest`)
Maintainer handoff for the vector-search feature of the object managers.

The methods are declared on `GraphObjectOperations`, which `StatelessGraphObjectManager` and the
deprecated `GraphObjectManager` both implement. This page was written when `GraphObjectManager` was
the only one, and names it throughout; what it says of it holds for both.

title: What it does
body:
What it does
Brings vector (approximate nearest-neighbour) search to `GraphObjectManager`, returning the same
typed objects `loadAll` does — paired with a normalized similarity score. Like the rest of the
manager, it works on both a `@GraphView` (searches the root fragment's embedding, returns the
projected view) and a plain `@NodeFragment` (searches and returns the bare nodes).

```kotlin
// infers the @VectorIndex on the view's root fragment — no magic string
val hits = graphObjectManager.loadNearest(PropositionView::class.java, queryEmbedding, topK = 20)
hits.forEach { println("${it.score} → ${it.value.proposition.text} (${it.value.mentions.size} mentions)") }

// disambiguate when a node has several embeddings; floor by similarity
graphObjectManager.loadNearest(PropositionView::class.java, "titleEmbedding", vec, topK = 20, threshold = 0.8)
```

Returns `List<Scored<T>>`, most similar first.

title: Design decisions (and why)
body:
Design decisions (and why)
- **`topK` is the ANN index's `k`, not a guaranteed result count.** It's a real, knowable number
  (the value passed to the index), matching every vector API people know. A "give me exactly K
  survivors" knob can't be honoured under selective filters anyway, so we don't pretend to.
- **Post-filter, documented.** The view's required-relationship `EXISTS` checks (and the optional
  `threshold`) prune the K candidates *after* the search — so **the result may contain fewer than
  `topK` rows**. Callers who need a fuller set raise `topK`. This keeps the vector path's `WHERE`
  byte-identical to the normal load path.
- **Score normalized to similarity, higher = better, on every engine** — so ordering and `threshold`
  mean the same thing regardless of backend: `(1 + cos) / 2` for cosine and `1 / (1 + d²)` for
  Euclidean, each in `[0, 1]`, as Neo4j gives them. The normalization lives in each grammar, and
  `VectorScoreCrossEngineTest` pins the score of a known pair on every store.
- **The property is inferred from `@VectorIndex`.** The embedding property is already annotated for
  the schema feature, so the common single-embedding case needs no property argument; a name is only
  passed to disambiguate multiple embeddings on one node. No `@Embedding` / auto-embed — Drivine
  stays out of embedding generation; the query vector is computed caller-side.

title: Backend support
body:
Backend support
All three native-vector engines are verified end-to-end against testcontainers (ranking, scoring,
post-filter, threshold) — see `VectorSearchNeo4jTest` and `VectorSearchCrossEngineTest`.

| Engine   | Vector head | Status |
|----------|-------------|--------|
| Neo4j 5  | `CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes(name, k, vec) YIELD node, score` — score is already normalized similarity | ✅ verified |
| FalkorDB | `CALL db.idx.vector.queryNodes(label, prop, k, vecf32(vec)) YIELD node, score` — the score is a distance, `1 - cos` or `d`, rescaled to `1 - score / 2` and `1 / (1 + score²)` | ✅ verified |
| Memgraph | `CALL vector_search.search(name, k, vec) YIELD node, distance` — the distance, `1 - cos` or `d²`, rescaled to `1 - distance / 2` and `1 / (1 + distance)` (not `similarity`, which is `\|1 - distance\|`) | ✅ verified |
| Neptune  | **throws** `UnsupportedOperationException` — no native vector index (inherits the grammar default) | ✅ throws |

### FalkorDB quirk: required relationships are filtered *after* projection

FalkorDB cannot evaluate an inline relationship pattern predicate in a `WHERE` over a node sourced
from a vector-index `CALL` — `WHERE (doc)-[:WRITTEN_BY]->(:Author)` fails with `Type mismatch:
expected Null but was Pointer`, because the node still carries its `vecf32` property and the
pattern-predicate evaluator trips on the Pointer. (The relationship *projection* comprehension
`[(doc)-[:WRITTEN_BY]->(a)|…]` is fine; only the bare predicate fails.)

So the vector path does **not** reuse the load path's pre-projection `EXISTS` checks. Instead it
projects every relationship and then filters the *projected* value of each required (non-null,
non-collection) relationship for `IS NOT NULL` **after** the projection `WITH` — equivalent for
required single relationships, and portable across all engines. See
`GraphViewProjectionAssembler.requiredRelationshipAliases` and `GraphViewVectorSearchBuilder`.

title: Code map
body:
Code map
- `manager/Scored.kt` — `Scored<T>(value, score)`; score lives here, not on the domain object.
- `query/grammar/VectorQuerySpec.kt` — resolved index + bound param names handed to a grammar.
- `query/grammar/CypherGrammar.kt` — `vectorSearchHead(...)` + `supportsVectorSearch` (default
  throws / false); implemented in `Neo4j5Grammar` and `FalkorDbCypherGrammar`.
- `query/grammar/MemgraphGrammar.kt` — Memgraph head.
- `query/VectorIndexResolver.kt` — resolves label/property/indexName/similarity from `@VectorIndex`
  on the root fragment (infer / disambiguate by name / error). Mirrors `VectorIndexSpec` naming.
- `query/GraphViewProjectionAssembler.kt` — shared projection core (root + relationships +
  aggregates + required-rel `EXISTS` + `WHERE` + `BuildContext` prolog plumbing).
- `query/GraphViewLoadBuilder.kt` — normal load (`MATCH` head) over the assembler.
- `query/GraphViewVectorSearchBuilder.kt` — view vector search (`CALL` head + scored RETURN +
  `ORDER BY score DESC`) over the assembler.
- `query/FragmentVectorSearchBuilder.kt` — fragment vector search (`CALL` head + fragment field
  projection + scored RETURN); no relationships, so threshold is the only filter.
- `query/GraphViewQueryBuilder.kt` — facade; `buildVectorQuery(...)` delegates to the vector builder.
- `manager/GraphObjectManager.kt` — `loadNearest(...)` overloads; branches view vs. fragment, reuses
  `TransformPostProcessor` on the inner `value` map, and snapshots for dirty tracking.

title: Generated Cypher (Neo4j, the `DocView` test fixture)
body:
Generated Cypher (Neo4j, the `DocView` test fixture)
```cypher
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('Doc_embedding_vector', $_vectorTopK, $_vectorQuery)
YIELD node, score
WITH node AS doc, score AS _score
WITH
    doc { id: doc.id, title: doc.title, embedding: doc.embedding, labels: labels(doc) } AS doc,
    [(doc)-[:WRITTEN_BY]->(author:Author) | author { ... }][0] AS author,
    _score
WHERE author IS NOT NULL          -- required relationship, filtered on the projected value
RETURN { value: { doc: doc, author: author }, score: _score } AS row
ORDER BY _score DESC
```

The required-relationship filter is a post-projection `IS NOT NULL` on the projected value (not a
pre-projection `EXISTS`) — see the FalkorDB quirk above. A `threshold`, when given, is `AND`-ed into
the same `WHERE` as `_score >= $_vectorThreshold`.

The row is wrapped as a single map column so the result mapper collapses it to one value; the
manager unpacks `value` + `score` into `Scored<T>`.

title: Tests
body:
Tests
- `query/grammar/VectorSearchGrammarTest` — each backend's head; Neptune + base openCypher throw.
- `query/VectorSearchBuilderTest` — index inference, disambiguation, error paths, Cypher shape.
- `manager/VectorSearchNeo4jTest` (testcontainer) — ranking, hydrated `Scored` views, the `<topK`
  post-filter proof (the nearest Doc, lacking an author, is correctly absent), and threshold.
- `manager/VectorSearchCrossEngineTest` (testcontainers) — the same ranking/prune/threshold
  assertions run against **FalkorDB and Memgraph**, verifying each engine's procedure, `vecf32`
  wrapping, and distance→similarity normalization actually execute and rank correctly.

title: Recall tuning (0.0.79)
body:
Recall tuning (0.0.79)
**`searchK`** — what the *index* is asked for, i.e. the HNSW beam width. `topK` becomes a post-filter
`LIMIT`, applied after the `WHERE` so over-fetching recovers rows the filter would otherwise thin away.

`k` is not just a row count: on a 9K-vector index a vector at true global rank 3 was missed at every
`k ≤ 100` and returned at rank 3 at `k = 200`. In Lucene-backed HNSW the result queue is the candidate
queue, so `ef_search == k`. Omitting `searchK` leaves the emitted query byte-identical.

On Neo4j, over-fetching also **re-ranks the beam by exact similarity** rather than by the index's
yielded score, because that score is computed against quantized vectors and does not order identically
to exact similarity — measurably so even on a 4-dim vector. Without the re-rank, over-fetching buys row
count on the filtered path but not row correctness. FalkorDB and Memgraph over-fetch without re-ranking.

Full rationale: [0.0.79-vector-search-k.md](0.0.79-vector-search-k.md).

**`partitionLabel`** — targets a per-partition index at runtime, so the search runs *inside* the
partition rather than being post-filtered. The label is bound, not interpolated (one query plan for all
partitions); the index name re-derives as `${label}_${property}_vector`, matching the create side.
Targeting is not identity — the projection is unchanged, and a node the partition's index yields
comes back only when it has every one of the fragment's labels.
Full rationale: [0.0.79-vector-partitioning.md](0.0.79-vector-partitioning.md).

**Short-yield reporting** — a vector search returning fewer rows than requested logs the numbers at
DEBUG on `org.drivine.manager.GraphObjectManager`, so post-filter dilution stops being silent.

title: Open follow-ups
body:
Open follow-ups
1. **Cross-partition search.** `partitionLabel` targets one partition; searching several needs one call
   per index, merged and re-ranked, which changes what `k` means. Deliberately deferred.
2. **Phase 2 — `nearest{}` DSL sugar.** `loadNearest` is the primitive; a `nearest{}` block
   composable with `where{}` (returning plain `List<T>`, dropping the score by design) is deferred.
3. **Search anchored on a non-root node.** A view always searches its *root* fragment's embedding; a
   `@VectorIndex` on a relationship target is not reachable (you'd search the target and traverse
   back). Not currently supported.
